Protect Against Spirits

  • Goddesses: Bastet, Hekate, Kupala

One of the most fundamental and frequently practiced intentions in all of magick. Protection encompasses any working designed to shield, guard, or defend a person, place, object, or situation from harm, whether physical, emotional, psychic, or spiritual.

The Nature of Protective Magick

Protective workings operate on the principle that energy can be directed to form barriers, deflect negativity, and create zones of safety. Unlike banishing, which removes something already present, protection is primarily preventative. It establishes defenses before threats arrive.

There are several distinct approaches to protective magick, each suited to different situations:

  • Shielding creates an energetic barrier around the target, like an invisible wall that deflects unwanted energy
  • Warding anchors protective energy to a specific place such as a home, a room, or a doorway, creating a standing guard
  • Binding restricts a known source of harm from causing further damage
  • Deflection redirects negative energy back to its source or safely into the ground
  • Concealment hides the target from hostile attention entirely

When to Work with Protection

Protection is often the first type of magick a new practitioner learns, and for good reason. Before opening yourself to new energies through spellwork, divination, or spirit contact, establishing strong protections is essential. Think of it as locking the doors before you settle in for the night.

Common situations that call for protective workings include:

  • Beginning a new spiritual practice or opening psychic channels
  • Entering environments with heavy or chaotic energy
  • Dealing with difficult people or toxic situations
  • Protecting a home, vehicle, or personal belongings
  • Shielding during vulnerable times such as illness, grief, or major life transitions
  • Before and after ritual work, especially when working with unfamiliar forces

Building a Protective Working

As the Correspondence Guide describes, start with your intention and follow the links. Protection connects to a wide web of allies across every grimoire, from minerals like Black Tourmaline and Obsidian, to plants like Rosemary and Basil, to entities like Archangel Michael and Hekate, to timing like Saturday and the influence of Mars.

You do not need every linked element. One protective plant combined with one protective stone and the right timing is more than sufficient. Choose the materials you have access to and that resonate with your practice.

Layering Protections

Experienced practitioners often layer multiple forms of protection rather than relying on a single working. A protected home might include a warded threshold, a protective sachet by the door, a charged crystal on the windowsill, and a spoken charm renewed regularly. Each layer reinforces the others, creating a stronger whole.

Maintaining Protective Workings

Protection is not a one and done act. Wards fade, shields thin, and charged objects gradually lose their potency. Regular renewal, whether through recharging, recasting, or simply refreshing your intention, keeps your protections effective. Many practitioners tie their protective maintenance to lunar cycles, renewing wards during the waning moon when banishing energy is strongest.

In Counter Magick and Protection

Magickal attack works by binding the victim's soul and deep mind, creating an unconscious blind spot that the attacker then exploits. This renders the victim accident-prone and unable to perceive or resist the influence directed against them.

A key distinction in protective workings is that between amulets and talismans. Amulets are charged with the intention of inducing harmony, generosity, expansiveness, security, and optimism in the deep minds of those nearby. Talismans are charged for a specific, defined purpose. Earth power and earth-based amulets operate through direct contact with the earth itself, drawing on both mineral and vegetable forces.

Holystones

A holystone must be naturally formed by the erosion of wind and water. It cannot be purchased; it must be found. When discovered, it is picked up in Hertha's name and hung near the hearth or in the most-used room of the home. No purification is needed. The holystone is used au naturel, exactly as found.

Witch Balls

Witch balls take two traditional forms. The first is a hollow silvered glass globe, hung from the ceiling or placed in the front hall. The second is the traditional fisherman's glass net-float of green bottle-glass, hung in Hertha's name. Both serve as protective presences within the home.

Portable Amulets

When carrying protective amulets, restrict to one at a time, excluding the witch jewel. As one's powers develop, the aim is to rely less on these portable batteries and more on one's own cultivated inner strength.

Cross-Stone (Staurolite)

The cross-stone, also called staurotides, is a crystal of ferrous aluminium silicate (staurolite) that occurs naturally in orthorhombic form, with three planes set at right angles to each other, forming the shape of a three-dimensional Greek cross or solid cross of nature. Symbolically, this shape encodes the seven mystical dimensions of space: north, south, east, west, the abyss above, the abyss below, and the holy centre, laying the groundwork for the complex Cabalistic Ararita formula. As a protective amulet, the cross-stone is suspended in a red cloth bag tied with red thread from the neck of the bearer, placing them under the protection of Hertha.

Sign of the Fig

An image of the hand making the phallic sign of the fig (fist clenched, thumb thrust between first and second fingers) carved in nephrite (jade), amber, coral, jet, carnelian, or any other fascination gem, suspended in red from the bearer's neck in Hertha's name, is considered a potent earthly amulet. An old iron key serves the same protective purpose, sharing similar sexual implications.

Elf-Shot

Ancient flint or stone arrowheads of pre-Celtic Pictish origin, always considered highly potent by witches in matters of protection. Employed in the same manner as the preceding amulets.

Siderite (Lodestone) Amulet Consecration

The siderite, a stone of magnetic iron oxide (lodestone or magnetite), is among the most prized protective amulets in witchcraft. By the light of the full moon, with the window open if working indoors, place the lodestone on a piece of talisman paper laid over the workbook. Consecrate it with as many drops of Sabbat oil as there are years in the bearer's life, plus one extra drop for the present year, chanting with each touch: May Hertha bless thee [N] with all her might and main. Visualize the drops of oil glowing as they touch the stone, infusing it with witch power. Tie the stone loosely in a red flannel or chamois leather bag bound with red ribbon. Seal with So mote it be.

Every full moon, remove the siderite, dip it in a glass of water, dry it, and sprinkle on a small pinch of iron pyrites dust or iron filings in Hertha's name. This is called feeding the stone. The siderite must be worn around the neck or carried in the pocket. Male practitioners have traditionally carried it near the genital organs to increase sexual vigour and potency; in this case, the Horned One is invoked alongside Hertha in the initial consecration.

Magickal Defence

Signs that a definite occult attack may be in operation include recurrent nightmares, sustained runs of unbelievably bad luck, psychosomatic disturbances and allergies, poltergeist manifestations, and in extreme cases, acute mental disturbance. All of these symptoms except poltergeist activity can have non-occult causes, and it is always best to consult a doctor or psychiatrist before assuming magickal origin. However, if a practitioner has been directly informed that they are being targeted, the pattern becomes harder to ignore.

Nightmares are generally not the attack itself, but the deep mind's cry for help to the conscious self. They will often recur with a specific repeated motif and, if magickally induced, will tend to correspond to lunar phases, reaching their peak at the new moon rather than the full. As an attack worsens, the deep mind's pleas may escalate to waking hallucinations: visual, aural, or olfactory sensory disturbances including disembodied voices, music, a high-pitched tone (historically called the astral belt by occultists), or imaginary odours, usually fetid in the case of attack.

Runs of misfortune are often taken as signs of a lodged curse but are more frequently self-inflicted by the victim's own deep mind. Skilled attackers diagnose the victim's psychological weak spots in advance, then aim the attack precisely at those built-in deep-mind blind spots. The most deadly attack is the least suspected.

The chief danger to avoid is surrendering judgment to fear. Paranoia is a known pitfall for otherwise competent practitioners. When attack is suspected, a trusted fellow practitioner should handle the divination, exercising scepticism. The pendulum, Vassago, and rune sticks are the most reliable methods. Tarot and the I Ching may also be used. The aim of divination is to establish the nature and, where possible, the source of the hostility. Motivations are generally either lust or hate.

The Fetch (Projected Attack)

A skilled magickal antagonist may project witch power into a definite shape and transfer consciousness into it, sending it forth to accomplish the witch's will. This projected shape or fetch is often animal in form, corresponding either to the ensouling emotion of the projector or to the coven totem. This process is identical to modern astral or etheric projection. The fetch may be perceived by the victim through inner vision or, very rarely, with physical sight if either party possesses materializing medium abilities.

The legends of the werewolf and the vampire both derive from this practice. The werewolf represents materialized witch power ensouled by destructive rage; the vampire, incubus, and succubus by lust. The artificially produced fetch differs from the magistellus or Watcher in that the witch transfers her own consciousness to the fetch and not to the magistellus, and that the fetch relies solely on witch power and deep mind, while the magistellus involves some exterior demonic or elemental agency.

Tradition holds that when a habitual fetch-sender dies, the vampire or werewolf personality can persist as a self-perpetuating psychic fragment, feeding on the magnetism of the sleeping living. This practice gave rise to the lore of lycanthropy, including its traditional methods of dispatching such entities. Should a projected fetch achieve any degree of materialization, wounds inflicted upon it may be transferred back to the projector's sleeping body through the process of repercussion.

Passive Defence

Passive defence is the most effective form of retaliation in occult warfare. When a magical attack misfires or meets adequate protection, the curse returns to its sender. As the craft saying goes: An the witch bide the issue! Skilled practitioners avoid this recoil by delegating the actual cursing to less advanced associates; regardless of who ultimately bears the consequence, the defended practitioner should proceed with all defensive preparations as surely as one would board up a house before a hurricane.

Attacks generally begin after sundown; consult an ephemeris or almanac for the exact sunset time. Primary defences are the grand magickal circle and the pentacle of protection, supplemented by the magickal power of iron and protective herbs, plus all active amulets and magistelli.

Herb Planting by Moon Phase

For herbs whose end product is the root, plant during the dark of the moon (waning). For herbs to be used for their leaves or flowers, plant during the waxing moon. When harvesting, pick in the lunar quarter corresponding to the type of magick intended: the bright quarter for constructive workings, the dark quarter for baneful or destructive ones.

Trituration (Sachet and Incense Preparation)

Sachet powders have two components: agents (flower essences, perfumes, gum resins) and a base (orris root, patchouli, rose petals, sandalwood, agarwood, cedarwood shavings, or similar). Method:

  1. Assemble all ingredients.
  2. Grind the base herbs well in a pestle and mortar.
  3. Grind the flower essences or perfumes into a portion of the herb base.
  4. Add any gum resins (frankincense, myrrh, benzoin) to the remaining herb base and powder as finely as possible.
  5. Combine the two powdered portions.
  6. Add oils or liquids last (honey, wine, blood). If the oil quantity is very small, dissolve it first in a small amount of pure alcohol, then blend in for greater mixing power.
  7. Allow to steep at least overnight. Add extra base if the result remains too liquid.
  8. Store in well-stoppered nonporous bottles, labelled, protected from bright light at a moderate temperature.

Protective Herbs

The following herbs are traditionally potent against sorcery, individually or in combination:

  • Holda (elderberry), berries or flowers, gathered at midsummer
  • Madwort (alyssum)
  • Marjoram
  • Dragon herb (tarragon)
  • Angelica
  • Fennel
  • Bay laurel
  • Asafetida grass
  • Holy thistle, replace after seven days
  • Bishop's-wort (betony)
  • Garlic flowers
  • All-heal (mistletoe), may be carved into a ring or bracelet
  • Dog roses
  • Arum lilies
  • Benet, holy herb, or avens (Geum urbanum)
  • Lucky-hands (unexpanded fronds of male fern, Dryopteris filix-mas) — dry over a Sabbat fire

The four most powerful of all protective herbs, held potent against all varieties of sorcery from time immemorial:

Trefoil, vervain, St. John's wort, dill, hinder witches of their will!

(Trefoil is any three-leafed plant such as clover.)

Protective Potion

To calm those who suspect bewitchment, steep powdered angelica, marjoram, bay, and fennel seed in hot wine. Chant a few words of benediction and reassurance and charge strongly with witch power.

Iron in Occult Defence

Iron has a definite jamming or scrambling effect on any magickal signal when used with intention. For this reason, iron and all metals are rigorously excluded from the dress of a candidate in magickal initiation rituals where a definite transmission of power is required.

Origins and Evolution

Hekate's origins trace to pre-Greek Anatolia and Thrace, where she appears as a great goddess figure before her integration into Greek mythology. She may have evolved from Bendidia, also known as Bendis, the primordial Thracian lunar goddess. As Dark Moon Goddess, Queen of the Night, and Ruler of Heaven, Earth, and the Underworld, Hekate holds the title Queen of Witches. Her name likely derives from a feminine form of Hekatos, an obscure Apollo epithet meaning "far-shooter" or "far-darter."

Literary Appearances

Hesiod's Theogony (circa 700 BCE): Presents Hekate as cosmically powerful, retaining privileges across sky, earth, and sea. Zeus honors her above all others, granting her power to give or withhold anything from mortals. She aids warriors in battle, athletes in competition, fishermen at sea, and shepherds with their flocks. She receives special honor as kourotrophos (child-nurse), blessing young people who seek her favor.

Homeric Hymn to Demeter: Depicts Hekate as witness to Persephone's abduction, emerging from her cave when she hears Persephone's cry. She approaches Demeter with torches to report what she heard (though not what she saw). After Persephone's return, Hekate becomes her permanent attendant and companion in the underworld.

Evolution Through Greek Culture

5th Century BCE - Chthonic Phase: Hekate becomes increasingly associated with necromancy, ghosts, and underworld sorcery. She appears at crossroads and haunts tombs with her pack of spectral hounds. This is when she becomes firmly established as Queen of Witches and mistress of harmful magick.

Hellenistic Period - Expansion: Syncretism spreads her worship throughout Mediterranean. She becomes identified with other goddesses in different regions while maintaining distinct identity as mistress of magick.

2nd Century CE - Chaldean Oracles: Hekate undergoes radical transformation into World Soul and cosmic principle. The Oracles present her as transcendent force governing universe itself, far beyond earlier chthonic associations. She becomes philosophical concept as much as goddess.

The Crone Misconception

Important clarification: Hekate is never portrayed as a crone in ancient sources. This modern association comes from confusion with other triple goddess frameworks and Wiccan wheel-of-the-year mythology.

Ancient depictions: Hekate appears consistently as young woman, often in triplicate form (three bodies or three heads) but always youthful. Her "triple" nature refers to her power over three realms (sky, earth, underworld) and her presence at three-way crossroads, not to maiden-mother-crone lifecycle.

The triple goddess error: The maiden-mother-crone framework widely popularized in modern Wicca does not reflect ancient practice. Ancient Greeks did not worship a universal triple goddess following this pattern. Hekate's ancient worship centered on her liminal power and command over boundaries, not on feminine life stages.

Cultural Context

Anatolian: Original cultural context before Greek adoption

Greek: Primary cultural development through classical and Hellenistic periods

Roman: Continued worship as Trivia at crossroads (the name Trivia literally means "three roads," from which the English word "trivial" derives, reflecting her dominion over three-way crossroads)

Chaldean: Mystical and philosophical transformation in late antiquity

Associated Symbols

Hekataion: Protective amulet depicting Hekate's triple form, placed at doorways and crossroads to ward off evil. These apotropaic images served as guardians of thresholds and boundaries.

Torches: Her most consistent attribute across all periods, representing her role as guide through darkness and illuminator of hidden knowledge.

Keys: Symbol of her role as keyholder and guardian of thresholds between worlds.

Titanic Nature

Titans are primordial forces that preceded the Greek gods, embodying the fundamental, ineradicable workings of Nature and Time. Hekate is counted as a fourth-generation titan, setting her apart from the Olympian gods as an older and more elemental power. Unlike the original twelve titans, she was never bound to the authority of the gods, moving instead freely between worlds, realms, aeons, and dimensions. She is sometimes called the Liminal One: neither any single thing nor its opposite, but the path by which opposing forces are reconciled. In this role she acts as a connector and mediator, opening the channels between this world and the ones sought beyond it, and carrying across them information, wisdom, will, and the very stuff of life.

Snakes: Associated with her chthonic power and wisdom, often depicted in her hair or wrapped around her body.

Dogs: Her sacred animals, whose howling announces her presence. Black dogs especially connected to her nocturnal processions.

Colors

Hekate's colors include black, gray, silver, and deep midnight navy blue.

Signs of Her Presence

Those who work with Hekate learn to recognize the signs of her nearness. Frequent encounters with the number three, the unexpected appearance of a stray dog that lingers in your space, or a prophetic dream may all indicate she has heard your requests. Being followed by dogs, particularly black dogs, signals that Hekate is reaching out.

Hekate's Procession

On nights sacred to her, Hekate roams the Earth accompanied by her pack of hounds and Wolves and a host of ghosts, blessing those who have left offerings for her. The howling of the wind and the barking of dogs announce her passage through the darkness.

Hekate at the Boundaries of the Oikos

Within Hellenic household worship, Hekate is one of three Gods who guard the Oikos from outside threats, working alongside Hermes and Apollo Agyieus. Her station is at the threshold of the home and just outside its perimeter fence, taking the same office She holds along the roads, sovereign and keeper of the place where ways meet. The doorway itself opens onto such a meeting, since several paths lead away from any entrance.

Where space allows, the household sets a niche beside the doorway for Her image together with the smaller working tools of the rite, the incense burner and the offering bowl among them. In a modern apartment, a shelf or ledge takes the place of the fence niche. Devotional images here should be three-dimensional, statues or carvings rather than flat pictures, which are reserved for ordinary household decoration.

Daily practice is uncomplicated. Outside of specific sacred days it consists of a simple offering and the burning of incense whenever the practitioner enters or leaves the home.

The Sow Thistle

The sow thistle (Sonchus oleraceus) is counted as one of Hekate's gifts to the world. Where the plant is spotted, the words "Open sow-thistle" spoken in the manner of "Open sesame" will reveal any concealed or hidden treasures in the immediate vicinity.

Role in Hellenic Household Worship

Within the household, offerings to Hekate include saffron, rosemary, garlic, red mullet, amphiphon (a sweet), styrax incense, and dry laurel leaves. Her emblems are the yellow veil, the torch, the double-edged knife, the key, a candle made of three combined colours, serpents, the scourge, and bronze. The colour linked to Her is saffron. Her sacred animals are the ferret, the dog, the bull, and the lioness. The oak is the plant and fruit sacred to Her.

Sacred Midwife Role

For millennia the office of midwife was held by consecrated priestesses of spirits with dominion over birth, among them Hathor, Hekate, Kybele, Tanit, and Tlazolteotl. These birth spirits were themselves understood as divine sacred midwives, with their priestess-midwives serving as their earthly representatives. The connection endured long after the rise of Christianity, when midwives came to be identified with witches, and the classic witch's broomstick is said to have been, in an earlier age, the professional emblem carried by Hekate's own priestess-midwives. Through this lineage, midwives preserved magickal and shamanic traditions for centuries. Sacred midwives such as Hekate remain eternally powerful, and may still be appealed to for protection, good fortune, and an easy, brief, and safe labor.

What is Magick?

Ancestral Magick

Magick may feel exciting to some and controversial to others. Those new to the subject may find it strange or even a bit disorienting at first. Most religious institutions frame it as supernatural and dangerous; secular culture frames it as irrational and naive. And yet, magick has a timeless appeal, and records of its practice stretch back as far as records exist.

As Gordon White explains in Star.Ships, the first structures humans built as a species were not houses. They were temples, where hunter-gatherer ancestors very likely went to commune with spirits and engage in magickal practice. Whatever the living may have told you about magick, your ancestors practiced it, and they will help you practice it too.

Defining Magick

Magick is the pitter-patter in your heart when seeing someone that catches your fancy, or the butterflies in your stomach that give you a thrill when your loved ones are near. Magick is the hair standing on end, warning you that something is about to happen. These things can be explained away with biological reasoning, but that makes them no less magickal.

Fantasy author Arthur C. Clarke's Third Law states: "Any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magick." Magick is simply the name for things science does not understand yet. That does not make them any less real. Whether journeying within oneself to follow the link between self and environment, or altering consciousness to reach other planes, the only difference is the destination. They both deal with the realm of the possible.

Place your hand on your heart. That pulse you feel under your hand? The lub-dub of the heart's chambers working in concert is one of the hallmarks of life. Life implies biological processes, and in humans, they start with electrical impulses. As much as science understands those biological processes and the human body, even surgeons admit they do not comprehend what makes the heart beat, or what causes this complex machine to stop working. Witches do. It is magick, plain and simple, while also being terrifyingly complex.

Art and Science

When asking a witch what magick is, one is likely to get several mixed answers. The most common is Aleister Crowley's definition: "Magick is the art and science of creating change in accordance with will."

The breadth of the definition is part of its appeal. There are as many ways to do magick as there are people practicing it. Some require deep study or training with an adept; others are entirely self-directed. Some rely primarily on visualization; others leverage physical materials. And the mundane actions that support a desired outcome are their own form of magick.

Magick can also be understood as prayer in 3D. Where ordinary prayer says "please make my life better," magick involves choosing a specific outcome and reinforcing it through corresponding actions. In the example of landing a dream job, the mundane work includes updating a résumé, activating a network connection, researching the company, and preparing for the interview. Magickal work identifies which additional actions and correspondences align with the desired outcome and layers them in.

Crowley did not put "art and science" in there by mistake. The art of magick is entirely separate from the science of magick. The art of magick is the difference between a painting by one of the masters and a paint-by-numbers copy. Creating magick has art involved, in the same way painting does. Anyone can paint and have fun with it, just as anyone can recite a rhyming couplet. What makes the difference between a rhyming couplet and magick is the spirit of the person reciting them.

Are the spells cast in popular witchcraft media real? Not yet, no. But they could be. Magick requires thought and intention, among other things. Saying the words is not enough. Thought and intent must be put into them.

Egregors and Thoughtforms

There is a concept known in magickal circles as an egregor (pronounced E-gr-g-Or). An egregor is a thoughtform that has been thought of by so many people, for so many years, in such a varied population, that it becomes its own autonomous entity. The idea is that figures like Santa Claus have been thought of for long enough that they became true spirits. They may not occupy a physical place on this plane, but they exist in spirit.

Magickal spells that exist in popular culture could be used in spells by witches, but just because something was on television does not make it real. The only thing real in pop culture magick is usually the dry ice.

The Role of Feeling

Magick should make you feel something. You should feel something before you start the spell, while creating it, and after you have finished the spell. If there is no feeling attached, there can be no magick.

This does not mean you have to experience extreme passion to work practical magick, but there needs to be some feeling to tap into. If you do not care enough about the issue, it is like a chocolate bunny in the spring: it looks good, but it is hollow. One can be passionate about a subject without being hysterical.

Making Magick

There is a disconnect between the brain and the heart when it comes to making magick happen. It comes from watching magick on TV and reading about it in books. New witches see fictional characters reciting "magick words" and something amazing results with sparkly special effects. In real life, there are no light cues or faint chimes to signal that a spell was effective.

What televised magick leaves out is the hair-raising knowing that comes with real magick. The tingle in your palms that says the energy was raised. You can have all of the aesthetics right and still not raise any energy. Ritual theater (the costumes, masks, robes, and the like) will only get you so far. The magick comes from you.

Psi-Magick

Psi-magick is magick worked solely with the mind, no candles, crystals, tools, or anything else. Many practitioners consider it the most advanced form of magick because it requires complete mastery of focus, visualization, and energy manipulation without physical aids. The practitioner becomes both the tool and the source.

What is a Magick Spell?

At its simplest, a spell is a deliberate, structured act of directing magickal force (heka) toward a specific outcome. The ingredient that elevates a sequence of actions from mere routine into genuine spellwork is the practitioner: your focused intention, your clearly defined goal, and the depth of feeling behind it. Precision matters. A sharply defined objective, a vivid mental picture of the result, and real emotional investment all increase the likelihood that the working will succeed.

You Are the Irreplaceable Component

Spells exist in an almost limitless variety. Some are elaborate and theatrical, some are startling, and some look so ordinary you would never guess magick was involved. Countless styles exist, each with its own preferred ingredients and methods, and if one approach does not resonate, another will. Uncomfortable with open flame? Build your spell around an enchanted bath. No bathtub? Brew a potion or work with knotted cord. If a particular ingredient is impossible to source, alternatives almost always exist. Many of the most potent magickal materials hide in plain sight among everyday kitchen staples.

Magickal energy is persistent and pervasive, and spells are the structured channels through which it is aimed. Yet out of every element in any spell you will ever cast, exactly one is truly irreplaceable: you. Your personal energy is the binding force, the animating spark that turns a collection of actions, words, and materials into a living magickal working.

Naturally Charged Objects

Certain substances found in nature arrive already saturated with magickal power. Iron, menstrual blood, salt, and specific botanicals all radiate their own energetic charge without any preparation or consecration. At the other end of the spectrum, some magickal tools, a wand, a ritual blade, a consecrated mirror, require painstaking spellwork over an extended period before they reach the level of power needed for serious use. The most heavily charged objects shoulder a significant portion of the work in a given spell, though no working is ever entirely effortless.

The Morality of Magick

Even practitioners who work with magick regularly sometimes hold limiting beliefs about how it operates. One common belief is that magick cannot be performed for personal gain, an idea likely popularized by the television show Charmed and not rooted in any serious magickal tradition. Another is the principle that magick must "harm none."

Harming none sounds straightforward but is nearly impossible in practice. Doing magick to obtain a job is simultaneously doing magick to prevent someone else from getting it. Other candidates may want or need it more. Whether intended or not, some degree of harm is always a possibility. And yet the world does not collapse from this. The person who does not get that particular job continues applying and may ultimately find something better suited to them.

The belief that magick must "harm none" is not rooted in rigorous moral philosophy. It tends to arise from a deeper wound: the belief that one cannot have what one wants because one does not deserve it. This wound has many sources, including organized religion, family dynamics, and cultural messaging. You can have what you want. You can have good things, you can be loved, and when that truth is genuinely internalized, the obsessive pull of desire begins to loosen.

For those still concerned about the ethics of working magick for personal gain, ancestral magick offers a natural moral framework. When petitioning the ancestors, one stands before the eldest elders and states desires aloud. This requires clarity and conviction. Whatever is being asked for must feel genuinely warranted. The ancestors' attention is not to be wasted on requests made in bad faith, repeated for problems of one's own making, or directed against others without real justification. The relationship itself cultivates discernment.

The Witchcraft Method

Some feel that science and magick are antithetical, but scientists make great witches. In a way, both witches and scientists use the Scientific Method. The Witchcraft Method mirrors this approach.

Step 1: State the Need

This could be a spell, or a small part in a more extensive ritual incorporating many elements including candles, quarter calls, and the like. "Money" is acceptable, but better results come from more specific intention: "I need money for a new car."

Whenever possible, state the need in the positive rather than negative. "I don't have money for a new car" is not as magickally effective as "I need money for a new car." The theory is that the mind does not grasp negative words when doing magick, which can impact the working.

The best wording, however, is "I have money for a new car." You are acting as though the goal has already been attained. This leaves room in the universe to provide what you need, or something better.

Step 2: Conduct Research

You will need correspondences for the stated need: plants associated with prosperity, stones for money, and the like. Write them all out first, then narrow the focus from there.

This method serves two purposes: it makes it easier to see patterns, and it has been proven that more information is retained when handwritten rather than typed. Use blue ink for a memory boost, as it differs from black typeface and stands out in the mind for easier recall.

Step 3: Write the Spell or Ritual

First, decide how complicated the working should be. Is this a simple issue with a simple solution, like a candle spell? Or is this a complicated matter that requires an in-depth ritual to build the power needed?

Step 4: Do the Thing

The minute you decide a spell needs to happen in Step 1, the clock starts ticking. Every moment you spend researching materials, choosing the working, and shopping for materials required is energy that goes toward the intended outcome. The more power, the more likely the intended result.

Step 5: Make Observations

The data you collect during and after the spell gets recorded in your Book of Shadows, just like a scientist would record findings. "A week later, I won the office birthday pool" or "thirteen days later, still no results."

Even if the spell does not work, it can be illuminating to look at the potential reasons why. Perhaps you look at the time the working started and find out the moon was void of course, or between signs. That can muddy the magickal waters, so try not to do workings when the moon is between signs. Your magickal calendar or ephemeris might have it marked as "Moon v/c 6:04 p.m."

Step 6: Form Your Conclusion

If your intention came to pass the way it was designed, excellent. If it did not, many factors could have contributed to the failure of the ritual.

Before you declare it null, wait for at least a full lunar cycle (twenty-eight days) for the intention to come to pass. You do not want to decide a working failed before it has a chance to work.

Step 7: Communicate and Replicate

The Witches' Pyramid says: "To Know, To Will, To Dare, To Keep Silent."

Exclaiming to your circle of friends that you have completed the "coolest spell ever" is not the best idea. It can introduce doubt into the spell from outsiders, from yourself if they are not 100 percent supportive, or from magickal practitioner friends who do not see the outcome the same way you do. Wait before declaring success.

When communicating the results of a spell, await the full results or 28 days before declaring it a failure. Spell work takes time.

Unintended complications from magick can happen. For example, you needed cash, but after the money came in, an unexpected bill came up. Perhaps in addition to keeping magickal records, you want to start an online journal, a blog, or even a channel to speak to other witches about your experiences. Being a magickal practitioner can feel lonely if you do not know anyone. If you feel that way, there are thousands of others like you who feel isolated and could benefit from your experiences.

Anatomy of a Basic Spell

This guide walks through a fundamental candle spell to demonstrate how the core elements of magick work together. Once you understand this structure, you can adapt it for any intention.

The Initial Requirement

Before any spell is cast, you need a personal goal. What do you want to achieve? What do you wish to prevent? What are your secret desires, your deepest fears? Magick spells are always cast for a purpose, even if it is a generic one like "personal happiness," "peace on Earth," or obtaining vague "good fortune." The more specific your desire, the more clearly articulated your vision, and the deeper your passion, the more likely it is that your spell will work.

Many Forms, One Purpose

Spells come in an extraordinary range of shapes. They draw on diverse powers and make use of all manner of elements, tools, and materials. Some of these are found raw in nature; others are crafted by human hands. Certain spells revolve around physical objects, while others rely entirely on spoken or written words. Some call for long lists of rare plants and minerals; others, often considered the most demanding because the practitioner must generate every bit of the energy transformation alone, need nothing beyond the force of personal will.

No single style of spell is inherently superior to any other. What exists is a spectrum of approaches, and certain styles simply click better for certain people. Discovering which methods resonate most strongly with you is one of the great pleasures and ongoing challenges of building a practice.

Where Magick Meets Other Arts

Some workings occupy a blurry boundary between magick and religion, or between magick and traditional healing. This overlap partly reflects magick's habit of absorbing any object, system, or technique that shows promise as a source of power. It also reflects the fact that the lines between different disciplines were not always drawn as sharply as they are in the modern world. The recognition of magickal force and the impulse to harness it for personal benefit may be the oldest human art and science. Religion, traditional medicine, astrology, alchemy, the aromatic arts, perfumery, music, dance, visual art, and more all trace their roots back to magick and shamanism.

Before You Begin

If you are working on behalf of another person, obtain their explicit permission first. Consent matters in magickal practice.

Gather your materials: an incense aligned with your goal, a corresponding oil, and a candle in an appropriate color. For healing work, purple or blue serves well. Bring everything to your altar or working space.

The Working

Settle your mind. The room should be quiet, your thoughts calm and focused. Light a charcoal disk in your censer and sprinkle incense over it. As fragrant smoke rises, direct your attention entirely toward your goal.

Visualization is essential. Picture the desired outcome clearly. If working for healing, see yourself or the other person in perfect health. Do not dwell on illness or problems. If negative images arise, dismiss them immediately. They work against your intention.

Open your oil. Dip two fingers of your dominant hand into it. Hold the candle in your other hand. Apply the oil from the wick end down to the middle, then from the base up to the middle, until the entire candle has a thin, shiny coating.

As you dress the candle, you are charging it. Your personal energy flows through your hands. The oil carries its own power. Both merge with the candle, fusing together through your focused will. Feel this happening.

Hold the dressed candle and speak to whatever powers or deities resonate with you. Ask for their aid. Then place the candle firmly in its holder. Add more incense to the censer. Light the candle.

Watch the flame for a few moments while holding your visualization. Then step away. As you leave, release all thoughts of the working from your mind. Let it go.

After the Working

Allow the candle to burn as long as practical. If you must leave, extinguish it with your fingers or a snuffer rather than blowing it out. Blowing is traditionally seen as disrespectful to Fire. Relight the candle when you return.

This working can be performed once or repeated over several days. Experience will teach you how many repetitions your goals require.

Expanding the Framework

The basic structure above can be elaborated in countless ways:

  • Timing: Perform the spell on a day ruled by a planet aligned with your goal. Sunday supports healing work.
  • Stones: Wear or place a crystal with appropriate properties nearby. Amber has long been associated with healing.
  • Ritual bathing: Precede the working with a bath steeped with herbs matching your intention.
  • Spoken words: Add invocations, prayers, chants, or words of power to direct your energy.
  • Clothing: Wear colors that correspond to your goal.
  • Music or movement: Some practitioners incorporate sound or dance to raise energy.

The possibilities are limitless. Start simple and add complexity as your practice develops.

How It Works

From the moment you select your materials, you set forces in motion. Concentration is power. Every second you hold your goal in mind, you send energy toward it.

When you anoint the candle, you transfer energy from the oil and from yourself. The incense creates an atmosphere charged with vibrations aligned to your purpose. These energies saturate the candle alongside your focused intention.

Spoken invocations add another layer, aligning your working with higher forces and contributing additional power.

As the candle burns, flame transforms solid wax into liquid, then gas. This physical transformation releases the energy you poured into the candle, sending it outward toward your goal.

Adapting for Different Goals

This same framework serves any intention. Change the candle color, oil, and incense to match your need:

  • Financial concerns: Green candle, prosperity oil and incense. Visualize bills marked paid, money flowing in, stability achieved.
  • Love: Pink or red candle, love-drawing oil and incense. See yourself with an ideal partner. Never target a specific person.
  • Protection: Black candle, protection oil and incense. Visualize yourself surrounded by impenetrable light.

Natural Materials for Spellwork

Things of nature that may be incorporated into spellwork include herbs, feathers, rocks, shells, crystals, minerals, spring water (for purity), rain water (for energy), storm water (for power), sea water (for cleansing), animal hair, fur, whiskers, and claw sheaths (naturally shed, used in association with characteristics of the animal). Soil may be used for seed and growth-related spells.

The Circle

A circle may be cast or not depending on the circumstances and the spell. Follow your intuition.

Ritual Complexity

Ritual may be as simple or as complex as desired. Rituals are a means of focus for the Practitioner, not for the Power.

Correspondences in Practice

Lists of correspondences bring together energies that are related to the goal. Trust your intuition, focus on the desired outcome, and see what method comes to mind as you review the relevant correspondences.

Constructing a Spell

The construction of a spell is determined by what is wanted, what will be written, what will be said, what steps will be taken, the timing, and the approach consistent with the goal and method. Spells are the vehicles of magickal workings. Any ritual, brew, charm, chant, prayer, amulet, talisman, or crafted item created for magickal purpose, utilizing the movement of energy, the speaking of a word or formula, and the generating of intent into manifestation is a spell.

Inscribing with Sigils and Bindrunes

Inscribing items with sigils and bindrunes (monograms of two to three runic letters invoking their combined magickal meanings) requires drawing up energy from the Earth or breathing on them to energize or enliven the inscription.

The Essential Truth

Magick does not work instantly. Results take time. You cannot perform a spell and expect everything to change overnight.

More importantly, you must support your magickal work with mundane action. A job spell accomplishes nothing if you never apply for positions. A healing spell works alongside medical care, not instead of it. A love spell requires you to actually meet people.

Magick demands full engagement. Psychic effort must be matched by physical effort. When you commit to both, your intentions manifest into reality.

Law of Similars

The Law of Similars (also called the Law of Sympathy or Doctrine of Signatures) is one of the foundational principles of magickal correspondence. It states that colors, shapes, and characteristics of a plant, stone, or other object give clues to its magickal function.

How It Works

According to this law, objects that look like or resemble something share an energetic connection with it. This resemblance creates a sympathetic link that can be used in magick.

Examples:

  • Red stones might be used in magickal cures for blood problems (color similarity)
  • Heart-shaped leaves might be part of a love spell (shape similarity)
  • Walnuts, which resemble brains, have been used for mental clarity and memory (form similarity)
  • Eyebright, a flower with markings resembling eyes, has been used for vision issues

Why It Works

Symbolic images affect the subconscious in specific ways. Advertisers understand this; it's no accident that certain products use specific shapes and colors to evoke particular feelings and associations. Magick works with these same symbolic connections intentionally.

Applications in Practice

Sympathetic Magick

The Law of Similars is the foundation of sympathetic magick, the principle that like affects like. When you work with an object that resembles your target or intention, you create a sympathetic link.

Poppets and Dolls

One of the most common applications is the poppet, a doll made to represent a person. What you do to the poppet symbolically affects the person it represents. This can be used for:

  • Healing: Bandaging the doll's injured area while sending healing energy
  • Protection: Wrapping the doll in protective materials
  • Binding: Restricting the doll's movement to restrict harmful actions

Correspondences

The entire system of magickal correspondences is built on the Law of Similars:

  • Colors correspond to intentions (green for money, pink for love)
  • Shapes correspond to purposes (circles for protection, triangles for manifestation)
  • Natural objects correspond to their resemblances (roots for grounding, feathers for air/communication)

Working with the Law

When choosing materials for spellwork, ask yourself:

  • What does this object look like?
  • What does its color suggest?
  • What does its shape resemble?
  • What qualities does it naturally possess?

These answers point toward the object's magickal correspondences and best uses.

Closed Practices

This grimoire includes rituals, techniques, and traditions from many cultures. Some of these practices are considered closed, meaning they require cultural belonging, lineage, training, or initiation to practice respectfully.

Closed does not mean "secret," "elitist," or "rare."

It means these traditions belong to specific living communities and are not appropriate to use without membership or permission.

This grimoire includes closed practices because some users are practitioners within those traditions, and having this knowledge organized can support them.

However, inclusion is not permission.

Whenever a ritual, tool, plant, or technique belongs to a closed tradition, a Closed Practice Warning appears in the Notes & Warnings section of that entry.

If you notice a ritual from a closed tradition that is not marked, please leave a comment so it can be updated.

⭐ Examples of Closed and Restricted Practices

(This list is not exhaustive, but it reflects what culturally rooted communities define as closed.)

🔒 African Diaspora Religions (Initiatory)

These require lineage, initiation, or elder permission:

  • Haitian Vodou
  • Louisiana Vodou
  • Santería / Lucumí
  • Ifá (Yoruba divination system)
  • Palo Mayombe
  • Candomblé
  • Umbanda & Quimbanda (vary by lineage)
  • Hoodoo (African American folk magic; learn from Black practitioners and within the community)

Important:

Hoodoo is a closed practice rooted in African American culture and history. It is not open for outsiders to take up.

🔒 Indigenous Practices of the Americas

Most Indigenous ceremonies and sacred medicines are closed unless you are:

  • a member of the tribe
  • a descendant
  • a sanctioned student
  • formally adopted into the community

Examples:

  • Ceremonial smudging (varies by tribe)
  • Use of white sage in Indigenous rites
  • Sweat lodges
  • Vision quests
  • Sun Dance ceremonies
  • Ayahuasca ceremonies & dieta (Amazonian lineages)

Burning herbs in general (rosemary, lavender, mugwort, cedar, etc.) is not closed.

🔒 Romani Magick & Folk Traditions

Romani spiritual practices and protective workings are closed unless you are Romani or apprenticed directly.

🔒 Lineage-Based and Initiatory Traditions

These require training, oaths, or membership:

  • Gardnerian Wicca initiations
  • Alexandrian Wicca initiations
  • Golden Dawn rituals
  • O.T.O. workings
  • Freemasonry rituals
  • Rosicrucian order rites
  • Hereditary or family-based witchcraft rites

🔒 Other Culturally Restricted Workings

Depending on lineage, some of the following practices may be closed or require mentorship:

  • Specific Curanderismo rites (not all; some are family-held)
  • Specific Brujería traditions
  • Certain Indigenous folk-healing ceremonies
  • Siberian, Mongolian, or Andean shamanic initiations

The word "shaman" originally comes from the Tungusic peoples of Siberia; the role itself is cultural and not universal.

⭐ What Is NOT Closed (Common Misconception List)

These are open for everyone to practice, though they may be culturally rooted:

  • Kitchen witchery
  • Herbal magick (non-Indigenous, non-ceremonial)
  • Candle magick
  • Color correspondences
  • Cartomancy & tarot
  • Astrology
  • Florida Water
  • Numerology
  • Basic folk magick
  • Burning non-sacred herbs (for cleansing or scent)

⭐ If You're Unsure

If you're unsure whether a ritual is closed:

  • Research its cultural and historical context
  • Look for sources created by members of the tradition
  • Ask respectfully
  • Choose an open alternative that serves the same purpose

Respect is not optional.

This grimoire exists to inform, not to appropriate.

When in doubt, choose reverence, research, and cultural humility.

Plant Grimoire

Introduction to Plant Magick

The art of working with plant spirits for healing, spellcraft, and transformation. This section covers the foundations of plant magick, from understanding plant consciousness to building your practice with herbs, wood, and botanical mixtures.

Flora held only a modest place among the goddesses of the Greek pantheon, yet her standing rose when her name was given to all the abundant plant life of the world. Flowers, plants, and fungi make up one half of this section, and trees the other.

Science can explain how a seed, given only darkness, soil, water, air, and sunlight, becomes something as magnificent as an oak. Even so, the moment green shoots break the surface remains as near to magick as anything a person can witness. For that reason the seed itself stands among our most significant sacred symbols.

Plants carry all the meaning of the Sun, since they draw their properties from the power they gather from it. The spiral spacing of leaves and the shapes of certain flowers can conceal the golden mean, the mystical spiral that expresses the mathematics of growth. In the Vedic tradition, plants with healing properties rank among the greatest gifts ever given to humankind and receive the same reverence as deities. We owe our knowledge of these useful plants to the intuition and experiments of ancestors who risked poisoning and even death to uncover their hidden natures.

The Garden of Life

For many thousands of years of human evolution, trees, plants, flowers, and herbs have surrounded us. The green world offered a lasting and beautiful backdrop to the early struggle for survival, stirring the senses in many ways. Beyond taste, sight, touch, and smell, plants speak through sound as well, since rustling leaves or the snap of a twig could warn of an intruder. Plants endure in the harshest climates and the unlikeliest places. The word "vegetable" descends from the Latin vegetare, meaning "to enliven," from vegetus, meaning "vigorous" or "active."

When humanity began to wonder about its own origins, it made sense to imagine that a God had shaped the first person in a Godlike form, using the same earth that gave rise to plants. The name Adam means "clay," and it is no coincidence that the paradise this first man inhabited was a garden. The plants around him were friends and companions, providing food, medicine, materials for shelter, shade on a hot day, and fuel through cold winters. They also gave the fibers that make fabric, and the first garment was a leaf.

Plants mark the turning of the seasons, dying and then returning each spring like long absent friends. With the rise of agriculture we learned to harness their energy for our own purposes and convenience. The variety in a modern kitchen, drawn from every corner of the planet, would have astonished our ancestors. That abundance rests on thousands of years of testing and experiment: eating plants raw, cooking them, smoking them, and combining them with other substances to see what might happen. Some experiments ended well, others badly. Even now certain mushrooms are listed as "edibility unknown," and many people likely died before poisonous plants were identified.

The Doctrine of Signatures

Out of necessity, our ancestors were a superstitious people. Searching for the secrets held within plants, they applied the Doctrine of Signatures, the belief that a thing relates to whatever it resembles. They had little else to guide them. The idea still carries influence despite advances in botanical science. The pomegranate and tomato became fertility symbols because of their abundant seeds. Folk names also reveal old interpretations. The pansy, also called heartsease, was said to cheer the heart and takes its name from the shape of its leaves. Hemlock earned the name "poison parsley" because it looks like parsley and is poisonous. The rule does not always hold, though. Mistletoe is called "all heal," yet the plant is poisonous.

Anyone with comprehensive knowledge of herbs was naturally accorded respect, for such a person could quite literally kill or cure. The Breton word for herb, louzaouenn, is also the word for medicine. This understanding of the plant kingdom reached even to the herbs and flowers that affect the mind, the plants that hold mind-altering chemicals.

Plants as Tools of Transition

Psychedelic and psychotropic substances act on the mind to offer an alternative view of reality, inducing dreams and visions and opening a gateway to another dimension, the realm of the Gods. These plants and their uses were preciously guarded, secrets held by those considered wise enough to read their messages: the shaman or sorcerer. To take such a substance was a rite of passage, a spiritual exploration wrapped in ceremony so the initiate would arrive safely at the other end of the journey.

Though we now understand these chemical constituents and how they affect us, the plants that contain them still hold sacred status, surrounded by extensive literature and myth. Alongside ayahuasca, opium, cannabis, peyote, and various mushrooms, several more common plant substances act in similar ways. Alcohol, for instance, is the result of plant material fermented with yeast and sugar.

⚠️
Ayahuasca, peyote, and related entheogenic rites are sacred to specific Indigenous traditions and are closed practices meant only for those within the originating cultures.

Flowers, Plants, and Fungi

Flowers are generally symbols of love, a fitting association since they are the sexual parts of plants. Because they fade and die so quickly, they also serve as a reminder of the transitory nature of the material world. In Welsh myth, Blodeuwedd, whose name means "blossoms," was a beautiful girl magickally constructed from thousands of flowers. Like the blooms that formed her, she proved fickle and betrayed her husband.

The symbolism of flowers seems limitless, with a myth for nearly every kind of flower on the planet, the Greeks being especially prolific. Flower and story work together to explain each bloom's "personality." Color also plays an important part in reading flower symbols. The Japanese art of flower arranging, Ikebana, uses flowers to write a kind of poetry tied to the cosmos, the seasons, the passing of time, and the elements, and it carries its own extensive symbolism. The flower also serves as a symbol of the soul. In Tantric and Taoist philosophy, the "Secret of the Golden Flower" is the attainment of spiritual union, an alchemical process that unifies the essence with breath, fire, and water, where the flower itself stands as an allegory for the Elixir of Life.

These flowers and plants are grouped together here, apart from trees, since some herbs are also flowers and some flowers carry value in herbal medicine.

Plant Grimoire

What Is an Herb

At its most basic, an herb is a plant whose fragrance or taste lends itself to cooking, healing, or perfumery. The term generally refers to the aboveground portions of the plant, mainly leaves and flowers, though definitions shift depending on how the plant is viewed and used.

In horticulture, an herb has a soft stem with less cellulose than other plants. Cellulose forms the rigid outer wall of the plant cell. Herbaceous plants are most often valued for their leaves and flowers, though all parts of a plant can serve healing, culinary, and magickal purposes. Any nonwoody, vascular plant could meet this definition.

🌿
Herbs vs. Spices: Spices fall under the broader umbrella of herbs but are differentiated by their origin in subtropical temperate zones. Spices are typically pictured as ground powder made from dried seeds, bark, or roots of aromatic and savory plants.

Key Herbalism Terms

  • Annuals: Plants with a growth cycle lasting only one growing season. They germinate, mature, flower, and die within a year, requiring replanting each season.
  • Binomial: The two-part Latin name identifying each plant. The genus name appears first, categorizing shared characteristics. The species name follows, singular and specific. For example, basil is Ocimum basilicum.
  • Forage: The act of locating and harvesting wildcrafted herbs in their natural environment.
  • Hardiness Zone: One of eleven geographical regions in the United States delineating climate conditions that affect herb cultivation. Each adjacent zone differs by approximately ten degrees.
  • Hydroponics: A soil-free method of plant cultivation where nutrients dissolve into circulating water and plants grow directly from the solution.
  • Organic: In cultivation, this means plants are raised without additives such as pesticides or fertilizer.
  • Perennial Herbs: Herbs that grow back year after year without replanting.
  • Wildcrafted: Herbs that grow in nature without human cultivation.

Ways to Work with Plants

Divination and Observation

  • Watch plant behavior for omens and signs
  • Press flowers in your book of shadows

Spell Components

  • Gather loosened leaves and petals for magick potions
  • Use plant matter in amulets and talismans
  • Add plant matter to incense and candles

Healing and Wellness

  • Blend herbs for poultices and healing teas
  • Make fragrant potpourris for closets and drawers

Living Plant Magick

  • Place live plants throughout your home or yard to encourage personal growth and well-being

Plants as Spell Components

If you think of a spell as a magick recipe, you begin to understand why the components matter so much. A good cook knows that the key to great food lies in the quality of the ingredients and how they are combined. The same holds true for spells.

  • Measure correctly: Proportions matter
  • Add at the right time: Timing affects potency
  • Allow time to work: Magick needs space to unfold

Anything that builds the energy of the working toward the right outcome qualifies as a good spell component. All ingredients must mesh on a metaphysical level.

✨
Remember: The witch themselves is the key component of any spell, adding a word, a touch, or a wish.

Building Your Plant Collection

You do not need to acquire everything at once.

  1. Select a few staples suited to the kinds of spells you want to cast
  2. Add more over time as your practice expands, just as a cook builds a spice collection
  3. Keep notes on what works and what does not as you become more proficient

Oil Grimoire

How Essential Oils Work

The therapeutic potential of essential oils, like other plant-derived remedies, is still being uncovered. Many medicinal herbs have been used since antiquity, and a great number have yielded the active compounds that underpin modern drugs, including quinine and cocaine, yet much of their precise pharmacology has yet to be mapped. This is especially true of aromatic oils, whose nature is concentrated and multifaceted by design. Only a small fraction of the world's flora has ever been examined for pharmacologically active compounds, and as more plant species become endangered, important sources may be lost before they are ever studied.

Modern research has largely confirmed the traditional understanding of medicinal plants, even as the language has changed. A herb such as basil, once described as a protection against evil or as good for the heart, with a scent that takes away sorrowfulness, would today be called an excellent prophylactic, nerve tonic, and antidepressant. Essential oils, like herbal remedies, can cover a wide field of activity. The same herb or oil (lemon balm being a clear example) can stimulate certain systems of the body while sedating or relaxing others. To understand how essential oils actually work, it helps to look at them through the lens of the body's major systems.

The Skin

Skin issues are often the surface expression of a deeper imbalance, whether a build-up of toxins in the blood, hormonal disruption, or nervous and emotional strain. Essential oils are well suited to this terrain because they can address such complaints on several levels at once. They dissolve readily in oil and alcohol, lend their scent to water, and so make excellent ingredients for cosmetics and everyday skincare as well as for the treatment of specific conditions. The activities listed below are particularly useful in this context.

  • Antiseptics for cuts, insect bites, and blemishes: thyme, sage, eucalyptus, tea tree, clove, lavender, lemon
  • Anti-inflammatory oils for eczema, infected wounds, bumps, and bruises: German and Roman chamomile, lavender, yarrow
  • Fungicidal oils for athlete's foot, candida, and ringworm: lavender, tea tree, myrrh, patchouli, sweet marjoram
  • Granulation-stimulating (cicatrising) agents for burns, cuts, scars, and stretch marks: lavender, chamomile, rose, neroli, frankincense, geranium
  • Deodorants for excessive perspiration and wound cleansing: bergamot, lavender, thyme, juniper, cypress, Spanish sage, lemongrass
  • Insect repellents and parasiticides for lice, fleas, scabies, ticks, mosquitos, ants, and moths: spike lavender, garlic, geranium, citronella, eucalyptus, clove, camphor, Atlas cedarwood

The Circulation, Muscles and Joints

Essential oils are absorbed easily through the skin and mucosa into the bloodstream, where they shape the character of circulation overall. Oils with a rubefacient or warming effect not only improve local blood flow but also reach the inner organs. They draw warmth and colour to the surface of the skin and can offer significant pain relief through their analgesic or numbing action. Some oils ease local inflammation by triggering mediators in the body that dilate the blood vessels, allowing blood to move more freely and reducing swelling. Others, such as hyssop, tend to balance the circulatory system as a whole, lowering blood pressure when it is too high and stimulating circulation when it is sluggish.

  • Hypotensives for high blood pressure, palpitations, and stress: sweet marjoram, ylang ylang, lavender, lemon
  • Hypertensives for poor circulation, chilblains, and listlessness: rosemary, spike lavender, eucalyptus, peppermint, thyme
  • Rubefacients for rheumatism of the joints, muscular stiffness, sciatica, and lumbago: black pepper, juniper, rosemary, camphor, sweet marjoram
  • Depurative or antitoxic agents for arthritis, gout, congestion, and skin eruptions: juniper, lemon, fennel, lovage
  • Lymphatic stimulants for cellulitis, water retention, and weight management: grapefruit, lime, fennel, lemon, mandarin, white birch
  • Circulatory tonics and astringents for swellings, inflammation, and varicose veins: cypress, yarrow, lemon

The Respiratory System

Nose, throat, and lung infections respond very well to treatment with essential oils. Inhalation is a particularly effective route. Once the oils reach the bronchi the larger part is exhaled directly through the lungs, and at the same time they prompt an increase in bronchial secretion, a protective response that benefits many respiratory ailments. Inhalation also carries the oils into the bloodstream more quickly than oral application. Most essential oils absorbed through the stomach are likewise excreted through the lungs, with only a small portion leaving through the urine.

  • Expectorants for catarrh, sinusitis, coughs, and bronchitis: eucalyptus, pine, thyme, myrrh, sandalwood, fennel
  • Antispasmodics for colic, asthma, dry cough, and whooping cough: hyssop, cypress, Atlas cedarwood, bergamot, chamomile, cajeput
  • Balsamic agents for colds, chills, and congestion: benzoin, frankincense, Tolu balsam, Peru balsam, myrrh
  • Antiseptics for flu, colds, sore throat, tonsillitis, and gingivitis: thyme, sage, eucalyptus, hyssop, pine, cajeput, tea tree, borneol

The Digestive System

External application of essential oils can influence digestive processes, even though the oils themselves are not taken orally. Herbal medicine, by contrast, draws on a wide range of remedies for stomach, gall bladder, and liver complaints, including dandelion, marshmallow, chamomile, and meadowsweet. Much of the effect of those remedies comes from the combined action of aromatic components, bitters, tannins, and mucilage, none of which travel with the volatile oil on its own. External use of essential oils on digestive issues is therefore useful but more limited in scope than internal herbal preparations.

  • Antispasmodics for spasm, pain, and indigestion: chamomile, caraway, fennel, orange, peppermint, lemon balm, aniseed, cinnamon
  • Carminatives and stomachics for flatulent dyspepsia, aerophagia, and nausea: angelica, basil, fennel, chamomile, peppermint, mandarin
  • Cholagogues for increasing the flow of bile and stimulating the gall bladder: caraway, lavender, peppermint, borneol
  • Hepatics for liver congestion and jaundice: lemon, lime, rosemary, peppermint
  • Aperitifs for loss of appetite and anorexia: aniseed, angelica, orange, ginger, garlic

The Genito-urinary and Endocrine Systems

As with the digestive system, the reproductive organs can be reached through absorption from the skin into the bloodstream, and also through hormonal influence. Rose and jasmine have a particular affinity for the reproductive system, offering a general strengthening effect as well as support for menstrual problems, genital infections, and sexual difficulties. Other oils carry plant hormones that mimic their human counterparts. Hops, sage, and fennel have been shown to contain a form of oestrogen that influences the menstrual cycle, lactation, and secondary sexual characteristics. Oestrogen also supports healthy circulation, good muscle and skin tone, and strong bones in both men and women.

Several essential oils also affect hormone secretion in other glands, including the thyroid (which governs growth and metabolism), the adrenal medulla (which manages the stress response), and the adrenal cortex (which oversees a number of processes including the production of oestrogen and androgen, the male sex hormone).

  • Antispasmodics for menstrual cramp (dysmenorrhoea) and labour pains: sweet marjoram, chamomile, clary sage, jasmine, lavender
  • Emmenagogues for scanty periods or lack of periods (amenorrhoea): chamomile, fennel, hyssop, juniper, sweet marjoram, peppermint
  • Uterine tonics and regulators for pregnancy, excess menstruation (menorrhagia), and PMT: clary sage, jasmine, rose, myrrh, frankincense, lemon balm
  • Antiseptic and bactericidal agents for leucorrhoea, vaginal pruritis, and thrush: bergamot, chamomile, myrrh, rose, tea tree
  • Galactagogues for increasing milk flow: fennel, jasmine, anise, lemongrass (sage, mint, and parsley have the opposite effect and reduce it)
  • Aphrodisiacs for impotence and frigidity: black pepper, cardamon, clary sage, neroli, jasmine, rose, sandalwood, patchouli, ylang ylang
  • Anaphrodisiacs for reducing sexual desire: sweet marjoram, camphor
  • Adrenal stimulants for anxiety and stress-related conditions: basil, geranium, rosemary, borneol, sage, pine, savory

The kidneys, bladder, and urinary system as a whole are harder to address through essential oils alone. Recent research suggests that the diuretic effects of essential oils are effectively non-existent. Traditional diuretic agents such as juniper, lovage, and parsley seed are also considered unsuitable as essential oils for internal use because of their toxicity and the risk of kidney damage. Herb teas of fennel, dandelion, or chamomile offer a gentler alternative. Bathing and the use of a douche can help control urinary infections, especially those tied to nervous or stress-related symptoms.

  • Urinary antiseptics for cystitis and urethritis: bergamot, chamomile, tea tree, sandalwood

The Immune System

Almost all essential oils carry bactericidal properties, and by encouraging the production of white blood cells they help the body resist and recover from infection. These qualities are why aromatic herbs and oils held such standing against tropical infections like malaria and typhoid, and during the plague epidemics of the Middle Ages. People who use essential oils regularly tend to maintain a higher than average resistance to illness, picking up fewer colds and recovering more quickly when they do.

  • Bactericidal and antiviral agents (prophylactics) for protection against colds and flu: tea tree, cajeput, niaouli, basil, lavender, eucalyptus, bergamot, camphor, clove, rosemary
  • Febrifuges for reducing fever and temperature: angelica, basil, peppermint, thyme, sage, lemon, eucalyptus, tea tree
  • Sudorifics and diaphoretics for promoting sweating and eliminating toxins: rosemary, thyme, hyssop, chamomile

The Nervous System

Recent research aligns closely with the traditional view of how essential oils act on the nervous system. Chamomile, bergamot, sandalwood, lavender, and sweet marjoram have been shown to sedate the central nervous system, while jasmine, peppermint, basil, clove, and ylang ylang stimulate it. A few results run counter to popular assumption: neroli proved stimulating and lemon proved sedative. Some oils are adaptogens, meaning they have a balancing or normalising effect on the body's systems. Geranium and rosewood, for example, can be sedative or stimulating depending on the situation and the individual.

Words like relaxing and uplifting often describe an odour and emotional response rather than a physiological effect, although the two are connected. Bergamot, lemon balm, and lemon can sedate the nervous system while reviving the spirit. Jasmine, ylang ylang, and neroli can stimulate the nerves and yet feel soothing and relaxing on a more subtle emotional level.

  • Sedatives for nervous tension, stress, and insomnia: chamomile, bergamot, sandalwood, lavender, sweet marjoram, lemon balm, hops, valerian, lemon
  • Stimulants for convalescence, lack of strength, and nervous fatigue: basil, jasmine, peppermint, ylang ylang, neroli, angelica, rosemary
  • Nerve tonics (nervines) for strengthening the nervous system as a whole: chamomile, clary sage, juniper, lavender, marjoram, rosemary

The Mind

The mind is perhaps the most discussed and least understood territory of essential oil work. There is no question that aromatic oils have been used throughout history to influence emotion and state of mind, and this is the basis for their long employment as incense in religious and ritual settings. Two olfactory nerve tracts run directly into the limbic system, the part of the brain concerned with memory and emotion, which is why scents can produce an immediate and powerful response that resists rational analysis.

Research at Warwick University in England and Toho University in Japan has set out to place these traditional understandings within a scientific frame. The findings describe two kinds of reaction to odours, called hard-wired and soft-wired responses. The hard-wired response is ingrained from before birth and operates purely on instinct, such as a baby's recognition of the scent of its mother's skin, or a sexual signal between adults. The soft-wired response is learned or acquired later, such as the fragrance of honeysuckle recalling a particular childhood garden.

This raises a real question. To what extent does the effect of an oil rest on its chemistry and physiology, and to what extent does it depend on belief and association? Once the conversation moves into psychological and emotional response, neat classification becomes much harder, and it makes more sense to weigh the temperament of the individual within a given context than to predict a fixed reaction.

The conclusion drawn at the 1991 Psychology of Perfumery Conference was that pharmacological effects tend to be similar from one person to the next, while psychological effects are bound to differ. The effect of an odour on a person depends on a number of factors.

  1. How the odour was applied
  2. How much was applied
  3. The circumstances in which it was applied
  4. The person to whom it was applied, including age, sex, and personality
  5. The mood they were in to begin with
  6. Any prior associations they hold with the odour
  7. Anosmia, or the inability to smell certain scents

The aim, then, is to seek out odoriferous substances that have an affinity with the person being treated, that compensate for what is lacking, and that allow particular faculties to flourish. This is the principle behind the so-called individual prescription, a blend tailored on every point to the identity of the person it serves.

Once individual need enters the picture, essential oils begin to show the full range of their nature. The rose is a clear example. In folklore and religious writing, especially within the Sufi tradition, the rose is associated with beauty, love, and spiritual depth, and it has an equally long history in physical care, used for skin problems, regulating the female cycle, supporting circulation, purifying the blood, and as a heart tonic. When the fragrance reaches the nose it carries all of these associations with it, working on mind and body at once, with the precise effect shaped by personal experience.

The dominant trend in modern thought is strictly dualistic, treating psychic and somatic events as mutually exclusive rather than inseparable. Trying to disentangle spirit from matter leads nowhere. Mind and matter are better understood as enfolded projections of a higher reality that is neither matter nor consciousness alone.
