Mineral Grimoire

Introduction to Crystal Magick

The art of working with the slow, concentrated energy of stones for spellcraft, healing, and transformation.

Ancient Origins

Long before people began prizing gems for their monetary value, they used them as magick charms. In early societies, only rulers, members of royal families, priests, and religious leaders wore gems.

The ancient Egyptians used stones for healing, protection, and other purposes, both physical and spiritual. Ancient peoples believed gemstones were "capable of human feelings and passions so that they could express jealousy and shock."

The reverence ran deeper than adornment. Egyptian burials wrapped the dead in gems and set carved stone amulets throughout the tomb, each placed for a deliberate protective purpose. Far to the east, the vibrational qualities of gems were recorded in Indian Ayurvedic medicine and in Chinese herbal tradition, where stones were understood to carry healing influence on body and spirit. Using crystals for healing is an ancient art whose roots reach back beyond any single civilization.

🏛️
Lost Knowledge: Many researchers believe crystals may have been sources of power and magick on the lost continents of Atlantis and Lemuria, and that crystals were used in building the pyramids and Stonehenge.

Born of the Stars

One enduring teaching holds that the stars and planets shaped gemstones from the slow decay of the earth's matter, and that each stone then came under the rulership of the planet that formed it. This is one reason so many crystals carry planetary correspondences, and why the heavens and the mineral kingdom are read as a single continuous web of influence.

Gems in Sacred Myth

Across traditions, the most awe-inspiring symbols were imagined in gemstone form. In Hindu myth the sacred mountain Meru, home of the Gods, turns a face of gold to the north, silver to the east, cat's eye to the south, and ruby to the west where the sun sets. The same tradition gives us the Kalpa tree, a world-tree built entirely of jewels, with fruits of ruby, leaves of green zircon and coral, shoots of emerald, a trunk of cat's eye, topaz, and diamond, and roots of sapphire. The Seven Heavens of Islamic faith are mapped in gems and metals, as are the twelve foundations of the New Jerusalem.

The breastplate worn by the High Priest of the Temple in Jerusalem held twelve gems credited with the power of prophecy. Those twelve stones seeded many of the associations that still link particular gems to the months and signs of the year.

The Doctrine of Signatures

A widely used method reads a gem's magickal purpose from its color. This color correspondence sits at the heart of how stones are matched to intention, since color carries a real and marked effect on mood. A stone's hue becomes a direct signpost to the work it supports.

Tapping the Magick of Stones

Today, precious and semiprecious gems are prized primarily for their beauty. Witches, however, recognize that crystals and gemstones serve many magickal purposes:

  • Spellworking - Amplifying and focusing intention
  • Divination - Seeking insight
  • Shamanic journeying - Accessing other realms
  • Meditation - Deepening practice and awareness
  • Dowsing - Finding what is hidden
  • Healing - Supporting physical and spiritual wellness

Living Entities

Like plants, crystals and gemstones are living entities, although they resonate at a slow rate that most people can't perceive.

💎
Crystal Energy: Their slow, concentrated energy enables them to keep working their magick for a long period of time, making them ideal for sustained spellwork and protection.

Ways to Use Crystals in Magick

You can include crystals or gemstones in virtually any spell to increase, focus, stabilize, or fine-tune your spell's potency:

  • Wear them to enhance your own personal energy field
  • Put them in amulets or talismans for portable magick
  • Set them near windows and doors to provide home protection
  • Meditate with them for deeper spiritual connection
  • Infuse magick potions with their energy
  • Dowse with a pendulum made of gemstone or crystal
  • Display them on your altar to attract positive energy
  • Offer them to deities or nature spirits in return for assistance
  • Gaze into them to see the past or future (scrying)

Birthstones and Zodiac Signs

Birthstones resonate with the qualities of the zodiac signs to which they correspond. Originally, people wore birthstones to enhance, balance, or moderate their own personal characteristics.

♈
Important: You should look at your birth sign, not the month of your birth, to discover your true birthstone. If you're an Aquarian, for example, your birthstone is garnet, regardless of whether you were born in January or February.

Clearing Stones Between Workings

Crystals and other stones can be used in more than one spell, but you must clear them after each working. Clearing is essential because using a crystal that retains vibrations from a previous spell can interfere with the outcome of a new spell.

Clearing Methods

Water, salt, incense, sunlight, and moonlight can all be used, alone or in combination, to clear stones. For example:

  • Wash a crystal in running water, place it in a dish of salt, then put the dish in sunlight
  • Smudge a stone with incense, then place it overnight in moonlight

The more clearing you feel the stone needs, the longer you leave it in the clearing medium. The important thing is that you feel the stone has been cleared of any magickal residue before you use it in another spell.

Building a Crystal Spellwork Tool Kit

Before purchasing crystals, take time to figure out which ones will help you the most. Grab your journal and answer these questions:

  1. What types of spellwork do you do the most? If you do a lot of abundance work, acquire crystals with this focus.
  2. What crystals immediately come to mind? Research these intuitively-chosen crystals for themes you had not considered. Add at least two to your tool kit.
  3. What crystals do you dislike? Why? Often, a crystal we do not like is one we ought to work with most. There may be a lesson that crystal wants you to learn. Choose one of these for your tool kit.
  4. Which element are you most drawn to? Include crystals representing each element, with your most-used element as a larger focus.
  5. How much space do you have for crystals? Resist the desire to buy large crystals when starting out. Tumbled stones and crystal chips work just as effectively.

Crystals by Intention

  • Abundance: Citrine, aventurine, jade, apatite
  • Love: Rose quartz, rhodonite, amazonite, lapis lazuli
  • Manifestation: Apatite, cinnabar, opal, carnelian
  • Mental clarity: Amethyst, fluorite, lepidolite, sodalite
  • Money: Pyrite, tiger's eye, goldstone, orange calcite
  • Spiritual: Moonstone, clear quartz, lemurian quartz, labradorite

Crystals by Element

  • Water: Blue lace agate, aquamarine, larimar, green tourmaline, chrysocolla
  • Fire: Garnet, fire agate, amber, citrine, carnelian
  • Earth: Tiger's eye, smoky quartz, black tourmaline, hematite
  • Air: Fluorite, aura quartz, aventurine, labradorite, kyanite
  • Spirit: Moonstone, amethyst, clear quartz, herkimer diamond, apophyllite

Storing Your Tool Kit

Keep working crystals in a bowl on your altar, in a wooden box, or in a velvet drawstring bag near your sacred space. You can decorate a box with colors and sigils to create a special home for your magickal workmates.

Connecting with Your Crystals

Connecting with your crystals and learning how their energy feels is essential for effective spellwork. By connecting with each one, you build a solid working relationship with each crystal spirit and can effectively assign each crystal its special job during your spellwork.

Sometimes a crystal does not feel suited for a specific spell, and you must respect their wishes and choose another. You can tell if a crystal does not want to participate by holding it and gauging its energy. The crystal may feel colder than usual, or you sense resistance. After your working, check back with any crystal that declined. Sometimes they just need a good cleaning.

Ways to Connect

  • Carry your crystal in your pocket or bag throughout the day. Hold it often.
  • Talk to your crystal. This opens the pathway to receiving messages during spellwork.
  • Sleep with your crystal under your pillow or on your bedside table. Ask it to communicate with you in dreams.
  • Meditate with your crystal to open the lines of connection and sense what it wants to offer you.
  • Journal about your crystals. Track thoughts, feelings, and messages to help you decide which crystal to use in each working.

Cleansing and Caring for Crystals

Cleansing crystals before and after use is good practice for spellwork, healing, or meditation. Crystals are sensitive to energy and will pick up and hold onto energy when handled. Clearing ensures the focus is directly on what the crystals need to do during a particular spell.

🌙
Selenite is self-cleansing and can cleanse other crystals. Place crystals in a selenite bowl and ask for them to be cleansed. Say thank you when finished.

Cleansing Methods

  • Smoke: Pass crystals through the smoke of your favorite herbs or incense, asking the smoke to clear unneeded energy. Rosemary smoke works well.
  • Moonlight: Place crystals under a full moon, or on a windowsill. Direct moonlight is not required; intention is what matters.
  • Sound: Use a singing bowl, bells, or music. Clapping your hands also works.
  • Reiki: A quick method if you are attuned.
  • Rice: Place crystals in a bowl of uncooked rice for as long as you are able. Any type of rice works.

Care Tips

  • Keep crystals dry and out of the sun. Some crystals, especially amethyst, fade with prolonged sun exposure.
  • If you have small children or pets, store crystals on a high shelf or in a drawer.
  • Keep altar crystals in a safe place to prevent disruption of ongoing spells.

Clear Quartz as Universal Substitute

Because they can most easily be programmed and reprogrammed, clear quartz crystals can be substituted for almost any stone in any spell.

Programming Clear Quartz

To substitute clear quartz for another stone:

  1. Take the crystal and hold it in sunlight or moonlight
  2. Say: "Crystal, for this spell you are given the powers of [name the stone whose energies are required]."
  3. After the spell has been cast, clear the crystal to restore it to its original state

Cleansing Your Tools

Any object may be spiritually cleansed using various cleansing techniques. Always make sure the technique will not harm the object. (Sprinkling Indigo Water on a crystal is fine. If you soak fabric in Indigo Water, it will turn blue.)

General Methods

  • Pass objects through incense smoke
  • Fumigate with a smudge stick
  • Asperge with cleansing waters: Holy Water, Marie Laveau Water, and Rose of Jericho Water are particularly effective; choose what suits your purposes best
  • Salt water provides a strong cleansing, providing the object will not be damaged by salt
  • Singing bowls will cleanse objects as well as areas and individuals

Cleansing Crystals

Crystals and gemstones absorb and store energy. Depending upon how they are used, they may need to be cleansed periodically and re-charged.

Whether to cleanse is a personal decision. Some practitioners never cleanse their stones, believing that whatever energy a crystal carries is part of its intended journey. Others cleanse immediately upon acquiring a stone and again after use or after others have handled it. Neither approach is wrong. Intuition is a reliable guide here. If the source of a stone is known and trusted, cleansing may not feel necessary. Some practitioners intentionally avoid clearing stones whose origin or journey holds meaning for them.

Some stones do not require cleansing at all. Black kyanite, for example, does not hold or accumulate a charge and needs no clearing. Programmable stones like quartz, on the other hand, absorb energy and vibration readily and benefit most from regular cleansing.

  • Bury the stone in the ground overnight or longer. Most potent if done outside, but a flowerpot filled with dirt will work too. Mark the burial spot if you wish to retain the stone.
  • Expose the crystal to sunlight and/or moonlight
  • Pass the crystal through incense smoke
  • Many clear crystals may be cleansed with salt water: collect ocean water or add sea salt to spring water
  • Many Charged Waters may be used to cleanse crystals, particularly Florida Water or Notre Dame Water
  • Salt may leach color from a vivid crystal or damage a fragile one like moldavite: bathe these in spring water with a few drops of Dr. Bach's Rescue Remedy or a similar emergency flower remedy formula

The new moon is the phase most aligned with crystal cleansing. Its dark, receptive quality supports the release and purging of accumulated energy. Additional methods beyond those listed above:

  • Smoke: Sacred herbs and resins are potent cleansers. White sage (Salvia apiana), palo santo, and copal are among the most effective. Passing stones through the smoke resets them to their base energetic frequency, clearing anything accumulated in transit or use.
  • Water: Running water and collected natural water are powerful cleansing mediums. Placing stones in a bowl of spring water or recently gathered ocean water clears unwanted energy and reconnects the crystal to the energy of the earth. Always confirm a stone is water-safe before using this method.
  • Sound and frequency: The solfeggio frequency of 417 Hz, rooted in Gregorian chant traditions dating to the eleventh century, is used specifically for clearing unwanted energy. Play this frequency near your stones or use a tuning fork calibrated to 417 Hz. Drumming and chanting are equally valid sound-based approaches.
  • Intention and breath: Slow, deliberate exhalation directed across a stone with focused clearing intention is an accessible and effective method. Conscious breath connects personal life force with the crystal's energy, resetting its vibration to align with a specific purpose.
  • Clearing stones: Selenite and black kyanite neither accumulate nor hold a charge, so they never require cleansing themselves. Simply touching either stone to another crystal transmutes and clears accumulated energy. Both can also serve as passive cleansers when placed near other stones in a collection.

Charging and Programming

When first acquiring a stone, it is natural to wonder whether it is already aligned with a specific intention or whether it needs to be directed. Crystals can be charged and programmed for focused work, particularly quartz. Due to its inherent electric charge, quartz carries a stronger natural frequency and a broader electromagnetic field than most other stones, making it especially responsive to intentional programming.

Charging: Place the stone outside or on a windowsill under the full moon. As the lunar light infuses it, hold a clear intention for how the crystal will serve. The full moon is associated astrologically with Cancer, a sign connected to intuition, emotional depth, and receptive wisdom. This is the optimal time to charge a stone with a specific purpose, whether that is clarity, healing, abundance, or something else entirely.

Programming: Once charged, hold the crystal in the nondominant (receiving) hand and cover it with the dominant (projecting) hand. Visualize the dominant hand transmitting the specific intention directly into the stone. This process is sometimes called coding a crystal. The stone then carries that energetic instruction until it is deprogrammed.

Deprogramming: When a crystal is needed for a different purpose, it can be decoded and reset. The new moon, aligned with releasing and letting go, is the most supportive phase for this process.

Cleansing Crystal Balls

It is crucial that crystal balls and scrying glass are kept cleansed, both physically and spiritually. A dusty crystal ball reveals nothing. A crystal ball covered with negative spiritual debris may reveal distortions.

Cleanse with any of the following:

  • A blend of spring water and vinegar
  • A charged water: Holy Water, Marie Laveau Water, and Notre Dame Water are particularly recommended
  • A water-based herbal infusion made with dried mugwort and/or anise seeds
  • Mugwort hydrosol

Add flower essence remedies to any of the above as desired. Mugwort flower essence enhances the crystal ball's powers. Dr. Bach's Rescue Remedy or a similar emergency formula will remove and assimilate disturbing or traumatic visions seen within.

Spirit Categories

An overview of the major categories of spiritual entities encountered in magickal practice, their origins, how they are traditionally approached, and what distinguishes each type.

Angels

The word "angel" translates directly as "messenger" in Greek, itself derived from the Hebrew. Unlike most other spirit categories, angels do not traditionally accept offerings. They are called through prayer, petition, and fragrance. High Ritual Magick, drawing on traditions attributed to King Solomon, compels angelic presence through sigils and talismans.

Angels oversee all areas of life. There are angels of conception, angels of specific countries, angels assigned to thieves, and individual guardian angels. The Talmud states that each person has eleven thousand guardian angels.

In Jewish mysticism, angels are described as beings of light. When an angel wishes to take physical form, it gathers earth, fashions it into clothing, and transforms itself. They are generally understood as dynamic, fierce beings of overwhelming radiance.

Angels and the Origin of Magick

According to Islamic and Jewish traditions, angels are directly responsible for humanity's ability to practice magick. The Creator generated magickal power, but angels taught humans to recognize and use it.

The Book of Enoch names specific teaching angels and their areas of instruction:

  • Semjaza: enchantments and root cutting
  • Armaros: resolving enchantments
  • Baraquiel: astrology
  • Kokabel: constellations
  • Ezequeeh: knowledge of the clouds
  • Araquiel: earth signs
  • Shamsiel: sun signs
  • Sariel: phases of the moon

Moral Status Across Traditions

Christian theology positions angels as purely good beings, with fallen angels losing their status entirely. Demons occupy the opposite end as purely evil. Islamic, Jewish, and Pagan traditions take a different view: angels are beings of power, not inherently good or evil. Some are benevolent, some are harmful, and some can be influenced in either direction.

Genesis 6:1-4 describes angels who desired human women and fathered children with them. According to the Book of Enoch, these angels shared knowledge of astrology, magick, witchcraft, and cosmetics, which was considered a significant magickal art in the ancient world.

Angelic Hierarchy and the Archangels

Angels are organized into ranks including Archangels, Throne Angels, Watchers, Seraphim, and Cherubim. The archangels command hosts of spirits, and many spells request their assistance, though whether the archangel appears personally or delegates varies by interpretation.

The four widely recognized archangels are Rafael, Gabriel, Michael, and Auriel (also spelled Uriel or Ariel). This grouping appears across Christian, Islamic, and Jewish traditions and likely predates all three. Some traditions recognize seven archangels, corresponding to the seven visible planets. Candidates for the additional three include Cassiel (Kafziel), Zadkiel, Samael, Chamuel, Jophiel, Raziel, Metatron, and Iblis. Most angelic names end with "-el," the ancient pan-Semitic name for the Creator, meaning "the Lord."

Enochian Magick

Enochian magick is a system of angel magick transmitted to Dr. John Dee through the medium Edward Kelley. Dee was a prominent astrologer and magickian who selected Queen Elizabeth I's coronation date and served as her advisor. He sought direct angelic communication but could not achieve it alone. Kelley, an alchemist with strong shamanic abilities, contacted the angels through mirrors and crystal balls. The angels reportedly identified themselves as the same beings who communicated with the biblical Enoch. Working with Dee's angelic system requires substantial familiarity with classical magick.

Demons

The modern understanding of demons as evil spirits stems from a reinterpretation of the Greek "daemon," which originally referred to a personal guardian spirit that could be benevolent, malevolent, or both. As Christianity gained institutional power, any spirit interaction not sanctioned by the Church was classified as evil, transforming the daemon into the demonic.

Within the classical grimoire tradition, "demon" typically refers to a low-level malevolent spiritual entity. These beings are generally anonymous, jealous, mischievous, and lacking in intelligence.

Orisha and Lwa

Origins

The orisha and lwa are closely related spirit beings originating from West Africa. The orisha come from Yoruba-land in modern Nigeria. The lwa derive from Fon traditions in Dahomey (modern Benin). The word "Vodou" means "spirit" in the Fon language.

These spirits have been venerated in their homelands for thousands of years. When their devotees were enslaved and transported to the Western Hemisphere, the spirits traveled with them. Traditional African religions were outlawed under slavery and devotees faced persecution, but the spirits endured. By the late twentieth century, they had re-emerged as the foundation of influential African-derived spiritual traditions.

Traditions and Variants

The orisha preside over Santeria and the Afro-Brazilian traditions of Candomble, Umbanda, and Quimbanda (where the Portuguese spelling "orixa" is used). Many of the same spirits appear across these traditions. Names and spellings vary by location, and personalities may manifest somewhat differently, but the core nature of each spirit remains consistent. Oya, for example, Spirit of storm winds and the Niger River, keeps that name in Cuba but is known as Iansa in Brazil.

The lwa preside over Haitian Vodou, New Orleans Voodoo, and Dominican Vodo. ("Lwa" is the modern Kreyol spelling; older French texts use "loa.") While the lwa represent a largely distinct pantheon, a few spirits are shared with the orisha traditions, and the behavior and manifestations of both groups follow similar patterns.

Spirits Common Across the Diaspora

Certain spirits were so widely distributed across Africa that they appear in virtually all African Diaspora traditions. Eshu-Elegbara, the trickster Master of the Crossroads, and Ogun, Spirit and Embodiment of Iron, are two of the most prominent. Their names shift depending on location, but their core essence remains consistent.

Thousands of orisha are said to exist, though only approximately forty maintain active interest in human affairs.

How Orisha and Lwa Operate

Vodou and Santeria are monotheistic faiths centered on a supreme creator deity. In Yoruba tradition, Olodumare created the orisha to supervise creation. Each orisha or lwa governs specific domains of life, and every area of life has its own presiding spirit. Each person also has presiding orisha or lwa, typically one male and one female, known as the "masters of your head," who serve as patrons, protectors, and advocates.

Each spirit has a distinct personality along with specific colors, numbers, foods, plants, and objects that carry its essence. Spells invoking a particular spirit draw upon these correspondences. Oshun, Spirit of Love and Beauty, is associated with the color yellow, the number five, water, cinnamon, and honey. Oya is associated with the color purple and the number nine. Spirits communicate through these same symbols and correspondences, and this system can be applied when working with spirits from other pantheons as well.

The Seven African Powers

The orisha most actively involved in daily human life are sometimes invoked collectively as the Seven African Powers:

  1. Elegba
  2. Ogun
  3. Obatala
  4. Oshun
  5. Oya or Orunmila (varies by tradition)
  6. Chango
  7. Yemaya

Petitioning the group as a whole ensures comprehensive coverage of blessings and protections. Commercial Seven African Powers products often depict them in their syncretic guise as Roman Catholic saints.

Ritual Possession

The orisha and lwa also work with independent practitioners outside formal religious structures and have been incorporated into some Wiccan, Pagan, and Goddess traditions. However, ritual possession, in which a spirit uses a person as a medium, occurs only within formal religious settings. This is a shamanic practice requiring proper initiation and supervision, not a magick spell.

The Exus and Pomba Giras

Eshu-Elegbara as Gate Guardian

Eshu-Elegbara is traditionally the first spirit petitioned in any ritual or spell. Because he controls all doors and access to roads, he determines whether a petition will be blocked or will reach its intended recipient. Similar to the Greek god Hermes, devotees contact Eshu first, make offerings, then request that he invite and escort any other desired spirits. Some traditions bypass this step, but many consider initial contact with a gate guardian to be proper spiritual protocol.

Eshu manifests different aspects of himself depending on location and audience. In his original West African form, he appears young and handsome. In the Western Hemisphere, he more commonly takes the guise of a frail old man with a cane or a playful child.

The Brazilian Transformation

In Brazil, Eshu evolved into a distinct class of spirit: the exus (singular: exu, pronounced "Eh-shoo"). Powerful, volatile, and dangerous, the exus emphasize the extreme trickster aspects of the original spirit. Because exus are closer in nature to humans than the other orixa, they are the spirits most frequently petitioned for practical matters such as money and love.

Every orixa has a personal exu who serves as that spirit's messenger. All Afro-Brazilian spiritual paths include this concept by definition.

The Pomba Giras

The female counterparts of the exus are known as Pomba Giras (singular: exua, pronounced "Eh-shoo-ah," though Pomba Gira, meaning "whirling dove," is the more commonly used term). The Pomba Giras represent a fusion of West African spirituality with Portuguese Romany traditions, as Romani people were deported to the Brazilian colonies during the same era as the African slave trade.

The most prominent Pomba Gira is Maria Padilha, a deified historical figure: Maria de Padilla, wife of Pedro the First of Castile and Leon. She also appears in European magick traditions.

Working with Exus and Pomba Giras

Beyond their role as orixa messengers, exus and Pomba Giras can be petitioned independently, particularly for workings that the orixa themselves may decline to perform.

Perception of these spirits varies by tradition. From African or Pagan perspectives, exus and Pomba Giras are no more volatile than many other spirits, and Maria Padilha in particular is recognized as a being of great power and generosity. Within traditions influenced by Roman Catholicism, exus are sometimes associated with the Christian devil, with emphasis on qualities like crossroads encounters and the scent of brimstone.

The Pomba Giras prefer T-crossroads as gathering places. They favor working with women but will also work with men upon request.

Traditional Offerings

Exus traditionally receive plates of yellow manioc flour cooked or drizzled with oil. They drink wine, rum, and cachaca. Pomba Giras prefer flowers over food and favor anisette or champagne.

Djinn

The djinn are spirits of Arabia and North Africa whose origins predate Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. They have since traveled the world alongside Islam and can be found wherever that religion has been established. The word "djinn" (also spelled "jinn") derives from old Arabic and is thought to mean "covert" or "darkness." These are the spirits known in Western popular culture as genies.

Origin Stories

In one tradition, the djinn were created before humans to serve as intermediaries between angels and people. In another account, Adam and Eve had thirty children rather than just those named in scripture. When God asked to see them all, Eve brought out only fifteen and hid the rest. God declared that the hidden children would remain in shadow forever, while those presented would live in the light. The visible children became the ancestors of humanity; the hidden ones became the djinn and other spirits.

Nature and Temperament

Some djinn are benevolent and willing to help humans. Others are temperamental, treacherous, jealous, and consistently malevolent. Many djinn may be pre-Islamic divinities whose status was diminished over time. The prominent djinn Aisha Qandisha, for example, has been speculatively linked to the ancient goddess Astarte.

Unlike the gregarious orisha, djinn tend to be cautious, secretive, and quick to withdraw. They are most active at night and generally avoid daytime appearances.

Aversions and Preferences

Djinn hate salt and fear iron and steel, all of which can be used to expel them. They are attracted and pacified by storytelling. They prefer heat, deserts, natural springs, ruins, and wild places, and they despise cold and snow. Their traditional offering involves pouring oil over flour.

Spiritual Orientation

Djinn are believed to hold their own spiritual affiliations. There are reportedly Islamic, Jewish, Christian, and Pagan djinn, and each prefers to assist humans who share their orientation. Islamic djinn in particular are said to resent petitions from anyone other than devout Muslims.

The Gnawa Tradition

The human custodians most versed in djinn lore, including summoning, appeasing, dismissing, and ritually channeling them, are traditionally the Gnawa people of North Africa. The Gnawa (sometimes spelled Gnaua, believed to derive from "Ghana") are themselves descendants of enslaved sub-Saharan Africans. Their relationship to the djinn parallels in some ways the relationship between orisha devotees and their spirits.

Fairies

Fairy is a broad, somewhat generic category encompassing a vast range of spirits that may or may not be related. The category includes devas, flower fairies (miniature winged plant spirits), and human-sized Fairy Folk. Unlike "orisha" or "djinn," which refer to specific types of spirits, "fairy" functions as an umbrella term.

Types and Cultural Variants

Spirits classified under this category span many traditions: dakini from Tibet, apsaras from India, peri from pre-Islamic Iran, Eastern European vila, and Romany keshalyi, urme, and ursitory. Some of the more beautiful female djinn are also sometimes categorized as fairies.

What connects these diverse spirits are shared associations with wild nature, forests, flowers, love, sexuality, women's power, and the birth process.

Fairies as Ritual Judges

Fairies often function as enforcers of proper ritual behavior. They reward those who conduct rituals correctly and punish those who do not. The vila, for instance, are known to punish deceitful men and those who abandon commitments. In the tale of Sleeping Beauty, the offended fairy's wrath stems from an improperly set offering table with an incorrect number of place settings.

This reflects a broader dynamic in spirit relationships: once a mutual relationship is established, the spirit expects continued offerings and interaction. With the rise of European Christianity, many of these customary payments and tributes ceased, leaving formerly honored spirits without sustenance.

Demotion of Deities to Fairy Status

Many once-powerful spirits were demoted to fairy status as Christianity expanded, particularly in Ireland. Aine, a powerful solar spirit, came to be classified as a Queen of Fairy, as did Maeve. These spirits retained their power despite the diminished classification.

In parts of Europe, particularly France, witches were accused of consorting with fairies rather than with the devil. During the French witch craze (roughly from the era of Joan of Arc through the end of the seventeenth century), a conviction for fairy association carried a sentence of hard labor. Attempts were even made to depict Joan of Arc as a devotee of the Fairy Folk during her heresy trial.

The Romany Connection

Anthropologists and historians have noted parallels between descriptions of fairies and early European encounters with the Romany: nomadic people dwelling in forests, associated with magick and divination, described as dark and small among predominantly tall, fair populations. Both groups share accusations of child theft in folklore. The Romany themselves maintain their own complex fairy traditions in which fairies are clearly spiritual beings.

Elementals and Related Spirits

Other spirit types sometimes grouped alongside fairies include elementals (salamanders, undines, and similar beings) and mermaids, all of which may be summoned to assist in spell-casting.

Offerings and Attraction

Full-sized fairies are said to prefer milk and berries. Thyme is strongly associated with fairy attraction. Flower fairies, the butterfly-sized winged nature spirits, can be petitioned to bestow and enhance botanical powers. They are drawn to gardens containing birdbaths, water sources, charms, statues, witch balls, and crystals. Plants they favor include berries, chamomile, Corsican mint, forget-me-nots, foxglove, hibiscus, hollyhocks, honeysuckle, lavender, lilac, milkweed, morning glories, pansies, peonies, primroses, vincas, and violets. Fairies generally prefer wildflowers over cultivated blooms.

A circle of ash saplings serves as a fairy dance ground. Circles made from clear quartz crystals work as an alternative. Stinging nettles are said in Romany tradition to guard the doorways to fairyland. Burning equal parts dried hollyhock and rosemary as incense outdoors attracts flower fairies.

Saints

Deification and Sainthood

The line between spirit and human is not always clear. Many spirits across traditions, from the orisha to figures of ancient Greece and Hawaii, may be deified humans. Chango, for instance, was once a king in Yorubaland who was deified after death and took his place among the orisha. The ancient Greeks demonstrated this process when Heracles and Psyche, both originally mortal, were permitted to enter the divine realm.

Saints, however, are definitively human in origin. Although the term is most strongly associated with Roman Catholicism, concepts of sainthood exist across many cultures, including African Diaspora, Buddhist, Jewish, and Muslim traditions.

Criteria for Sainthood

Roman Catholic sainthood requires a lengthy, bureaucratic process of proving miraculous deeds through official beatification and canonization. Other traditions use different criteria. In many cultures, a person whose magickal power (known as heka in Egyptian tradition, baraka in Islamic and North African traditions) is so potent that it persists after death, remaining accessible for healing and magick, is recognized as a saint. This is typically an informal process: word of miracles spreads, shrines appear, and practitioners gather.

The behavior of these saints is not always exemplary. Some are described as devout and charitable, while others display what might be called excessive tendencies. Regardless, the saint's power remains accessible to those in need.

Marie Laveau

Marie Laveau, born in 1792 and known as the Pope of Voodoo, has attained this form of sainthood. Thousands visit her grave in New Orleans annually to petition for favors. She holds a strong reputation for resolving legal difficulties, as she did during her lifetime. The traditional method of contact involves knocking three times on the front of her tomb or drawing three x's in red brick dust or chalk on the stone. Common offerings include salt water or seven dimes.

Saints in Magickal Practice

The intersection of sainthood and magick, sometimes called "folk Catholicism," has existed for centuries. Several Vatican-approved saints are frequently invoked in magick spells, including Saint Anthony, San Cipriano, Saint Martha the Dominator, Saint George, and John the Baptist. When invoked for magick, saints are treated like any other spirit: offerings and payment are made for miracles requested and received. Each saint has favored numbers, colors, fragrances, and gifts.

A saint's magickal associations may diverge significantly from their official hagiography. Saint Anthony, for example, appears in nearly as many love spells as Aphrodite.

Unofficial Saints

Unofficial saints are those recognized for consistent post-mortem miracles without official Church approval. This phenomenon is tied specifically to the Roman Catholic tradition, which is the only system requiring a formal bureaucratic process for conferring sainthood. In traditions without official criteria, such as Judaism, all saints are effectively unofficial, with popularity and demonstrated power serving as their validation.

Unofficial saints may be accessed in magick spells in the same manner as any other spirit.

Identification and Syncretism

Syncretism is the process by which one spirit is identified or fused, to varying degrees, with another. Although most commonly associated with modern African Diaspora faiths, the practice extends back thousands of years.

Ancient Origins

When the ancient Greeks began to travel and encountered other cultures with their own pantheons, they developed a system of identification. Rather than accept entirely foreign spirits, they looked for correspondences with their own deities. Hathor, the Egyptian Spirit of love with an affinity for perfume and music, was declared to be Aphrodite. The Persian Anahita, a deity of romance and fertility who also possessed a martial aspect, was identified as both Aphrodite and Athena.

This process attempts to locate one spirit within another based on shared domains and attributes. Sometimes the identification is clean and intuitive. Other times it creates confusion, as spirits rarely map onto each other in a one-to-one fashion.

Syncretism Under Persecution

Syncretism goes a step further than identification. One spirit wears the mask of another. When a pantheon is outlawed, devotees continue their practice by presenting their spirits in the guise of acceptable ones.

This is precisely what occurred among enslaved Africans in the Western Hemisphere. Forbidden from practicing their own religions but permitted Roman Catholic chromolithographs of saints, they searched the images for coded references to the orisha and lwa. Identifications were often made quickly and visually.

Some of these pairings work remarkably well. Ogun, Spirit of Iron, was syncretized with the Archangel Michael because Michael's most famous image shows him wielding a sword. The two share genuine common ground: both are tireless warriors on behalf of human safety, and Michael carries his own associations with iron.

Other pairings are more unexpected. Chango, the intensely virile Spirit of Fire and Lightning, was syncretized with the virgin martyr Saint Barbara because her chromolithograph depicts a lightning bolt.

Elegba, the road-opening trickster, was syncretized with Saint Peter on account of Peter's keys.

The Fluidity of Spirits

Spirits are fluid in nature, and shape-shifting comes naturally to them even without deliberate syncretism. India's Durga is an aspect of Parvati. In a moment of extreme crisis, Durga unleashed Kali, her own alter ego. All three are aspects of a single being, yet all three are also distinct entities.

The first generation to engage in syncretism is fully conscious of the process. After that, the lines blur. At what point do the spirits genuinely fuse? Saint Peter, syncretized with Elegba because of his keys, may have effectively become Elegba, or the reverse. After several generations, the original spirit behind the mask may no longer be remembered, yet the magickal behavior persists.

Syncretism From Above

Syncretism did not always originate with the oppressed. Religious authorities sometimes deliberately presented it to make a new faith more palatable. The Celtic Spirit Brigid, known as the Druid's daughter, became identified with Saint Brigid. The two merged so thoroughly that distinguishing where one ends and the other begins is nearly impossible. The Irish solar spirit Aine was demoted to a Queen of Fairy, remaining accessible to old devotees in a diminished role. Maeve underwent the same transformation.

Sometimes this process backfired. Missionaries in Guatemala attempted to syncretize the spirit Maam with Saint Simon. The resulting figure, Maximon (also known as Brother Simon), a spirit of primal male energy, defied all boundaries and took on a life of his own. When the Church then attempted to associate him with Judas Iscariot or the devil, the outlaw image only deepened his devotees' loyalty. Rather than merging with an official saint, Maximon emerged as a powerful unofficial saint in his own right.

Hidden Spirits

Sometimes syncretism occurred so long ago that the original spirit underneath has been entirely forgotten. The only indication that syncretism may have taken place is when a saint behaves in notably un-saintly ways within magickal practice. This applies especially to the three saints most prominent in magickal Catholicism: Saint Anthony, Saint George, and John the Baptist. Many practitioners believe that beneath their respective masks lie Hermes, Baal, and Adonis.

Santeria itself takes its name, "religion of the saints," from syncretism. Some practitioners emphasize the Roman Catholic side, others the African roots, and for many, the saint and the orisha have fused so completely that separation is no longer possible.

Working with Deities

A practical guide to establishing relationships with gods and goddesses, understanding ethical considerations, and approaching divine beings with respect.

Simple Rules for Working with Divine Beings

Don't Mix Pantheons Carelessly

Try not to mix pantheons in a single working. If you have a working relationship with deities from pantheons that have a tumultuous past, you know your own practice best. However, just slapping names on a candle can have disastrous results, especially if the cultures represented had wars over it.

Build Relationships First

If you're going to work with the gods, get to know them. Develop a relationship with the deities that carry a deeper meaning for you. It will make your magick more effective, it can deepen your personal practice, and it helps practitioners stay within appropriate bounds and keep from infringing on Black or Indigenous cultures who have already lost so much. Besides, in doing your magickal homework, perhaps you will meet the divine of your dreams and find a way to build relationships.

Deity Work is Optional

Just know that gods and spirits are not a mandatory part of magick. If you're:

  • Uncomfortable working with gods outside of the religion you were raised with (if any), or
  • Concerned about trampling on someone else's faith expression or practice, or
  • Atheist

...that is okay. Magick works without deity involvement.

Practice Ethical Self-Examination

Examining one's own inherent prejudices, feelings, and any potential bias is what makes for responsible, ethical witches.

Etiquette for Working with Deities

Certain rules apply when working with divine helpers, as in any relationship:

  • Ask for assistance - Guides, guardians, and deities respect your free will and may not intervene unless invited to do so.
  • Show respect - Treat deities as honored teachers and allies, not servants.
  • Avoid micromanaging - When seeking aid from divine beings, turn over the reins and allow them to carry out your request as they see fit.
  • Do not seek help for harmful purposes - Benevolent deities will not support harmful causes, and you do not want to attract malevolent entities.
  • Express gratitude - Thank the beings who assist you and consider giving them an offering.

Ways to Attract Divine Assistance

Deities may come to you in dreams, meditation, or visions. Throughout history, countless people have experienced visitations from divine beings. Such appearances can happen to anyone, anytime.

If spontaneous contact does not occur, other methods can catch a deity's attention:

  • Research thoroughly - Learn as much as possible about the deity you wish to attract through myths, spiritual literature, and folklore.
  • Create a dedicated altar - Set up and dedicate an altar to your chosen deity.
  • Display sacred imagery - Collect and display artwork depicting the deities you wish to petition in a prominent place.
  • Make appropriate offerings - Discover what specific deities prefer (particular plants, foods, stones) and place these on your altar or in a special outdoor location.
  • Stay receptive - Keep an open mind and heart when working with deities. Trust your intuition to tune into higher frequencies.
  • Cultivate belief - Trust that deities will communicate with you. Doubt closes the door between you and divine beings. When dealing with supernatural forces, you'll see it when you believe it.

Protocol for Established Traditions

When working with deities from living traditions (Tibetan Buddhism, Vodou, Santería, Hinduism, etc.), respect existing protocols. Seek proper initiation or empowerment where required. Do not innovate or combine incompatible systems.

Deities tied to specific cultural and religious contexts carry the full weight of those systems. Working with deities from closed practices requires proper entry into those systems.

Study the tradition thoroughly or work with qualified initiates.

The Reciprocal Relationship

What do deities gain from this arrangement? Relationships with divine beings are reciprocal. Devotees provide veneration, offerings, and attention; deities provide guidance, protection, and assistance. Either party may initiate contact. Deities sometimes appear in dreams or visions to offer their patronage voluntarily.

This exchange is not transactional in a cold sense, it is relational. The most powerful working relationships develop over time through consistent devotion, not single requests made in crisis.

Finding Your Deities

Many practitioners feel called to specific deities. Pay attention to:

  • Recurring themes - Do certain myths, symbols, or cultures keep appearing in your life?
  • Ancestral connections - What did your ancestors worship? These connections can be powerful.
  • Personal resonance - Whose stories move you? Which deities do you find yourself thinking about?
  • Signs and synchronicities - Repeated encounters with a deity's symbols, animals, or imagery may indicate their interest in you.

Some practitioners work with a single patron deity. Others maintain relationships with multiple deities from one or more pantheons. Your practice should fit your needs and circumstances.

When Deities Don't Respond

Sometimes requests go unanswered. Possible reasons include:

  • The deity is not the right match for you or your request
  • Your approach was inappropriate for that tradition
  • The timing is wrong
  • What you requested is not in your best interest
  • You haven't built sufficient relationship yet

Don't take silence as rejection. Consider approaching differently, choosing a different deity, or examining whether your request truly serves your highest good.

Color Magick Practices

The History and Symbolism of Color

Colors are proven to have a profound effect on the human psyche and on our moods. They resonate with the elements, the directions, the seasons, the planets, and astrological signs as well as holding huge significance in their own right.

Colors and particular shades of them confer an immediate identity and make a strong statement. For example, in the green, purple, and white of the Suffragettes (green for hope, purple for dignity, and white for purity), or in the red and white stripes of the old-fashioned barber's pole (where the white represented the color of flesh and the red was the blood sometimes drawn by the cut-throat razor).

The significance of colors is proven by the high value that our ancestors placed on certain plants or substances that could be made into dyes, such as the Imperial Purple of Rome that was produced from a mollusk valued more highly than gold, or the saffron crocus that produced the sacred color of the same name. Prior to the development of chemical dyes, the creation of colors that did not fade in the Sun or wash away was a combination of art, science, and magick, akin to an alchemical process.

The impact of the Sun shining through stained glass, painting the interiors of churches with living colors that shimmered and danced, in a medieval world where color was often a privilege of the wealthy few, can only be imagined. Warriors in Ancient Britain daubed themselves in blue pigments in order to look more fearsome to their enemies. The power of red was once so powerful that corpses were daubed in red ochre in the belief that the color had the same life-giving properties as blood.

The seven colors of the rainbow, which break down into 700 shades visible to the naked eye, are associated with the seven planets, the days of the week, the Seven Heavens, and the seven notes of the musical scale.

The Power of Color

Color therapy operates on the principle that colors create beneficial effects on different organs and systems in the body. By exposing yourself to specific colors, you can support healing, shift emotional states, and align your energy with your intentions.

Practitioners often do this instinctively, wearing green after a breakup to encourage forward movement, or choosing red when confidence is needed. Color therapy simply brings this natural tendency into conscious practice.

A note on black:

Black has many negative connotations to the general public like death, mourning. To witches, however, black is a color of power, for it contains all the other colors. It's also reminiscent of mystery and the night, the time when witches often gather to work magick. In spellworking, black is associated with the planet Saturn and used for banishing, endings, and inner strength.

Practical Applications

Wearing Color

The most direct way to work with color energy is through clothing:

  • Red for energy, courage, and confidence
  • Violet to enhance divine connection
  • Green for healing and moving forward

If a needed color doesn't suit your outfit or situation, wear it as an undergarment or carry a swatch of fabric in your pocket.

Candle Magick

Burning colored candles infuses your space with specific energies:

  • Red candles build confidence for challenging situations
  • Yellow candles encourage outgoing, conversational energy at gatherings
  • Violet candles create introspective, meditative atmospheres

Choose candles intuitively based on what feels right, or deliberately select colors that align with your needs.

Methods for Identifying Needed Colors

Physical Color Collection

Create a set of color samples, one for each rainbow color plus white and black. Sources include:

  • Hand-painted cardboard squares
  • Magazine clippings
  • Paint manufacturer color charts
  • Colored tiles or fabric swatches

Practice: Sit quietly with your collection. Notice which color draws you without conscious decision. This is what your body needs. Gaze at the chosen color for 20-30 minutes, breathing deeply and allowing your system to absorb its energy. Your body signals completion when you feel restless or lose interest.

Daily variation: Each morning, choose the color tile that resonates and keep it visible throughout your day. The color works both when you actively look at it and when you absorb it subliminally while working.

Imagination Method

When physical samples aren't available, work with color through visualization:

  1. Close your eyes and mentally go through each color
  2. Ask yourself: "Do I need more red? Orange? Yellow?" and so on
  3. When you identify the right color, imagine breathing it in as pure light
  4. Continue until you feel saturated with that color's energy

This technique works as effectively as physical samples once you've familiarized yourself with the practice.

Pendulum Dowsing

Use a pendulum to identify which colors your body needs:

  1. Establish responses: Hold your pendulum and determine which movements indicate "yes," "no," "I don't know," and "I don't want to answer"
  2. Test accuracy: Ask questions you know the answers to (e.g., "Am I male?")
  3. Query colors: Systematically ask if you need each color: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet
  4. Note results: You may need multiple colors depending on your current state

Once the pendulum reveals your needs, absorb those colors through any of the methods described.

Key Principles

Colors affect practitioners constantly, whether consciously acknowledged or not. The difference between color therapy and everyday life is simply awareness and intention.

Physical exposure (wearing, viewing, surrounding yourself) works powerfully, but imagination and visualization can be equally effective once you've trained your sensitivity.

Your body knows what it needs. Trust the colors you're drawn to, through intuition, pendulum, or simple attraction, and absorb their energies through whichever method feels most natural to you.

Closing Reflection

The world is vibrant with color, each hue carrying its own energy, medicine, and teaching. While you may naturally gravitate toward certain colors, every color has value and purpose.

Some colors resonate based on personal preference. Others connect through name, birth date, and astrological correspondences, becoming personal colors that carry special significance in magickal and healing work.

Color and Moon Magick

While silver and white are most commonly associated with the moon, color in magickal practice is tied to both celestial bodies and general energetic themes. There is no universal rule. Card Grimoire

How Cartomancy Works

Cartomancy, like all forms of divination, operates within a framework of internal logic. The details of this framework vary across cultures, but the underlying principles share common ground that the subconscious mind responds to. The most important of these principles, and the primary concept behind sortilege (divination by drawing lots), is synchronicity.

Synchronicity

Synchronicity acknowledges connections between simultaneous events that have no determinable correlation with each other. In both magick and divination, synchronicity is attributed to the idea that all things are connected.

This principle comes into play in many modes of divination, not only in all varieties of sortilege but also in theriomancy (divination by observing the movements of birds and animals) and astrology. Animals and birds are not scrambling around to deliver coded messages. They are part of the ever-unfolding universe, part of the great universal pattern of becoming. The theriomancer's task is to discern shifts in that pattern by observing the movements and behaviors of various creatures.

Astrologers do not claim that stars influence our lives. The signs of the zodiac are named for twelve constellations but are not the constellations themselves. The zodiac consists of twelve equal sectors of the sky, each precisely thirty degrees in the 360-degree celestial circle surrounding our world. Astrologers observe the patterns of the planets as they move through these sectors. Gravitational fields are irrelevant. The visible planets, like everything else, are part of the unfolding universe, part of the divine pattern that connects all things.

When practicing cartomancy, the cards drawn at random are also part of this great pattern. Just as the zodiac gives meaning to planetary movements, the reader provides context for the cards they draw. That context can be as simple as a single daily card or as complex as a twelve-card layout, but synchronicity is the underlying principle regardless of how the cards are drawn and placed.

Intuition

Good readers do not rely on synchronicity alone. They also rely on intuition. Every language is limited in what ideas it can convey through its vocabulary, and playing cards have a vocabulary of only fifty-two "words." The advantage of playing cards is that their imagery is abstract, making each card far more open to interpretation.

Let the cards speak. This can be difficult at first while learning to associate each card with a general interpretation, but it gets easier with familiarity. If a particular card seems to mean something other than what published sources suggest or what its numerological and elemental correspondences would indicate, go with instinct.

Cards may also take on variant meanings to better reflect the reader's age and environment. If a card consistently communicates something different from its standard interpretation, do not be afraid to follow that intuition. Trust your instincts.

A variant meaning can also appear as a one-time occurrence. Perhaps the Five of Spades usually indicates unexpected obstacles, but during one reading, a strong impression arises that something fun and exciting will soon happen. This is something normally expected from Diamonds or Hearts, but if that is what the Five of Spades is communicating in that moment, trust that sixth sense.

The Personal Card

Some readers have a personal card that represents themselves. This card most often indicates the reader only when they are the querent. When reading for another person, it typically carries its ordinary meaning. However, if intuition insists the personal card represents the reader regardless of who the reading is for, follow that instinct.

Keeping Imagination in Check

While it is important to listen to the sixth sense, it is equally important not to let imagination run wild. Keeping a journal of readings can help. Watch for personal bias. If most readings seem to involve the same theme over and over, personal desires may be interfering with true seership.

The journal does not need to be elaborate. Once the reader is comfortable trusting their intuition, the journal can be set aside, but it is an extremely helpful tool when first learning to read cards.

Developing a Relationship with the Deck

A good reader develops their own relationship with the cards over time. This is reflected in the decks they use, any unique interpretations they develop, and how and where they choose to read. For some, cartomancy is a private and personal activity. Others are comfortable reading at gatherings, fairs, or for anyone who asks. Some readers practice only in a quiet, secluded space, while others can draw cards anywhere.

Approach the cards with respect. If they are treated like a parlor game, that is exactly what they will become.

The Daily Card

When beginning to work with cards, draw a single card each morning. Do not immediately look up its meaning. First ask what, if anything, the card is saying. Consider both the suit and the numerological significance, but trust intuition as well. Only then look up the meaning if it does not come to mind.

Keep the card in mind throughout the day. How does it apply to the events unfolding around you? Unless the same routine is followed every day, the cards will shift their meanings to adapt to activities and environment. What a card reveals depends partly on where you are, who you are, and what your immediate plans are. If there is no chance of meeting anyone that day, a court card that normally represents a specific type of person might instead speak to a quality the querent needs to cultivate in themselves. This is where intuition comes into play.

Drawing a daily card builds familiarity with the deck. Even after mastering every card's meaning, a daily single-card reading helps maintain and sharpen the skill.

How Often to Read

As a general guideline, allow one day per card drawn before repeating a reading for the same person. A single card can be drawn every day. A three-card reading should not be repeated for the same querent until three days have passed. A twelve-card reading should be spaced at least twelve days apart, though many readers prefer to wait two or three months between full readings.

These are minimums. Reading too frequently for the same person causes the messages to break down into a garbled mess. However, this applies per querent: there is no reason not to give twelve-card readings to five different people in one sitting, since each person is only receiving one reading. Likewise, drawing three cards for one question does not prevent drawing three more later that day for an entirely different issue.

Building a Practice Routine

For solo practice, consider this schedule:

  • Daily: One-card reading each morning
  • Weekly: Past-present-future reading on a specific day and time (such as Friday evenings or Sunday afternoons). Write down the interpretation to refer back to as the week unfolds.
  • Quarterly: A twelve-card reading, timed with something meaningful like a solstice or equinox, or simply on a set schedule.

Record interpretations in a journal, including any personal meanings that emerge over time.

Reading for Others

Practicing on other people is one of the best ways to gain experience, especially with complex layouts. Start with close friends or family who understand the learning process. Reading for others reveals how the same card shifts meaning depending on the querent's age, gender, relationships, and circumstances.

For those who do not have willing participants or who are not yet comfortable reading for others, try doing readings for people without their presence. Nothing seen in those cards should be shared with anyone, since consent was not given. Choose people of different ages and backgrounds to develop a feel for how the cards read for diverse querents.

If skill and demand eventually reach a point where charging for readings seems appropriate, research local regulations first. More importantly, be aware that accepting payment creates a conflict of interest. Querents become customers, and on some level there is now a motive to please rather than to read honestly. Some readers navigate this successfully, but it is a real obstacle to be aware of.

Choosing a Location

Reading at home offers the most control over the environment. Setting the stage before pulling out the cards is another way to prepare the mind, much like meditation or prayer. Choose a comfortable seat at an open working surface. If there is a particular chair or table that feels especially empowering, use it consistently. Over time, the simple act of sitting down in that chosen workspace will signal the mind to focus on divination.

Consider reading by candlelight. Turn off electric lighting and use a single white or beeswax taper candle for illumination. This directs attention to the immediate area where the cards are laid out and allows outside distractions to fade. Some readers use two or three candles for religious reasons, but one is sufficient.

Incense can also enhance the atmosphere. A simple divinatory blend: equal parts dried garden sage (Salvia officinalis) and dried rosemary (Rosmarinus officinalis), burned over a charcoal block. A few drops of nutmeg oil can be added for extra potency. This is more than necessary for a quick one-card or three-card draw, but it pairs well with a twelve-card reading. The same blend can be used to pass individual cards through the smoke, attuning them to the purpose of divination.

These are all aids, not necessities. Readings away from home may not allow candles or incense, and that is perfectly fine. Creating an empowering home environment does not confine the practice to that location. Readings can happen anywhere, as long as there is a deck of cards on hand.

Setting Boundaries

At gatherings, benefits, or parties where readings are offered, stay grounded. Take breaks and allow time to center between readings. There is no obligation to read for anyone who creates a feeling of discomfort. If that happens, lay out the cards, then simply say that no impressions are coming through. This allows a graceful exit without insulting the querent. There is an intimacy in looking at someone else's fortune, and it should never feel compelled.

Even on days when a morning card has already been drawn, new questions can arise later. If the morning's Four of Spades warned of an annoying day and now friends are inviting you out, draw another card to see if the energy has shifted. Think of it as a clarification card for the day itself.

With enough practice, the cards come alive and speak in ways that transcend any finite set of interpretations.

Ethics of Divination

When interpreting cards for another person, the reader looks beyond the ordinary exterior that person presents to the world. There is an intimacy to divination. For this reason, it is essential to set boundaries, both for the reader's protection and for the querent's. Readers who ignore the ethics of divination are likely to make enemies and develop bad reputations.

Personal Ethics and Boundaries

Tarot readers work without an international governing body or a shared code of ethics. There's no oath comparable to the Hippocratic Oath binding readers to a universal standard, so shaping a personal ethical framework is left to each individual. While no reader can control what a querent does with a reading afterward, understanding the weight that words carry within a reading remains a real responsibility.

Not every reader chooses to cover the same ground. Some feel comfortable answering any question a querent brings, believing it's their role to read whatever comes up. Others draw lines around specific topics, such as declining to speak to a medical diagnosis and instead referring the querent to a doctor while still exploring how they can build a healthier relationship with their body. Keeping a referral list of trusted professionals, lawyers, doctors, therapists, financial advisors, can help when a querent's needs fall outside what a reading can responsibly offer.

Suspected affairs are one of the more delicate situations a reader will eventually face. Consider in advance how a wrong read on that kind of question could affect a querent's relationship, and how you'd feel if it did.

Third-party readings, where a querent asks about someone who isn't present, such as an ex's current activities or a new partner's pregnancy, raise their own questions worth thinking through ahead of time.

Reading for children brings its own considerations. Most parents ask out of love and a genuine wish to know their child is okay, but it's worth deciding in advance how you feel about reading for an older teenager on their own, and whether you'd want a parent present for that kind of session.

These boundaries aren't fixed forever. As a reader's knowledge and experience grow, their sense of what they will and won't do often shifts too. As long as a reader stays aligned with their own inner compass and feels good about how they show up in a reading, that's the real measure of ethical practice.

Consent

Never read for anyone without their consent. Reading for someone is not the same as reading about someone. Even in solo readings, other people will appear in the cards. If the Five of Hearts and Seven of Spades suggest a new romance, someone else is obviously involved. In a twelve-card layout, at least a third of the cards almost always represent other people.

Drawing cards for absent people as a practice exercise is acceptable, but the reader is ethically bound not to share anything seen in those cards with others. The reading exists solely for skill development.

Likewise, if a personal reading reveals something about another person, that information should not be disclosed. If the cards suggest a partner is considering leaving, the reader can pay closer attention or have a conversation about the relationship, but cannot cite a card reading as the source of suspicion. People who understand divination know that a reader might pick up on things, but nobody wants to feel surveilled. Furthermore, not everyone wants to know what the future holds. Some find it uncomfortable, and others object for personal or spiritual reasons.

The Power of Words

Words carry weight. When giving a reading, the reader must avoid manipulating the querent in any way. Everyone has a personal agenda, things and outcomes they prefer over others. The ancient Delphic teaching to "know thyself" is crucial here. An ethical reader is mindful of their own biases and takes care not to let them color the reading. The goal is to help the querent, never to steer them.

Using a reading to pursue personal interests, such as implying a romantic connection with a querent, is a severe breach of ethics that accomplishes nothing beyond damaging the reader's reputation.

Influences, Not Destiny

There is a world of difference between saying "your marriage is doomed" and saying "you may be facing some marital challenges in the near future." The first implies an unalterable fate, a futile existence without free will. The second simply suggests possible influences ahead.

Speaking in absolutes can become a self-fulfilling prophecy. Telling someone their marriage will fail does not help them. It may actively contribute to the failure. But overly optimistic absolutes are equally dangerous. Telling someone they will receive a promotion might lead them to stop putting in the effort required to earn it. There is a world of difference between "you are going to get a promotion" and "I see some very positive influences concerning your career."

The future is constantly unfolding from the present, shaped by actions and decisions. What divination reveals are probabilities, not certainties. An ethical reader always ensures the querent understands they have control over their own destiny.

Handling Difficult Readings

Sometimes the cards show what appears to be a crisis. In a twelve-card reading, the Four of Clubs in position 2 (resources) could indicate the querent is oblivious to what is happening around them. The Six of Spades in position 7 (partner) might show depleted energy in the relationship. The Queen of Diamonds in position 8 (partner's resources) could suggest another person with an agenda has a significant presence in the partner's life.

Superficially, this looks like infidelity. But the ethical reader does not blurt out that conclusion. First, there is the inevitable margin of error; the interpretation could be wrong. Second, expressing it bluntly could become a self-fulfilling prophecy, leading the querent to take actions that destroy a salvageable relationship. Third, the querent has the right to shape their own destiny.

Instead, suggest that the querent be mindful of the relationship and perhaps talk with their partner about how to strengthen it. Frame the other person's presence as something the querent can address. Express what the cards show as influences rather than fate, empowering the querent to take action rather than feel helpless.

It is equally important not to lie. If the cards clearly show something difficult, pretending everything is fine betrays the querent's trust. Honest framing, expressing challenges as influences that can be navigated, respects both the truth and the querent's autonomy.

The Margin of Error

Divination is not infallible. Sometimes predictions are completely wrong. Maybe the cards were interpreted incorrectly, or circumstances shifted. This margin of error is actually a good thing. It confirms that the future is not set in stone. If a reading shows challenges to a marriage, the querent can take steps to overcome them. A failed relationship is not a foregone conclusion.

If there were no influence over destiny, divination would be pure voyeurism. The entire point of reading cards is to illuminate the path so the querent can navigate it with greater awareness.

When to Decline a Reading

There is never an obligation to read for someone. Reasons to decline include:

  • The person is a skeptic who views divination as a joke or intends to disprove the reader's ability
  • Something about the person creates an uncomfortable feeling, even if it cannot be identified
  • The cards produce a result the reader does not feel equipped to share responsibly

In any of these cases, lay out the cards and then explain that no impressions are coming through. This exits the situation gracefully. If the person has paid for a reading (such as at a charity benefit), return the payment when declining.

If choosing to read for a skeptic, follow the same ethical guidelines as with any other querent.

Never Offer to Change the Future

As a card reader, the role is that of an observer. Never offer to help the querent alter their future through magickal means. This applies to querents who are not close friends or family. Anti-divination laws were originally enacted because of individuals who posed as readers and then "helped" their clients avoid misfortune, a scheme that inevitably involved relieving the client of a substantial sum of money. Offering spellwork to querents risks association with that kind of activity, regardless of intent.

Exercise Eight: Your Tarot Reading Ethics

These scenarios work as case studies for examining personal ethical standpoints on tarot. Each one presents a hypothetical situation or question posed by a pretend querent during a reading. Consider each question and reflect on how it would be handled.

Scenario One

Querent question: "My boyfriend recently broke up with me. I want to know what my current ex is doing and if he's with anyone else."

Scenario Two

Querent question: "I just interviewed for my dream job, and I know it's competitive. I want to know how I can get this job."

Scenario Three

A client arrives for a reading and brings her sister along. The sister isn't receiving a reading of her own, she simply wants to listen in. The client seems reserved, though, giving the impression that she may not want her sister present. How would this situation be handled?

Scenario Four

A querent explains that they've lost a family heirloom somewhere in their apartment and asks whether the tarot cards can help locate the missing item. What would the response be?

Scenario Five

Querent question: "Can the tarot cards tell me the winning lottery numbers?"

Scenario Six

Partway through a reading, a querent turns out to be seventeen years old. Would the reading continue? What minimum age requirement would apply going forward?

Scenario Seven

Querent question: "Am I going to get pregnant this year?"
