Rune Grimoire

Choosing Your Path

Selecting a runic system is a personal journey. You may resonate with one specific system or use different ones for various purposes. While ancestral connection is a common starting point, it is not the only criterion, especially for those without access to family histories. Runes are fluid constructs that transcend time, useful for navigating both the past and the present.

Exploring Ancestral Roots

Genealogy can be revealing but also challenging, potentially uncovering generational trauma. However, confronting these histories can open pathways to healing.

  • Reclaiming: For those whose lineages were disrupted or who feel disconnected, reclaiming a system can be empowering. It offers a sense of self and connection to the migrations that led to your current life.
  • Language & Naming: Understanding the origins of names and language impacts your interaction with the oracle. Just as marginalized groups reclaim language as an act of defiance, choosing a runic system can be an act of claiming personal power.
  • DNA Testing: While not 100% accurate, DNA tests can reveal general migration patterns. Comparing these with family stories can provide insight, though ancestry never prohibits you from using a system that calls to you.

A Starting Place: The Present Moment

If family records are lost, connect with your present environment.

  • The Land: Acknowledge the history of the land you occupy.
  • Migration: Consider your own life's movements. Frequent movers might resonate with the exploratory energy of Norse runes. Those deeply rooted in one place might find kinship with the tree-based Ogham runes.
🧭
The Vegvísir

This eight-rayed symbol, often associated with Vikings, is likely a modern reconstruction from the 1800s (appearing in the Huld manuscript). Despite its debated ancient origins, it has taken root in the collective consciousness as a powerful symbol of protection and guidance through "storms," both literal (climate change) and metaphorical.

Practical Experimentation

To determine which system calls to you, try writing your surname or magickal name in different scripts.

  1. Norse: Write phonetically from right to left along a horizontal stave.
  2. Ogham: Carve vertically from bottom to top along a central stave.
  3. Theban: Transcribe directly using the cipher alphabet.
  4. Witch Runes: Select symbols that feel poignant to your identity.

Observe which form pleases your eye and resonates with your soul.

Cultural Associations & Elemental Correspondences

Understanding the cultural "flavor" of a system can help align it with your personality or zodiac sign.

Norse Runes (Earth, Fire, Water)

  • Vibe: Powerful, mutable, transformational.
  • Best for: Those attracted to themes of creation, destruction, distant travel, and overcoming obstacles.
  • Elements: Volcanic fire (creation/transformation) and icy water (endurance/travel).

Ogham Runes (Air, Earth, Spirit)

  • Vibe: Cyclical, nature-based, reverent.
  • Best for: Those who see death as a rite of passage and are deeply connected to the earth and seasons.
  • Elements: Earth (inspiration/devotion) and Air (rapid change/growth).
  • Context: Druidic culture emphasized the cyclical nature of life and the connection to universal consciousness.

Witch Runes (Visual/Psychic)

  • Vibe: Intuitive, symbolic, direct.
  • Best for: Visually oriented practitioners and those developing psychic abilities.
  • Usage: Excellent for psychometry, talismans, and quick fortune-telling. Since they are non-alphabetic, they rely on pure symbolism rather than linguistics.

Understanding Energetic Properties

Before engaging with different energetic properties, you must first reclaim your power and understand your receptive abilities. Once you are self-aware, you can interpret the subtle energies inhabiting both the rune's material and its symbol.

Elemental Properties

  • Air: Ranges from gentle breezes of new growth to formidable winds of transformation and destruction.
  • Fire: Can be the illuminating candle flame or the raging wildfire that reduces substances to their purest form. Represents change through redirection or destruction.
  • Water: Manifests as nourishing rain or deep, unknowable mysteries and complex emotions.
  • Earth: The life-giver and repository for generations, sustaining all life and absorbing it back in death.

Runes and Divination

Divining is subtle work requiring active engagement. Like thermodynamics, energy is transferred from the rune maker to the object, and between the petitioner and the source.

Source Points:

  • Spiritual: Deities (Goddess/God)
  • Ancestral: Spirits of ancestors
  • Secular: Elemental confluences or the subconscious self

The Magickal Force: Your magick is the "outside force" (inertia) that sets things in motion.

Energetic Principles

Identify your energetic source to establish a clear connection.

1. Spiritual Energy:

  • For witches on an initiatory path.
  • Involves invocations to deities, directions, and elements.
  • Practice: Dedicate rune sets as formal pathworking or explore pantheons (Norse, Celtic, Greek) to find resonance.

2. External Energy:

  • For witches focused on wellness, weather, and environment (Green/Hedge/Kitchen witches).
  • Based on elemental and ancestral energy rather than formal deity worship.
  • Practice: Use runes in the presence of elemental representations (candle, water, salt) to establish a link.

3. Internal Energy:

  • For secular or solitary witches relying on intuition.
  • Requires high levels of self-examination.
  • Practice: Engage in meditation to clear the mind. Treat the oracle as a trusted confidant or ancestor. If needed, seek a like-minded partner for objectivity.

Pathways and Choice

Modern practitioners (Heathens, Druids, Wiccans) all use runes for divination, drawing from reconstructed traditions or personal gnosis.

Gnosis: Empirical spiritual knowledge gained through personal experience rather than books or lore. When multiple practitioners receive the same messages independently, it validates without requiring published sources.

Three Pathways:

  1. Solitary Secular Practitioner:
    • Read for yourself or others for personal guidance.
    • Rely on intuition and instinct.
    • Choose your system by preference, affinity, or how you wish to be perceived.
  2. Tradition, Craft, or Practice:
    • Use runes ritualistically alongside psychometry, meditation, and astrology.
    • System chosen through elder knowledge, ancestral origins, or cultural affiliation.
  3. Initiatory Path:
    • Runes as conduits to higher spiritual powers.
    • Incorporated into coven work with reverence for deity, nature, and oracle.
    • Techniques: Grounding and centering before readings, cleansing runes before and after, invoking guiding powers.

Conclusion: Consciously choosing your energetic properties and pathway empowers you as a rune-master. The depth of your practice depends on your preferences, needs, aptitude, and ability. The only wrong way to use runes is as pure entertainment with disregard for their origin, historical application, and modern power.

Reclaim Your Power as a Witch

Runes bring the past alive while empowering the present. Reclaiming runes is a valid exercise for any witch, regardless of tradition. Whether you follow an initiatory path or an unconstrained spiritual practice, there is no wrong way to experience magick.

  • Historical Context: Witches were once feared and persecuted for their perceived threat, healing abilities, or nonconformity. Using runes connects you to this lineage of power and divination, a staple of occult practice for millennia.

1. Declare Your Power

The first step is acknowledgment. Even in initiatory paths, true initiation comes from the Gods and personal transformation. The outward trappings merely honor the internal shift. Acknowledge yourself as a creator of magick. No one else can declare when you have awakened.

2. Own Your Power

Be true to yourself as an ethical learner. Tap into your sources of power by attuning with moon phases and practicing mindfulness. Be honest about your psychic strengths, whether empathy, clairvoyance, or other abilities, and embrace them.

3. Use Your Power

Power is multifaceted. Approach it as an expression of your highest aspiration for the good of all. Never confuse "empowerment" with "power over others."

  • Responsibility: Extend your seeking of autonomy to all beings. Avoid creating chaos or imbalance.
  • Safety: If celebrating fire festivals, take precautions. Understand your strength in both the physical and metaphysical worlds.
🔥
The New Burning Times

The witch hunts of the 16th and 17th centuries persecuted many who were not actual witches. As your understanding of humanity grows, so should your acceptance of "otherness." Acknowledge modern equivalences of persecution based on actions or appearance as part of your path.

Witch Runes

Witch runes differ significantly from stave runes (like Norse and Ogham) in both form and symbolism. They consist of thirteen pictographic symbols, often painted or inscribed on round tiles or stones. Along with the Theban alphabet, they are one of the two systems of writing and divination most strongly associated with modern witchcraft.

Origins and History

While their exact origins remain unknown, this system of folk magick was popularized in the 1970s, largely due to Dana Corby and her work The Witches' Runes. Interest continued through the late 20th century with works like Susan Sheppard's A Witch's Runes.

  • Theories of Origin: Suggestions range from Eastern Europe to Northeastern Scotland.
  • Pictish Resemblance: The forms bear similarity to early carvings by the Scottish Picts.
  • Ancient Connections: The rudimentary designs resemble symbols found in Egyptian hieroglyphs, Slavic light symbols, and early Bronze Age carvings.

Symbolism and Associations

Witch rune symbols are pictographic, meaning their form often directly reflects their meaning (e.g., the Eye looks like an eye, Rings look like rings). This directness removes immediate secrecy but retains occult depth through context.

  • Celestial: Sun, Moon, Star.
  • Elemental: Flight (Air), Wave (Water), Harvest (Earth), Romance (Fire).
  • Polarity: Man and Woman reflect the duality seen in many traditions (Goddess/Consort), though gendered polarity is not a prerequisite for modern practice.
  • Protection: The Eye serves as a talisman and ward.
  • Fate: Scythe, Crossroads, and Rings connect heavily to predictive magick.

Why Use Witch Runes?

Modern witches appreciate Witch runes for their adaptability and aesthetic appeal. They are among the most modern occult motifs, offering:

  • Versatility: Can be drawn on paper for charms/jars or inscribed on candles.
  • Simplicity: Easier to interpret than alphabetic systems because they are pictographic (cannot spell names).
  • Directness: Simple forms allow for quick understanding and visual parity.

Divination Methods

Psychometric Divination (Pendulum Work)

  1. Setup: Arrange all 13 runes in a 6-inch circle (Sun at 12 o'clock).
  2. Connect: Ground yourself and hold a pendulum over the empty center. Establish "yes" and "no" movements.
  3. Ask: Speak your question/intention aloud to create vibrational energy.
  4. Probe: Move the pendulum over specific runes to gauge positive or negative influence based on the pendulum's response.

Holding Space (Casting)

  1. The Vessel: Cup your hands (palms not touching) with runes inside to create an energetic opening.
  2. The Focus: Instead of a direct question, state the situation (e.g., "The issue is my relationship").
  3. The Breath: Repeat the issue three times while shaking the runes. Exhale deliberately into your hands, then drop them.
  4. Interpretation:
    • Dominant Rune: The first one you notice.
    • Guide Rune: The one farthest away.
    • Combinations: Runes touching each other modify meanings (e.g., Scythe + Flight = fast ending; Eye + Wave = healing/forgiveness).

Uses in Magick

  • Divination & Psychometry: Used for readings and reading object energy, though spreads are often less complex than those for Elder Futhark.
  • Spellwork: Ideal for casting spells, scribing candles, and emblazoning charms.
  • Grimoire Work: Used to add context and embellishment to magickal records.
  • Secrecy: Historically, esoteric symbols allowed witches to record spells and communicate safely during times of persecution, acting as ciphers for the craft.

Theban Runes

The Theban alphabet, also known as the Runes of Honorius, originated in the medieval period. While its precise roots remain unclear, it is attributed to Honorius of Thebes and first appeared in Book Three of Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa's Three Books of Occult Philosophy. Agrippa's work was a cornerstone of Renaissance discourse, inextricably linking magick and religion.

Agrippa's Feminism

Agrippa was a revolutionary voice against the misogyny of his time. His 1529 publication, Declamation on the Nobility and Preeminence of the Female Sex, challenged the deep-seated patriarchal belief in the inferiority of women, establishing him as a significant early feminist figure.

Aesthetics and Modern Usage

Next to Norse runes, the Theban alphabet is the most widely used system in modern witchcraft. Its graceful curves and complex patterns contrast with the rudimentary staves of earlier rune systems, showing unmistakable Indo-European influences.

Application in the Craft

Theban runes are prized for their elegance and their utility in maintaining secrecy. They are frequently used in grimoires to:

  • Label and consecrate tools
  • Create and record spells and charms
  • Record memories
  • Dedicate objects for special use

Ogham Runes

Druidic Mystery and Oral Tradition

The Druids, a Celtic class of priests and mystics, left no written manuscripts. They revered nature and passed traditions orally. Consequently, modern Druidry is a reconstruction. This evolution does not invalidate the practice; like language, tradition fluxes and refines over time.

History of the Ogham Runes

Theories on Ogham origins vary. Some suggest it arose after the biblical fall of the Tower of Babel. Others propose early Irish Christians created it to conceal communications from Latin-reading rivals, or simply as a symbol of Irish distinctiveness.

While some scholars argue Ogham was purely written, poet Robert Graves suggested it had phonetic equivalents and functioned as a spoken language. This aligns with the oral nature of Druidic mystery.

Structure and Meaning

Ogham script consists of hash marks or tallies etched along a central line.

  • Fews (Feda): The individual characters.
  • Aicme: Families of five letters, united by a common motif.
  • Tree Ogham: Each letter is named for a specific tree, imbuing it with occult significance.
  • Calendar: The system functions as a calendar, with thirteen months associated with specific trees.

Robert Graves also theorized a system of hand gestures where finger parts corresponded to letters, creating a secret sign language.

Archaeological Evidence

Ogham dates back to at least the fourth century. Surviving examples appear on tombstones and in manuscripts like the Book of Ballymote.

  • Inscriptions: Often indicate possession or lineage (e.g., "Stone of [Name], son of [Name]").
  • Orientation: Early stone carvings read vertically from bottom to top. The Book of Ballymote presents them horizontally.

Modern Usage

Modern witches use these cipher-like symbols for divination, celebrating love and family, and marking property.

Using Ogham for Divination

Creating an Ogham Set:

Make an Ogham set by burning or painting the markings onto larger twigs, popsicle sticks, or pieces of dowel rod. These become your casting sticks. Toss them onto a casting cloth and interpret their positions and relationships.

The Casting Cloth:

A useful design features a circle divided into different sections, with each section pertaining to a different area of life: Health, Happiness, Relationships, Work, Home, and other areas meaningful to your practice.

Interpreting the Cast:

  • Sticks outside the circle: Remove first. Not relevant to the matter at hand.
  • Sticks touching other sticks: Most important. Their connection indicates a significant relationship between their meanings.
  • Sticks half in and half out: May reveal what is entering or leaving the current situation, energies in transition.
  • Sticks face down: Of minor input, present but not dominant influences.

Beyond Divination:

Ogham may also be used for sigil creation, talismans and amulets, and as markers around your space for protection or encouragement. Get to know the fews and Ogham sticks, familiarize yourself with their timing and the trees they represent, and they will soon become a magickal tool that is portable and profound.

Dream Grimoire

Dream Journaling

Dreams offer direct access to subconscious wisdom, future glimpses, and problem-solving insights. Ancient Babylonians believed spirits sent dreams to humans. Egyptians considered them divine gifts. The earliest recorded dream belongs to King Thotmes IV, carved on a granite tablet between the paws of the Sphinx.

Working with your dreams strengthens your intuition and improves spellwork.

Why Keep a Dream Journal

  • Process waking experiences. Dreams often rework daily events and reveal solutions.
  • Receive warnings. Some dreams prepare you for challenges ahead.
  • Spot opportunities. Future glimpses help you recognize and act on possibilities.
  • Identify patterns. Recurring themes reveal what your subconscious is processing.
  • Build rapport with your subconscious. The more you engage, the more your dreams reveal.

How to Record Dreams

  1. Prepare your tools. Keep your book of shadows and a pen within arm's reach of your bed.
  2. Write immediately upon waking. Capture images before they fade into daily busyness.
  3. Use shorthand. Complete sentences are unnecessary. Focus on key images, feelings, and details.
  4. Suspend judgment. Record everything without filtering or analyzing.

What to Document

  • People. Who appeared? Were they familiar or unknown?
  • Setting. Where did the dream take place?
  • Emotions. What did you feel during and after the dream?
  • Standout images. What symbols or objects drew your attention?
  • Date. Always timestamp your entries.
  • Waking context. Note relevant events happening in your life at the time.

Lucid Dreaming

Lucid dreaming allows you to become aware within a dream and direct its course. Developing this skill while asleep strengthens your ability to direct your waking life with intention.

Listening for Animal Spirits

Hearing Spirit's Second Song

Animals exist as both physical beings and spiritual guides. Beyond their material presence, they carry a "second song", a spiritual counterpoint that connects practitioners to necessary parts of the psyche and offers guidance through symbolic presence.

How to Tune In

Hearing an animal's second song begins with tuning in to the world around you. This means noticing not just what crosses your path, but what sparks your imagination or persistently tries to get your attention.

Physical encounters: An animal appearing unusually close, behaving strangely, or crossing your path in unexpected ways.

Subconscious presence: When an animal seeps into your daydreams, nighttime dreams, meditation, or shamanic journeys repeatedly.

Synchronicities in the physical world: Finding feathers, seeing photographs, noticing the animal on clothing or symbols, encountering representations in unexpected places.

Persistent patterns: When the same creature appears through multiple channels over time, it's time to take note.

Recognizing the Call

Sometimes an animal will reveal itself gradually, appearing first in one form (a dream), then another (a photo), then physically. Other times the encounter is immediate and striking: a falcon flying ten feet from your face, a snake appearing on your doorstep, a spider building a web in your workspace.

The key is awareness. Many encounters go unnoticed because attention is scattered or coincidence is assumed. When you begin to pay attention, patterns emerge.

Using This Grimoire

  1. Look up the animal in the Animal Database

Animal Grimoire

A Guide to Birds

Birds occupy a unique place in the magickal world. They move between earth and sky, bridging the ordinary and the unknown. When you look up at a bird in flight, something in you reaches upward too. That pull is not restlessness; it is aspiration. Watching birds encourages growth, curiosity, and the drive to become more than you were yesterday.

Birds and the Element of Air

In Western magickal tradition, birds are most closely aligned with the element of Air. Air governs the mind: thought, wisdom, knowledge, and intuition. Because birds live primarily in the sky, they carry these qualities as part of their nature. For centuries, people across cultures have sensed this connection instinctively, treating birds as messengers between worlds, heralds of spiritual communication, and carriers of meaning.

That said, not every bird is purely an Air creature. A bird's color, habitat, and behavior can link it to other elements as well. Waterfowl, for instance, also carry the energy of Water. When reading any entry, consider the whole picture.

Why You Noticed That Bird

Birds are everywhere, and yet certain encounters stop you. A hawk crossing your path on the highway. A cardinal perched where you least expected it. The fact that you noticed is meaningful in itself. Bird symbolism is built on that pause, that moment of recognition. The entries in this grimoire are here to help you interpret what you felt in that moment and give it language.

Reading the Seasons

Each bird entry notes which season it is most active in, or which season reflects its energy. Seasons carry their own current of meaning:

  • Spring: New beginnings, seeds planted, fertility, fresh endeavors
  • Summer: Fullness, expansion, sustained growth
  • Autumn: Harvest, ripening, resolution, preparation
  • Winter: Rest, introspection, stillness, the quiet before renewal

Element Reference

Some bird energies cross into more than one element. This is not a contradiction; it reflects the layered nature of the natural world.

  • Air: Intellect, knowledge, wisdom, communication, freedom
  • Fire: Inspiration, creativity, passion, vitality, purification
  • Water: Intuition, dreams, transformation, emotion, purification
  • Earth: Stability, abundance, nourishment, grounding, plenty

Color Reference

A bird's coloring carries its own layer of meaning. Colors vibrate at distinct energetic frequencies, each with its own associations:

  • Black: Encompasses all things, grounding, richness, fertility
  • Brown: Nurturing, comfort, stability, hearth and home
  • Red: Vitality, passion, courage, activity, cheer
  • Blue: Healing, truth, happiness, tranquility
  • Green: Health, growth, abundance
  • Yellow / Gold: Joy, clarity, solar energy, wealth
  • Orange: Creativity, vitality, enthusiasm
  • Purple: Spirituality, respect, richness, command
  • Grey / Silver: Wisdom, peace, neutrality, lunar energy, illusion
  • White: Purity, blessing, purification, peace, innocence

How Entries Are Organized

Each bird entry in this grimoire follows a consistent structure so you can find what you need quickly.

Name and Classification

Entries typically cover a bird at the genus level (for example, owl) and note any species-specific associations within that entry (barn owl, great horned owl, and so on). For spiritual purposes, the difference between closely related subspecies rarely changes the core symbolism. If you saw a blackbird, the energy it carries is largely the same whether it was a European or American species.

For reference, here is how taxonomic classifications work from broadest to most specific:

  • Order: The widest grouping, organized by shared general characteristics
  • Family: A narrower group sharing more specific traits within an order
  • Genus: A further refined group sharing even more specific qualities within a family
  • Species: The most precise classification, identifying one distinct kind of bird

Geographic Distribution and Habitat

Where the bird lives and what kind of environment it prefers. Most entries focus on North American species, since encountering a bird in your own neighborhood gives its message immediacy.

Physical Description

What the bird looks like. Size measurements are general averages across male and female.

Interesting Facts

Behavior, calls, and mating habits that are relevant to the bird's symbolic character.

Myths, Folklore, and Cultural Associations

How the bird appears across cultures, legends, and mythology. Many pieces of bird lore have no traceable origin and exist simply as part of a long folk tradition. Where a cultural source is known, it is noted.

Omens and Divinatory Meaning

What seeing this bird may be communicating to you.

Associated Energies

A quick summary of the bird's traditional correspondences, drawn from symbolism, mythology, and cultural perception.

Associated Seasons and Elements

Which season and element best reflect the bird's nature.

Color Associations

The energetic meanings connected to the bird's primary colors.

Related Entries

Where relevant, entries will point you toward related birds whose symbolism overlaps or complements. For instance, if you are reading about egrets, the heron and stork entries will offer additional insight, as these birds are closely related and often mistaken for one another.

Bird Divination Through History

Across nearly every recorded culture, birds have served as intermediaries between the human world and something beyond it. Their freedom of movement, their presence in the sky, and the strangeness of their calls made them natural candidates for divine communication.

The practice most familiar to Western readers is augury, the Roman art of reading omens from bird behavior. Trained augurs divided the sky into regions and interpreted a bird's flight path, direction, and behavior within that grid. The results informed military decisions, political appointments, and public ceremonies. It was a formal institution, not casual superstition.

Other specialized practices developed alongside it:

  • Ornithoscopy (ornithomancy): Broad study of bird omens, with particular attention to flight patterns
  • Alectryomancy: Observing a bird peck through grain arranged around a circle of letters, reading the sequence as a message
  • Haruspication: Examination of a sacrificed animal's organs for omens, including those of birds
  • Oomancy (ovomancy): Reading patterns formed by egg whites dropped into water

Other traditions developed their own systems independently. In Tibetan practice, the calls of ravens and other dark birds were read as omens, with meaning shifting based on the time of day, the direction of the call, and the circumstances of the listener. Birdsong as message appears across cultures worldwide, each with its own interpretive vocabulary.

What the Historical Record Tells Us

Most bird divination was never written down. It was the domain of specialists: priests, shamans, and augurs who passed knowledge through practice rather than text. What survives in written records is fragmentary, and much has been lost entirely.

What this means in practice is that bird divination has never had a fixed dictionary of meanings. It was always contextual, shaped by the observer, the question, and the moment. That flexibility is not a weakness in the system; it is the system. There is no single authority to defer to, which means your own perception and developing intuition are not a lesser substitute for the real thing. They are the real thing.

Modern Bird Divination

Working with birds as guides today requires no initiation and no fixed rulebook. The meaning you draw from an encounter is built from your own attentiveness, accumulated over time.

A personal system of bird symbolism should remain fluid. What a particular bird means to you in one season of your life may shift considerably in another, and that evolution is a sign that the system is working. Your intuition is the instrument, and it grows more precise with use. If a crow causes you to double back and check something you left behind, that is a valid and complete communication, regardless of what any historical text would say about it.

The following approaches can help you build and refine your own practice.

Learn the Bird

When an encounter catches your attention, look into the bird itself. What does it eat? Where does it live? Is it a predator, a scavenger, a songbird? The specifics of a bird's life add texture to any symbolic reading. If it is a predator, the birds it hunts may be relevant too. Relationships between species, whether through predation, competition, or shared habitat, can become part of what you are being shown.

Listen as Well as Look

Many birds are far more often heard than seen. Thrushes, whip-poor-wills, and countless others make their presence known primarily through sound. A call heard at dusk through the trees carries as much potential meaning as a sighting. Learning the calls of birds common to your region is a practical investment; field recording apps and audio databases make this easier than it has ever been.

Working with Birds Spiritually

Direct engagement with bird energy goes beyond observation. There are active practices for working with the powers and qualities that birds represent, from meditation and visualization to physical ritual and devotional work.

Look for Freeform Guidance

For quick directional guidance, go outside to a park or garden, settle yourself, and wait for the first bird to appear. Rather than identifying it and consulting its symbolism, simply observe:

  • What direction did it come from?
  • How many are there?
  • What are they doing: flying, foraging, calling, still?
  • Do they land, or do they pass through?
  • If they fly, how high?

The simplest traditional reading uses left and right. A bird appearing to your left is generally read as a no or an unfavorable sign; to the right, a yes or a favorable one. Left-handed practitioners often invert this. Another reading associates left with the past and right with the future, suggesting where the root or resolution of a situation lies. A bird appearing directly ahead may signal that the answer is already in front of you. One appearing or calling from behind suggests that something is not yet ready to be revealed.

If a bird moves toward you, traditional folklore reads it as a favorable omen; if it moves away, unfavorable.

Employ Bird Energy as Spiritual Guidance

When you want to work with a bird's energy but cannot go outside, or when you want to seek guidance from the bird kingdom without knowing which bird to approach, there are several ways to make contact:

  • Flip through this grimoire with your eyes closed and open to a page at random.
  • Use a commercially available bird oracle deck; there are several well-regarded options available.
  • Create your own set of bird cards from index cards or printed images, annotated with keywords and personal notes, and draw from it intuitively.

Alternatively, use the Find a Bird Guide meditation to let a bird come to you.

Totems and Spirit Guides

A totem is an animal, plant, or other entity that serves as an emblem or spiritual anchor for a group or individual. In many Indigenous traditions, totems are assigned rather than chosen, representing ancestral relationships and carrying specific responsibilities and taboos.

A spirit guide is more personal: an entity that accompanies, protects, or advises an individual, particularly in spiritual work. In shamanic traditions, guides were essential companions for journeys into other states of awareness, helping the practitioner navigate and return safely.

In contemporary practice, these concepts are often used more loosely to describe animals whose energy resonates deeply with a person, or whose symbolism recurs meaningfully across their life. Working with a bird in this way is less about claiming a fixed identity and more about entering into an ongoing relationship with a particular quality or intelligence that the bird represents.

Working with a Specific Bird

If a particular bird keeps appearing in your life, turning up in art you receive as gifts, crossing your path repeatedly, or appearing in dreams, it may be trying to establish a relationship. Pay attention to it. Read about it. Learn how it lives.

You can honor a bird you feel drawn to by keeping an image of it in your space, wearing jewelry that depicts it, or simply speaking to it when it appears. Educate yourself about the real animal: its habitat, its diet, its behavior. Supporting conservation efforts for species at risk is another meaningful form of acknowledgment.

If you want to deepen the connection intentionally, use the following meditation:

Attune to a Specific Bird

The Birds of the Air

Air is the element most frequently associated with birds, and for good reason: most birds fly in some way, shape, or form. Only a few are completely limited to land or water. If the birds you wish to work with are earth- or water-based, you can tweak the meditation below to reflect their elemental affinity: imagine yourself settling on the surface of the water, into the leaves of a forest floor, or whatever your chosen bird might do in the environment it prefers. (Working with a bird from a snowy habitat? Use a water meditation, but think cold.)

This meditation is not dependent on the laws of physics. It is imagination, pure and simple, meant to help you explore the energy of the element of Air, and how it pertains to birds.

Attunement to Air

Let a Guide Come to You

Sometimes you need a guide to address issues that you are not consciously aware of. If you are open to the idea of working with a bird that chooses you instead, that bird will be the right one for you at this moment in time.

Find a Bird Guide

Honor Your Guide

Once you have established a relationship with a bird guide, maintaining it with regular acknowledgment is simply good practice. Display or create art featuring the bird. Wear something that represents it. Leave offerings suited to the real animal if it is native to your area, taking care to research what is safe and appropriate, and to check local regulations on feeding wildlife.

For birds whose habitat is far from yours, a symbolic offering at a home altar or shrine serves equally well. Another meaningful option is donating to a conservation organization or bird sanctuary working to protect the species. Local wildlife centers and biodomes also frequently welcome volunteers.

The relationship you build with a bird guide is ultimately a relationship with a particular quality of energy in the world. Tending it enriches your practice and, over time, your understanding of yourself.

Animals in Spell-casting

Spell-casting draws on the power of animal allies and familiars, not their physical bodies. The magickal energy carried by specific animal species can support your workings when approached with respect and clear intention.

The End of Anatomy-Based Spells

For much of recorded history, cultures around the world folded animal body parts into their spellwork. Whether those practices ever delivered genuine results is beside the point. The natural world has been thrown severely out of balance, and workings that depend on animal remains are no longer viable. Every such spell ultimately depends on the cooperation of the presiding Animal Spirit, and those spirits will not lend their power to practitioners who cause harm to the creatures in their care. Anatomy-based workings risk actively backfiring. Magick is not static; it shifts with the conditions of the world it operates in. Techniques that served one era must be rethought for the present.

The historical prominence of these practices may also be exaggerated. Outside observers and storytellers have always gravitated toward the most sensational elements of magick. Hoodoo, for instance, is a deeply sophisticated tradition, yet popular imagination reduces it to the notorious black cat bone while ignoring the enormous body of plant-based and spiritual work that actually defines the system. Historical context matters as well. In periods when people raised and butchered their own livestock, leftover parts found secondary uses as a matter of course, magickal uses among them. A Romany protective amulet known as "eyes of the crayfish" sounds grisly until you discover it refers to calcium deposits scraped from the inside of a crayfish shell, one that was already destined for the cooking pot.

Image Magick: The Ancient Alternative

Animal spells can be updated for modern practice without sacrificing potency. Candles molded into animal shapes, charms cast in metal or carved from gemstone, and sculpted figurines all channel a species' inherent energy while leaving living creatures untouched. A copper hummingbird charm, for example, pairs the bird's longstanding role in Central American love magick with the complementary energy of the metal itself. Consecrating such a charm to the animal's spirit deepens its power, something that simply cannot be achieved with body parts obtained through suffering.

This is not a modern concession to squeamishness. Animal image magick is among the oldest and most potent branches of the art. The Biblical golden calf was exactly this: a magickal image that fused animal symbolism with metallic energy, shaped by collective human fear and longing into a powerful conduit. A living calf would have been far easier to come by, but the crafted image held greater magickal force.

Sacrifice Belongs to Religion, Not Magick

Animal sacrifice is a religious act, and it is entirely separate from spell-casting. Every major religious tradition has practiced it at some point. Some still do, others have moved on. In every case, rigorous training and formal initiation are prerequisites. No tradition permits untrained individuals to perform sacrificial rites on their own.

Where magick brushes up against religious territory, symbolic substitution is the long-established norm. Petition Aphrodite with a dove-shaped candle rather than injuring one of her sacred birds. Present Hekate with a miniature stone dog rather than a living animal. This is not a softened modern adaptation. More than two thousand years ago, worshippers who could not afford formal temple sacrifices, or who simply preferred private devotion, offered small stone fetishes to Hekate and obtained the results they sought.

Decoding the Grimoires

Many of the classical European grimoires trace their lineage to fragments of Alexandrian spell-books that circulated through Europe, Arabia, and North Africa long before the invention of the printing press. The professional magickians of Roman-era Alexandria developed an intricate coded vocabulary to keep their formulas out of unauthorized hands. That cipher was eventually recovered and translated from a collection known as the Greek Magickal Papyri.

The decrypted results are revealing. A formula calling for "heart of a hawk" actually specifies wormwood. "Lion's tongue" turns out to be turnip. "Hercules' semen" is arugula. A "physician's bone" is sandstone. Many, and quite possibly all, animal references in these texts originally pointed to plants and minerals. But centuries of hand-copying without the accompanying key led later magickians to read the ingredients at face value, never recognizing the professional shorthand underneath.

This kind of coded terminology is not limited to antiquity. Certain contemporary Amazonian shamans still maintain a secret professional lexicon specifically to prevent their knowledge from being exploited by outsiders.

The practical lesson is simple: never perform a working that makes you uncomfortable. Botanical and mineral ingredients are routinely named after animals. Deer's tongue is a grass prized for promoting eloquence. Swallow's blood is a red mineral powder with no blood whatsoever. Dragon's blood, one of the most widely used spell ingredients on the planet, is resin tapped from the Indonesian tree Dracaena draco, so named for its vivid red color. (A completely separate substance also called dragon's blood appears in Peruvian magickal practice, equally botanical and entirely unrelated to the Indonesian variety.)

Animal-Sourced Fragrances and Their Substitutes

Four historically significant magickal fragrances originate from animal sources: civet, musk, ambergris, and castoreum. In practical terms, only synthetic reproductions are available today, since the genuine materials are extraordinarily scarce and prohibitively expensive. Because scarcity has always been the norm, botanical stand-ins have existed for centuries:

  • Musk substitute: Ambrette (Abelmoschus moschatus), an Indian shrub also known as musk mallow, prized for its aromatic seed
  • Ambergris substitute: Labdanum, a resin harvested from the rock-rose (Cistus creticus, Cistus ladanifer). Cretan labdanum is said to offer the closest approximation, though French, Moroccan, and Spanish sources also produce usable material

When Spells Involve Living Animals

Certain workings call for a living creature's participation. Any animal involved must be treated with the same care and respect extended to a human or spirit collaborator, and must emerge from the spell in the same or better condition than when it entered. Spells that incorporate cuts of meat assume the practitioner acquires them the same way they would for an ordinary meal. Many workings call for eggs, honey, or milk. Practitioners who avoid animal products can simply choose from the enormous number of spells that require none. Magick and everyday life are not separate domains. If something clashes with your ethics outside of a ritual context, it will clash inside one too.

Collar Protection Magick

A pet's collar is a natural framework for protective spellwork. Any charged object can be fastened to it, and incorporating knot magick into the attachment strengthens the working further. Common additions include:

  • Clear quartz to amplify the animal's aura and provide a layer of energetic shielding
  • Rose quartz to extend the protective force of your love around the animal
  • Other crystals, protective amulets, religious medals, or similar charms selected to suit the animal's needs

Always charge and consecrate objects before attaching them to the collar. The collar itself can also be consecrated as a whole protective unit once everything is in place.

Magick Day Protection

Certain days of the year are believed to carry an extra charge of magickal power. Spells performed on these days benefit people and animals alike. The most important dates for animal protection include:

  • Beltane / May Day / Walpurgis (May 1): Fire rites dominate. Driving cattle between twin bonfires is the classic Beltane blessing for health, fertility, and protection. Water charged with a crystal ball on May Day shields cattle from bewitchment.
  • Midsummer's Day / Saint John's Day (June 24): Both fire and water rites are traditional. Animals may be led through flaming hoops of hemp, blessed with burning branches of hazel or rowan, or bathed in ocean waves or salted water. Some practitioners substitute the exact date of the summer solstice.
  • Saint George's Day (April 23): Traditionally the day livestock were first led out to pasture. Sunwise processions around the barn or field, torchlit parades, and elaborate blessing rites involving palm fronds, barley, and holy water are all performed on this date.

Barn and Livestock Protection

Folk traditions for shielding domestic animals from malevolent magick center on the barn and its immediate surroundings. These practices layer multiple forms of protection and can be combined freely.

  • Birch trees planted near the barn ward off harmful magick. If the barn is already standing, transplant birch trees as close as possible.
  • Red and white ribbons tied to the birch trees, or to other nearby trees, reinforce the protective boundary.
  • Lilies and primroses planted around the barn's perimeter create a living protective ring. Keep them maintained and replace as needed.
  • A hatchet buried sharp side up beneath the barn's threshold forces any malevolent energy to be cut as animals cross over it entering and leaving.
  • Horseshoes posted above the barn door protect animals just as they protect humans. In the Hungarian tradition, drawing a horseshoe over the door with black chalk serves the same purpose.
  • Silver water: Keep a piece of real silver (a small charm or coin) in a dish or bucket of water out of the animals' reach. Sprinkle the animals with this water once a week, then replace with fresh water.
  • Rose of Jericho Water sprinkled over the animals once a week provides an additional layer of cleansing and protection.

Cattle Spells

SATOR Spell

The SATOR square is one of the oldest known word squares, used historically in protective and binding magick. This version channels its power directly into the livestock.

  1. Write the following on a piece of paper:
SATOR
AREPO
TENET
OPERA
ROTAS
  1. Grind it up and add it to the cattle feed. Have the cows eat the words.

Dog Spells

Child's Dog Hair Medicine Bag

Dog hair carries the loyal, protective energy of its owner. This simple charm extends that protection to a child.

  1. Fill a medicine bag with loose dog hair.
  2. Add any other lucky charms, as desired.
  3. Give to a child to wear or carry for protection.

Greyhound Spirit Protection

A home where a well cared for, happy greyhound lives will allegedly never be haunted by malicious spirits.

Pacify Threatening Dogs Spell (Christian Pow-Wow)

Pow-Wow strongly incorporates the use of spoken charms. This one is used to soothe a threatening dog and provide protection, excellent for those forced to walk past a snarling, snapping canine.

The charm must be repeated three times before you reach the dog (or the dog reaches you!):

Dog, hold thy nose to the ground!
God has made thee, me and hound.
In the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Ghost.

Then form the sign of the cross three times.

This spell as recorded in 1820 by John George Hohman in his definitive Book of Pow-Wows: The Long Lost Friend omits the last line of the charm, but includes the crosses.

Pacify Threatening Dogs Spell (Pagan-Friendly Version)

Historically, there have always been two movements within the Pow-Wow community: those who emphasize Christian orientation and those who do not. Rhymes were adapted as needed and continue to evolve. This pagan-friendly version calls upon those Greek divinities that exert great influence over hounds:

Dog, hold your nose to the ground!
Creator made you, me and hound.
In the name of the triple goddess, Selene, Artemis and Hecate.

Repeat three times. The cross, as a pre-Christian symbol of protection, may still be formed. A pentacle, crescent moon, downward facing triangle or other shape may also be substituted, as desired.

Rhodium Oil Spell to Lure Dogs Away

This perfume oil allegedly attracts dogs and was once used by thieves in order to lure dogs away. Play with the proportions until you achieve an effective fragrance. It may work on other animals too. Experiment and see.

Rhodium Oil consists of:

  • Essential oil of cedarwood
  • Essential oil of rose geranium
  • Essential oil of palmarosa
  • Essential oil of sandalwood
  • Blend with a carrier oil, such as jojoba oil.

Rhodium Oil may be used in various ways:

  • Wear it as a perfume
  • Use the oil to mark a trail

Stop Dogs Barking Spell

Place leaves of hound's tongue in your shoes, beneath your feet. Alternatively, carry within a charm bag.

Familiars and Allies

Animal Spells

Spellwork involving animals falls broadly into two purposes: protecting animals from physical and spiritual harm, and channeling animal power to benefit humans. The animals who actively participate in magickal workings, lending their own energy and gifts, generally belong to one of two categories: familiars and allies.

Familiars

Keeping animals as companions purely for affection is a relatively recent idea. In earlier centuries, those who formed unusually close bonds with animals often attracted suspicion and accusations of witchcraft, particularly if the creatures in question were cats, birds, rabbits, black dogs, reptiles, or amphibians.

The word "familiar" captures the essence of the relationship. A familiar is a real, living animal with whom a person shares a deep psychic and emotional connection. The dog that insists on sleeping beneath your bed, the cat that shadows you through every room, the bird content to ride your shoulder all day: each of these is a potential familiar.

Sometimes the familiar's mere presence is enough to kindle and amplify magickal work, even without deliberate participation. For other practitioners, consciously cultivating the psychic bond between human and animal unlocks a source of profound power and fulfillment.

Typical Familiars

Most familiars are animals capable of sharing a household: cats, dogs, rabbits, birds, toads, and snakes top the list. But anyone who lives or works in close quarters with other species may discover unexpected magickal connections as well.

Wild Familiars

A wild animal that stays wild can still become a familiar, though in these cases the animal invariably initiates the bond. A bird or a colony of bees might visit the same person daily. Scandinavian witches were traditionally known to favor flies. Wild dolphins have been observed singling out a particular human for repeated interaction. People living near forests or wilderness areas sometimes develop a sustained, personal relationship with an individual creature over time.

💛
A familiar cannot be forced. The bond is rooted in love, respect, and genuine chemistry, and it must form on its own terms.

Allies

Because a familiar must be a specific creature with whom you share a personal bond, the range of animals available is naturally limited. But what happens when a working calls for a rhinoceros, a crocodile, a dragon, or a unicorn?

All familiars are animal allies, but the category of ally reaches far beyond what a familiar can offer. An animal ally is fundamentally a spiritual relationship, and because it can unfold entirely in the spirit realm, there is no limit on which creatures may be approached. One may also petition the presiding spirit of an entire species rather than any single animal.

There is no cap on how many familiars or allies a person may have.

Discovering Allies

Alliances with animals cannot be forced, but they can be invited. A common belief holds that every person is born with the alliances they need, whether animal, botanical, or spiritual. The work lies in recognizing those connections and learning to draw on them effectively.

Methods for uncovering allies include card-based divination systems and dreamwork. Any animal or species that keeps appearing in your life, whether in dreams or waking encounters, may already be an ally or may be signaling its willingness to become one.

The Nagual

Across Mexico and Central America, certain practitioners are believed capable of shapeshifting into animal form. Such a person is called a nagual, and a coyote trotting down the road might be an ordinary animal or a transformed practitioner. In the state of Oaxaca, however, the concept takes a different shape. The nahual (the Oaxacan spelling) is understood as a guardian spirit received at birth, a sacred gift bestowed by a child's parents.

Animal Images

Prehistoric cave paintings rank among the oldest surviving human artifacts, testifying to a deep magickal connection between people and animals stretching back millennia. Portable figurines of specific animals, typically shaped from clay or stone, have been used since antiquity for healing, hunting, protection, and the development of psychic power.

Zuni Stone Fetishes

The Zuni people of New Mexico elevated this practice into a refined art. Their stone fetishes are small carvings of individual animals, originally made for ceremony and the hunt. Traditionally, carvers sought out stones that already suggested the form of a creature, requiring only minimal shaping to bring the animal into view. Because the charm is found rather than manufactured, the animal spirit has the chance to choose the person instead of the other way around.

Working with a Stone Fetish:

  1. Look for stones whose natural shape already hints at a particular creature. When you encounter the right one, you will know it. Like holed-stones, these are gifts from the Earth.
  2. Charge and consecrate the fetish by placing it inside a magick box alongside images, food, and botanical activators. Corn pollen was the traditional offering used to awaken the fetish; substitute whatever feels sacred and appropriate to you.
  3. Store the fetish in its box or container when it is not in active use. Feed it on a regular schedule to maintain its power and keep it activated.

Living Animal Allies

The Leni-Lenape Tradition

Some traditions favor a tangible companion over an abstract guardian. In Leni-Lenape practice, a newborn is given an actual animal, most often a puppy or kitten, to serve as a personal protector and lifelong partner. The creature is raised alongside the child, and no two children share the same animal. This is a bond meant to last a lifetime.

If the animal dies, it is believed to have shielded the child by absorbing some threat of harm, particularly illness or accident. A ceremonial burial closes the bond, and a new companion is given to the child without delay. If the child passes first, funeral rites release the animal from its obligation.

Dedicating Animals to Spirits

Living creatures can also be consecrated to a specific spirit rather than bonded to a human. This creates a three-way connection linking human, spirit, and animal. Spells for animal healing, protection, or recovery of lost animals often recommend dedicating the animal to a spirit as part of the working.

Spirit Protectors

The following spirits have earned a reputation as renowned protectors of specific animals. Incorporate them into spells for healing, protection, or locating lost animals as needed.

Cats: Artemis, Bastet, Freya, Hekate, Lilith

Big Cats (tigers, lions, leopards): Dionysus, Durga, Hathor, Kybele, Sekhmet

Dogs: Artemis, Hekate, Ogun, Saint Roch

Horses: Anat, Demeter, Epona, Poseidon, Rhiannon, Hayagriva

Toads: Agwe, Heket

Snakes: Athena, Ezili Freda Dahomey, Lilith, Mami Waters, Simbi, Asherah

Cows: Brigid, Hathor, Hermes, Isis, Lakshmi, Maeve, Shiva

Fish: Atargatis, La Baleine, La Sirene, Yemaya

Pigs: Demeter, Seth

Animals in general: Aphrodite, Artemis, Baba Yaga, Faunus, Hathor, Lilith, Saint Anthony (the spiritual detective: petition for assistance when anything or anyone is missing)

Overview

Bats are ancient creatures, having inhabited Earth for about 50 million years. Nearly one thousand species exist, comprising nearly one quarter of all mammal species. Bats are unique as the only mammal capable of true flight. Virtually everywhere bats are found, they are identified with witchcraft, perceived as witches' familiars, mounts, and alter egos.

Physical Form and Behavior

Bats inspired awe because their form was ambiguous: they resemble a cross between an animal and a bird. In ancient Asian belief, bats were understood to be the most perfect bird because they nurse their young. Most bats are nocturnal, sleeping through the day hanging upside down in huge colonies, emerging at dusk from the caves they inhabit in huge swarms. Animals that live in caves, grottoes, or underground are metaphysically perceived as being especially close to Earth, privy to her deepest secrets.

Medieval European Associations

Medieval Europeans associated bats with dragons, magical winged creatures that live in caves and grottos. This association proved unfortunate, as by the Middle Ages, dragons were targets for questing knights, and small bats are much easier to kill than fire-breathing dragons. Dragons were also associated with Satan, and this association rubbed off on bats. They became closely associated with devils, demons, and the anti-Christ. Medieval artwork frequently depicts Satan with bat's wings, while angels were consistently painted with wings of white birds.

In medieval Europe, the sight of a flying bat was often interpreted as a transformed witch. Witches were believed to transform into bats, to ride bats like horses, and to smear their broomsticks with bat's blood to achieve lift-off. In 1322, Lady Jacaume of Bayonne, France was publicly burned at the stake as a witch. The evidence was that swarms of bats had been observed flying about her house and garden.

Vampire Bats and Dracula

The original major fear regarding bats was that they would become entangled in a woman's hair, not that they would suck blood. With the exception of a very few blood-consuming species, bats eat either fruit or insects. Vampire bats are indigenous only to the Western Hemisphere, ranging from Argentina to Mexico. They were never found in Central Europe, where the concept of an undead creature who survives by sapping the vitality of the living has existed since time immemorial.

Vampire bats received their name from the mythic vampire, not vice versa. Bram Stoker incorporated blood-consuming bats into his novel Dracula, whose success forever changed perceptions of bats and mythical vampires. The concept of a mythic blood-consuming "vampiric" spirit was well-known in Central and South America prior to European contact, where blood-consuming bats exist and have associations with death and blood sacrifice.

Positive Associations

Not all associations with bats are negative. The Kogi people of northern Columbia associate the vampire with human fertility. Their euphemistic expression for a girl who begins to menstruate is that she has been "bitten by the bat." According to the Kogi, the bat was the very first animal to be created, emerging directly from the Creator's body. Some tribes in New Guinea also perceive bats as fertility symbols.

In China, bats are regarded as especially auspicious, their very name a pun for luck. The Chinese five-bat design (Wu Fu) represents five blessings: longevity, prosperity, health, righteousness, and a natural death. Bat images abound in Chinese art and ornamentation.

African Folklore

Bats figure prominently in African folklore. In East Africa, bats are witches' mounts. In the Ivory Coast, bats represent souls of the departed, while in Madagascar, bats are souls of criminals, sorcerers, and the unburied dead. Bats have powerful associations with death and ghosts.

Magical Uses and Substitutions

Associations of bats with witches and magic inspired the use of whole bat corpses and various anatomical parts (hearts, wings, blood) in magick spells. References to bat's wings in magick spells may refer to holly leaves, which may always be substituted. Bat nuts (dried ling nuts), which if held from one angle resemble bats, may be substituted for bats in any spell. Bat's blood may have been a euphemism for another magical ingredient, perhaps a resin. Since the 1920s, commercially marketed Bat's Blood Ink is scented red ink.

Conservation and Modern Practice

Negative associations have taken a deadly toll. Many species of bats are extremely endangered due to loss of habitat and extermination as vermin. This terribly upsets the balance of nature: bats are genuine fertility figures, responsible for pollination of many plant species, particularly in the desert. Bats are also responsible for insect control, and one bat can consume as many as 600 mosquitoes in one hour. Modern witchcraft practices suggest that maintaining a bat house on your property will bring joy and good luck.

Longevity and Immortality

Like the Taoist Immortals, bats dwell in caves, and so they too became emblems of longevity and immortality. Some eastern bat caves have remained unchanged for thousands of years, and the bats living within them are revered as sacred.

The Night Devouring the Day

The bat's nocturnal nature has also drawn darker meanings. It is seen as a symbol of the night devouring the day, said to swallow the light because it stirs at dusk, the threshold between day and night. Indigenous peoples of Brazil tell that a bat swallowing the Sun will herald the end of the world, and the Maya regarded the bat as a harbinger of death.

Keeper of Hidden Knowledge

The same nocturnal habit makes the bat, like the owl, a creature with access to hidden knowledge and secret information, able to perceive in darkness what daytime creatures cannot. Before echolocation was understood, the bat's effortless navigation through the night was a source of fascination that only deepened its air of mystery.

A Good Mother

Because female bats are the only flying creatures that suckle their young, the bat is also honored as a symbol of the good mother.

Overview

Bears are conspicuous in witchcraft lore by their very absence. They are creatures so sacred that many fear to mention their name. Bears are the animals of shamanism par excellence. Throughout Northern lands, whether North America, Europe or Asia, bears are the original sacred animal, sponsors and symbols of shamanic healing societies. They are the teachers and perhaps originators of shamanism. Because bears dig in the Earth, they are understood as the original root-workers and possess profound connections with healing, herbalism, and root magick. Bears are simultaneously sacred and dangerous creatures, benevolent and frightening, possessing powers too strong for the uninitiated to withstand.

Sacred Names and Euphemisms

In traditional shamanic cultures, bears were worshipped and venerated. These bear cultures typically never utter the name "bear": that would be like taking the Lord's name in vain. Euphemisms are substituted: "Big Brother," "Old Honey Thief," and the like. In a similar manner, ancient Greeks never mentioned the name of the Lord of the Dead; Hades, which names his realm, and Pluto, meaning "The Rich One," are both euphemisms.

Ancient Bear Religion

Bear religion is among Earth's original religions. Fairly soon after people began worshipping mothers, they began worshipping bears, too. Sometimes both were worshipped simultaneously. Paleolithic goddess statuettes depict huge mother bears nursing petite human infants. Bears possess a great resemblance to humans. They stand upright and eat a similar diet. In a Native American story, a boy abandoned in the woods discovers that out of all the forest animals, the only animal that he as a human can live with comfortably is the bear.

Cave Bears and Neanderthal Shrines

Ursus spelaeus, the cave bear, appeared on Earth approximately 300,000 years ago and was physically similar to the modern brown (grizzly) bear. Cave bears were huge, weighing up to one ton and perhaps 30 percent taller than brown bears. They hibernated in caves, where they also gave birth and frequently died, leaving their skeletons behind.

Among the very first indications of human spiritual traditions are ancient cave bear shrines. In Alpine grottoes dating to c.100,000 BCE, cave bear skulls are marked with red ochre and carefully arranged alongside ritual hearths. Bear skulls were also arranged on stone slabs and placed in wall niches. The caves contain altars, flagstone flooring, benches, and tables. This is literally Neanderthal religion; Neanderthal people built these shrines. The bones of at least 30,000 cave bears formed a deep layer in the Dragon Cave near Mixnitz, Austria.

Distribution and Endangerment

Vestiges of the sacred nature of bears survive in place names, like Berne, Switzerland, city of the bears. Europe is now largely devoid of bears. They have lost virtually all of their former territory in North America as well. Atlas bears once ranged from Morocco to Libya; the last Atlas bear is believed to have been shot in 1840 in the Tetuan Mountains. Bears of one type or another are indigenous to all continents except Australia and Antarctica. A healthy adult bear has no enemies other than people. Wherever bears survive, they are endangered because of loss of habitat and extermination as a competitive species, for sport, and for museum collections. Bears' bodies are valued in East Asian medicine, making them targets for poachers.

Norse Berserkers and Odin

The ancient Norse associated bears with the shaman god Odin. Warriors who fought under his protection were known as "berserkers" (berserk means bear shirt). They fought naked but for bear skins, ritually channeling bear power, temporarily incorporating the bear's spirit to become fierce, formidable, and virtually unbeatable, striking terror into their opponents as they went berserk. In a sense, they become temporary were-bears; their comrades, also under Odin's protection, were wolf warriors.

Native American Bear Spirituality

Bear-centered spirituality survives wherever traditional Northern shamanism survives, particularly among Native Americans. Native American bear doctors and bear societies still exist. Among the few explicit linkages of bears to witchcraft occurs in the Ojibwa tradition of bear-walking, a form of shape-shifting sorcery.

Artemis and Greek Tradition

Bears were sacred in warmer climates, too. The Greek goddess Artemis's name may derive from her affiliation with bears, which were among her most sacred animals and sometime her alter-ego. Her young temple priestesses were known as "bears."

Fairy Tales and Hidden Meanings

The few references to bears in European fairy tales usually tell of men doomed to wear the bear's form because of unhappy encounters with witches, as in Snow White and Rose Red and some versions of East of the Sun, West of the Moon. These stories read negatively if one assumes that transformation into a bear's shape is negative; reading between the lines, if one understands wearing the bear's skin as a secret reference to shamanism, different conclusions can be drawn.

Black Bear's Teaching

Ursus americanus

Watching Black Bear stand upright on hind legs might briefly fool you into thinking a human approaches. This bipedal capacity makes her a bridge between earth and sky, positioning Black Bear as humanity's mirror-self, a wild sister still connected to healing wisdom and primal instinct we've largely forgotten.

Black Bear speaks to the part of us longing to hibernate all winter, then emerge renewed with creative energy trailing behind like cubs at our heels. Her teaching is simple: stop fighting seasonal cycles. Call on Bear to help you rediscover your natural rhythms and reclaim your wildness.

When nights lengthen and cold arrives, Black Bear retreats into dreaming without resistance. She embodies the understanding that dark nights exist for dreaming, requiring no justification. By contrast, human cultures characteristically resist the long night, filling it with artificial light and social activity. Black Bear's teaching is that the slowing, deepening, and even the subtle sorrow of winter are appropriate seasonal textures to be aligned with rather than escaped. Her medicine is the healing that comes through surrender to natural cycles.

Honeybee: Solar Navigation

Apis mellifera

Honeybee flies a zigzag path searching for pollen patches. Upon discovering one, she returns home to dance, showing her sisters the exact angle where sun hits the pollen location. Through this aerial communication, her sisters triangulate the feast's location. Bee's internal compass proves incredibly accurate, and she can locate the sun even on cloudy days.

The sun traditionally represents expansive, moving energies: our passions and our ability to manifest them in the world. When life feels cloudy and dull, call on Honeybee to help you navigate toward joy. During dark times, she reminds you that clouds pass and your passion and purpose will reveal themselves again.

Honeybee's Lessons

Two and a half million years ago, our ancestors' brains grew exponentially. The human brain uses incredible amounts of glucose, which honey provides. Some say Honeybee played a key role in our evolution. Ironically, our big brains cause overanalysis and rumination, two things most likely to extinguish our inner fire and dampen passion.

Honeybee creates honey surplus (her own liquid sunshine) to sustain her hive through winter months.

Made of interlocking hexagons that bees build cooperatively and efficiently, beehives are highly organized places with nurseries for young and rooms where worker bees pack pollen and nectar into wax-capped cells.

Sweetness and the Ancient World

In the ancient world the bee was an insect of great importance, since the honey it produced was one of the few naturally sweet substances then available and also served as a good preservative. That importance shows in the bee's appearance on the coins of Ephesus and in Minoan imagery that depicted a figure as half woman and half bee. In Egypt the bee stood as a symbol of the Lower Kingdom.

The bee is an emblem of industry and mutual cooperation, though it carries a spiritual side as well. The golden honeycomb served as one of the symbols of a goddess whose priestesses were believed to live on within the bodies of bees. These priestesses were called Melissae, a name drawn from the same root as the words for honey and bees. Their male counterparts, equivalent to the drones, were called Essenes and were eunuchs. Because bees produce wax, they came to be closely linked with places of Christian worship such as abbeys, where monks and nuns used that wax to make candles for the church.

Order, Immortality, and Sacrifice

Bees stand as symbols of order and of immortality. A queen needs to mate only once to spend the rest of her life producing offspring, and the drone whose task it is to impregnate her splits in half once that task is done. The workers feed the drones, which cannot feed themselves, but once the queen is mated the efficient workers simply stop feeding them and let them starve before dragging them to the entrance of the hive. Because a bee dies when it uses its sting, it became a symbol of great heroism and sacrifice, unlike the wasp, which can sting again and again.

Prophecy, Transmutation, and Sacred Geometry

The bee performs an elaborate dance to reveal the whereabouts of a particularly rich crop of flowers. Bees are believed to hold magickal powers to foresee the future and are regarded by many as deities in their own right. For this reason it has long been customary, over hundreds of years, for the beekeeper to tell the bees of a death in the household and to send word of the deceased to them. Because bees feed on the nectar of flowers, and so ultimately on sunlight, they act as agents of transmutation, making something from nothing. They are mystical creatures that both understand and embody some of our most ancient and powerful symbols, building their honeycomb from thousands of perfectly symmetrical hexagons, a structure that holds the secrets of the Flower of Life and of the six pointed star, or hexagram.

Birds as Divine Communicators

Birds have walked, and flown, this world far longer than humankind, and though we see them every day they have always carried more than meets the eye. Their oldest symbolic role is that of messengers between the worlds, bearing word from the spiritual realms and from the Gods, and few symbols are as universal.

An Ancient Bird Cult

The place of birds in human imagination runs very deep. Among the prehistoric cave paintings at Lascaux is a scene now called the Death of the Bird Man, a hint that some form of bird cult may reach back as far as Upper Paleolithic times. Writing in Jung and His Symbols, Joseph L. Henderson called the bird the most fitting symbol of transcendence, an image of intuition working through a medium, one able to gather knowledge of distant events by entering a trancelike state.

Birds, Fate, and Augury

The link between birds and destiny is woven into language itself: in the Qur'an the word for bird stands also for fate, and in Greek the words for bird and omen are one and the same. Orthomancy, divination by watching birds, was practised the world over. Diviners noted a bird's flight, its kind, its calls and cries, and sometimes read its entrails. The Romans would settle no important matter without first consulting their augurs, and the Latin root that gives us augury, an omen or portent, lies in the word for bird, as does inauguration. The practice was far from Roman alone, being shared by Tibetans, Indians, Native Americans, Mexicans, Egyptians, Mayans, and Celts. Whole sacred sites were founded on bird signs, among them Mexico City, Rome, and the place of the Omphalos at Delphi.

The Gift of the Alphabet

Far-reaching, too, is the idea that birds revealed the secrets of the alphabet. The best-known tale holds that Hermes, messenger of the Gods, devised the letters by watching the flight of birds, and of cranes above all. Robert Graves, in The White Goddess, records that the secret signs were kept in a crane-skin bag, fitting enough given that Alaskan peoples used the skins of cranes, swans, and eagles for bags, these being the strongest. Little wonder that we lend our Gods and their messengers the marks of birds: wings, feathers, and the power of flight that stands for both bodily and spiritual transcendence and for movement in a realm closed to humankind. Hermes wears wings not only on his sandals but on the caduceus that is his emblem; and in a neat circle of meaning, the feather or quill became a favoured tool for setting down the written word, the bird speaking once again.

Symbolism & Medicine

Danaus plexippus - Monarch Butterfly

Butterfly's journey toward flight begins with an inward turn. Before she can earn her wings, she must examine everything she's been and digest it completely. This quiet, womb-like work requires total isolation from the world as she begins her self-deconstruction.

In her chrysalis sanctuary, Butterfly performs the ultimate sacrifice: she dissolves herself entirely into cellular soup. Only then, having surrendered all her past forms, can she consult her inner blueprint and begin pulling proteins together into wings. When Butterfly appears in your life, she signals a time to begin your own shedding, to digest your history, and prepare for transformation.

The Alchemy of Becoming

The caterpillar's metamorphosis isn't metaphor-it's biological magick. Before transforming, Caterpillar gorges on leaves in a frenzied pre-transition feast, stoking the energy she'll need. Once sated, she creates a protective shell and begins the messy work inside.

Within the chrysalis, she literally eats herself, breaking down every component until nothing remains but undifferentiated cellular material. This living soup contains all the raw materials needed to build her future body. From complete dissolution, she reassembles herself, growing structures she never possessed before, wings that will carry her into an entirely new way of being.

Navigating Your Own Metamorphosis

Butterfly's biological process illustrates the stages of deep transformation:

Nourish first - Reserves must be built before the dissolution phase begins

Release completely - Prior forms must be broken to their essential elements rather than preserved

Create sanctuary - The transitional stage requires protected time and space

Trust the blueprint - The pattern of what will emerge is already present within the raw material

This biological process mirrors the observable stages of significant change. Understanding Butterfly's medicine offers a framework for navigating transformation with greater clarity about its natural progression.

Soul and Spirit

Unlike the bee, which moves from flower to flower with great purpose and intention, the butterfly seems to flutter about almost aimlessly, with no great ambition behind its beauty. The Greek word for butterfly, psyche, is also the word for soul, and winged creatures are widely thought to be able to communicate with other worlds and with higher powers. One belief held that human souls incarnated into butterflies between lifetimes. The bond between spirit and butterfly appears across the world. The Celts believed the butterfly was a human soul in search of a mother, while the Aztecs believed that the last breath of a dying person took the form of a butterfly.

The butterfly's lifecycle is visible at every stage, from grub to caterpillar to pupa, and on to the chrysalis that opens to reveal the butterfly. This made it a symbol of transmutation and metamorphosis. Because of the period of gestation within the chrysalis, which resembles a tiny tomb, it is also an emblem of death and resurrection.

In Japan the butterfly is the archetypal symbol of femininity and vanity, though two butterflies together stand for love and marriage.

⚠️ The following belief belongs to the Blackfoot, a Native American people. It is part of a closed practice that is sacred to that tradition and should be practiced only by those within the originating culture.

Some Native American peoples, particularly the Blackfoot, believe the butterfly brings dreams. They use a stylized butterfly symbol, resembling a Maltese Cross, embroidered onto babies' cribs and clothing so that the children sleep well and have sweet dreams. When a butterfly is painted on the wall of a tribal lodge, it signals that any other patterns drawn there were not the work of a person alone but were inspired by the Great Spirit, for whom the painter acted only as a conduit.
