Overview

The cat, that animal which famously does not come when called, has long been an emblem of independence and of free, independent, autonomous women. Historically, attitudes toward cats parallel those toward women: when women have been respected and honored, their psychic gifts cherished, cats are beloved, sometimes deified; when women are perceived as dangerous and perverse, cats have been degraded and demonized. No other animal in the Western world is as identified with witchcraft as the domestic cat, particularly black cats.

Nature and Characteristics

Cats are beautiful, intelligent creatures that cannot be ruled. The entire concept of obedience is foreign to their nature. Cats perform various services for humans, but only on their own terms; they can only be enticed, not commanded. Cats epitomize the pleasure principle: sensuous creatures, they crave warmth, fine foods, soft fabrics, the choice seat in the house. Nocturnal, independent and mysterious, cats come and go as they please. Although domestic creatures, cats are never entirely tame.

Sexual Associations and Fertility

Cats have profound associations with sex. Both male and female cats have reputations as lusty, prodigiously sexual creatures. Since at least the time of Aristotle, cats have been used to symbolize lasciviousness and sexual insatiability. Cats are affiliated with sexually autonomous female deities like Bastet, Diana, Freya, Hathor, Hecate, Cybele, and Lilith. By the eighteenth century, "cat" had become slang for a prostitute.

Cats possess lush fertility. Felis, the scientific name for cats, derives from the Latin root fe, "to bear young." Other words from this source are feline, fecund and fetus. Cats, like frogs, are often considered weather harbingers, announcing the start of fertilizing rain. Jewelry depicting a mother cat surrounded by a large litter of kittens was a popular fertility charm in ancient Egypt.

Early Domestication

The earliest indication of intimate relations between people and cats derives from a burial in Cyprus, dating back approximately 9500 years ago. A carefully buried cat was discovered inches from a human burial. The cat's bones were arranged to parallel that of the human and displayed no signs of butchering. It appears to have been a beloved companion animal.

General wisdom suggests cats were first domesticated in Egypt, where domestic cats were bred at least four thousand years ago. As Egyptian culture became increasingly agrarian, stored grain attracted vermin, who attracted cats, who quickly demonstrated their usefulness. Cats became sacred guardians of the grain. Wide distribution of domestic cats occurred only after the Egyptian kingdom lost its independence to Rome. Not until the fourth century CE were domestic cats widely distributed in Italy.

Bastet: Egyptian Sacred Cat

The most famous sacred Egyptian cat is Bastet, whose titles included Mistress of the Oracle and Great Conjuress of the Casket. She is depicted as a cat, often bejeweled, or as a woman with a cat's head, sometimes surrounded by kittens. Bastet has dominion over sex, fertility, marriage, magic, music, childbirth, prosperity, joy, dance, and healing. She provides protections against infertility, the dangers of childbirth, evil spirits, illness and bodily injuries. Bastet offers special protection to women and children and serves as matron of magicians and healers.

Egyptian Magic and Cats

In Egyptian magickal practice, cats were admired as hunters, and hunting served as a metaphor for overcoming dangerous forces. A tawny wildcat helped the sun-god Ra defeat the evil serpent Apep. In Book of the Dead illustrations, a cat slices a snake's body in two with a knife.

This spell animates a cat amulet (specified as lapis lazuli, though faience was more common):

"Oh cat of lapis lazuli, great of forms, mistress of the embalming house, grant offerings to So-and-so in the Beautiful West!"

Being "great of forms" meant having multiple manifestations or bau, a sign of how powerful a deity was.

Sacred Cat Mummies

Thousands of mummified cats and kittens were deposited at temple sites and cemeteries as offerings to Bastet. Most were hastened to the afterlife by human hands (snapped necks or drowning provided embalmers with bodies for mummification). Some "cat mummies" contained only earth and pebbles. It was the wrapping and priestly blessing that mattered when offering a cat mummy and asking for divine intervention.

From Lioness to Cat

In her earliest forms, Bastet had a lioness's head like her sister Sekhmet. The two may represent different aspects of the same primordial power: Sekhmet the fierce, destructive heat of the sun, and Bastet the gentler, protective warmth. Later, Bastet appeared as a beautiful woman with the head of a domesticated cat.

Worship of Bastet reached its zenith during the reign of Osorkon II (874-853 BCE). Bastet's annual festival in Bubastis was Egypt's most popular festival, renowned for parties, revelry, and drunkenness. The festival celebrated female sexuality and generative power. Celebrants would shout sexual obscenities, dance wildly, and perform anasuromai, the ritual act of lifting up the skirts to expose the vulva, associated with laughter, healing, and defiance of grief.

Even house cats maintained their mysterious, sacred nature in Egypt. Herodotus reports that anyone convicted of intentionally killing a sacred animal was sentenced to death. When a pet cat died, it was customary for the human family to shave their eyebrows as a sign of mourning and respect.

Freya and Norse Tradition

Cats have potent associations with Freya, Norse Lady of love, romance, sex, fertility, childbirth, shamanism, enchantments, witchcraft, and death. An oracular, sexually autonomous spirit, Freya's chariot is drawn by her familiars, two huge gray cats named Bee Gold (honey) and Tree Gold (amber), who embody Freya's twin qualities of ferociousness and fecundity. Cats are Freya's sacred animals; a traditional method of petitioning or pleasing the goddess was to offer pans of milk to cats. To be kind to a cat is to entreat Freya's blessings.

Eventually cats would be tortured and killed specifically because of their associations with Freya. After the introduction of Christianity, Freya became among the most demonized of spirits, coming to embody the stereotype of the seductive witch. Cats shared Freya's demonization.

The Witchcraze and Persecution

By the Middle Ages, cats had become so identified with witchcraft that in 1484, Pope Innocent VIII issued a decree, understood by many scholars as the official start of the Witchcraze, denouncing cats and their owners. Any cat in the company of a woman could be assumed to be a familiar. Pope Innocent commanded that when a witch was burned, her cats were to be burned with her. He decreed that all European cat-worshippers be burned as witches. He authorized the killing of cats even without an accompanying witch.

A vicious cycle emerged: the destruction of European cats is believed to have encouraged the proliferation of rodents, which in turn encouraged the spread of deadly disease, blamed on witchcraft and heresy, which in turn led to fear, panic, and more killing of cats. The degradation and destruction of cats parallels that of women and their increasing loss of autonomy.

Cats in Witch-Hunter Beliefs

According to witch-hunter perceptions, cats played various roles: Cats were believed to be common familiars. A close relationship with a cat was considered telltale evidence of witchcraft, sufficient to warrant death for woman and cat. Cats provided witches with magical transportation. Witches rode to sabbats on cats' backs or traveled in feline form. Shape-shifting witches were believed able to assume the form of cats.

Sometimes the cats are the witches. Cats are traditionally Hungarian witches' alter egos. Witch-hunter Jean Bodin insisted that all cats are witches in disguise. Nicholas Remy argued they were demons instead. Hungarian witch-lore suggests cats become witches between ages 7 and 12, though shaving a cross into the cat's fur was believed sufficient to prevent this. According to Somerset folklore, cats born in May were especially inclined to be witches in disguise and hence were frequently killed.

Documented Witch Trials

Not all legends are fictional. In 1586, Anna Winkelz Ipfel was burned as a witch in Bergtheim, Germany for allegedly disguising herself as a black cat. In 1607, Bartie Paterson was hanged as a witch in England. According to witnesses, Bartie transformed into a cat and, together with other witches disguised as cats, "sang" in the backyard. In March 1607, Isobel Grierson was brought to court in Scotland, charged with witchcraft. She allegedly invaded the Clarke household in the middle of the night in the form of a cat, accompanied by other cats. Isobel was burned to death.

In 1233 Pope Gregory IX declared that heretics worshipped the devil in the form of a black tom cat. In Slavic areas, especially Russia and Poland, the ovinnik, guardian spirit of the threshing barn takes the form of a huge disheveled black cat with glowing eyes. Offerings of blini or the last sheaves of grain are offered to him in exchange for protection and divination services.

Ritual Killings

The torture and killing of cats occurred in various contexts: in conjunction with human witch trials, as random acts of violence, but also as organized, documented ritual killings. In Paris, it was customary to burn a sack or basket filled with cats in the Place de Greve on St John's Eve, a tradition also popular in other parts of France. Although Louis XIV abolished the Parisian custom in 1648, it continued in the provinces until at least as late as 1796. Various French towns built bonfires to burn masses of cats on the first Sunday in Lent. Cats were burned in Alsace at Easter.

Black Cat Superstitions

Although all cats are associated with witchcraft, the black cat is most powerfully identified. Black cats' special identification with witchcraft is not limited to Western European or Christian perspectives. Chinese, Hindu, Japanese, Jewish, North African, and Romany witch-lore make the same connection, although whether it is understood to be a sacred or malevolent connection depends upon cultural and individual perceptions.

People tend to fear or love black cats, frequently revealing their attitudes toward witchcraft. The major superstition regarding black cats is that they bring bad luck should they cross your path and people will cross the street to avoid them. This isn't so ridiculous if one recalls that black cats were once commonly believed to be witches in disguise. In Britain, however, black cats are lucky; white cats are identified with bad luck, perhaps because of associations with ghosts and death.

Tabby Cat: Unquestioned Worthiness

Felis catus

Twitching in sunlight, Tabby Cat dreams ancestral visions of savannahs and sleeping in rocky crevices. As a wild cat descendant, Tabby still bears stripe and spot remnants. But she's pleased to have moved indoors—adopting humans was brilliant strategy, she purrs, stretching and kneading paws.

Tabby never questions whether she's earned the warm window sunpatch or evening tuna. She never doubts her worthiness. Tabby licks a paw to smooth the fur behind her ear. You are already enough, she reminds you. Breathe into that knowing.

Independence and Interdependence

Some theorize that domesticated cats, compared to their ancestors, remain permanently in a kitten-like developmental stage, never acquiring the capacity for independent hunting or self-care, with humans serving as surrogate mothers. Yet Tabby Cat's aura of self-sufficiency and independence stands at odds with this notion, suggesting that dependence and autonomy are not mutually exclusive states.

Mountain Lion is the wild, full-grown cousin of Cat. Mountain Lion elevates Tabby Cat's teachings, helping us grasp not only our own worth but others' worth; to watch and observe for understanding; and to move through the world balancing power with intentional action. Mountain Lion leads herself without worrying who follows—ironically, this sometimes leaves her with a trail of initiates.

Amulet Uses

A cat whisker or claw carried as an amulet bestows magical power and luck.

Cross-Cultural Cat Lore

Even the most ordinary household cat carries a mystique and the promise of the supernatural powers people have attributed to cats for thousands of years. In the West the cat, especially the black cat, belongs to the witch as her familiar, her companion, and her alter ego. It shares magickal secrets and arcane knowledge that it cannot explain to ordinary people, since they do not speak its language, and an unspoken understanding passes between the witch and her grimalkin that surpasses any language used by other creatures. The Saga of Eric the Red preserves a full description of a witch and prophetess skilled in rune-craft whose costume included a hood lined with white cat skin and cat-skin mittens.

The ancient Egyptians honored the cat so highly that they revered it as the deity Bast. Cats whose fur carried three different colors, or whose eyes were of differing shades, were especially prized for their Bast-like appearance, a reminder that power did not belong to the black cat alone. Egyptian priests believed that cats carried the magnetic forces of nature, so that close company with them opened access to those powers.

Artemis, also called Diana and goddess of the hunt, was associated with the cat, itself renowned as a hunter. When a cat sleeps it curls into a circle with its head touching its tail, a shape close to the ouroboros, and like that ancient mythical creature the cat became a symbol of immortality.

The cat does not enjoy an honorable reputation everywhere. In the Buddhist tradition it is regarded with suspicion as a base, earthly creature lacking respect, because it was absent at the death and spiritual liberation of the Buddha, when it should have been present. The only other creature missing was the serpent. This connection between cat and serpent appears in the Kabbalah as well, and in Christianity, where a cat placed at the feet of Christ carries the same negative imagery as the snake.

Although the black cat is the archetypal good luck symbol in the West, the reverse holds in Islam, where cats are viewed favorably unless they are black, since djinn can take the shape of black cats. The magickal powers of the cat are ambivalent, used either for or against people, a trait tied to the indifference with which a cat treats its prey. In Western tradition the cat has nine lives, while its Eastern counterpart manages with only seven.

A Persian belief echoes the idea of the witch and her familiar. Some people are born with a hemzad, a spirit that accompanies them throughout life in the form of a cat. The cat's blood was thought to be especially potent for writing charms, which further underlines the magickal nature attributed to the animal.

In parts of Africa the clairvoyant powers of the cat are also renowned, and medicine bags made of cat skin were believed to hold supernatural powers.

The Calf

When Moses received the Ten Commandments from God on Mount Sinai, he was gone longer than expected. Growing restless, the Israelites asked Aaron to make a god for them to worship. Aaron gathered all the gold trinkets and jewelry the crowd could muster, melted the metal down, and built a statue of a Golden Calf that was given worship and prayers. Meanwhile an angry God told Moses what was happening, that the people were worshipping false idols, and that he intended to destroy them all. Moses interceded to spare the Israelites and destroyed the statue.

The story becomes clearer in light of Egyptian belief, where the calf was the child of the great goddess Isis and one of the forms taken by her son Horus. The Egyptians worshipped a golden calf called the Horus of Gold, and the Israelites likewise held this so-called false god in great regard, willing to give up their wealth to build his effigy. It would have made sense for Aaron to provide his people with the object they desired as a focus for their worship.

As a symbol of innocence and a creature commonly used in ritual sacrifice, the calf came to be associated with Christ. The fatted calf was one kept especially well fed so that its meat would be particularly tasty, and it was slaughtered only on very special occasions, such as the biblical tale of the prodigal son returning to his family.

The Vedic tales of India refer to the Sun as the golden calf.

The Cow

Because its milk is a staple food for so many people, the cow is one of the most useful animals in the world. It was among the first animals domesticated by humans, and its symbolism is rich. The cow is emblematic of fertility, abundance, wealth, the universal Mother, and rebirth, and it is also a gentle and compliant creature.

It is no surprise that the cow is widely thought of as a mother figure. In Egypt the cow was personified as Ahet, the mother of the Sun itself, and Egyptian women wore amulets of the cow-headed goddess Hathor in her guise as the Creator to make themselves fertile. In Europe the cow was likewise the mother-ancestor of all living things, called Audumla, the milch-cow. In Greek myth one of the names for the great Cow was Europa, meaning full Moon, and the stars were said to be the children of Europa.

The cow was also regarded as a psychopomp, a creature able to lead the souls of the dead to the Underworld. There was once a custom of bringing a cow to the sickroom so that the dying person could grasp its tail while breathing a last breath. This role is still honored in the Nepali festival called Gai Jatra, the cow festival, in which every family that has lost a member during the year joins a procession leading a cow, or a child dressed in a cow costume when no animal is available. The cow is believed to guide the soul on its final journey, including a passage through the Milky Way, the band of stars said to be milk splashed by the great Cow that mothered the Universe.

The sacred cow is a fundamental part of Hindu iconography. In India the cow is so revered and treated so gently that it often causes a traffic hazard as it wanders along busy city roads. The Hindu faith respects all animals and holds vegetarianism as a tenet, and the god Krishna was a cowherd for a time, one of his names being Bala Gopala, the child who protects the cows. Hindu deities rule over every part of the cow. In times of famine a cow that gives limitless milk is far more useful alive than as a dead beast that would provide meat only briefly.

The Bull

The sacred standing of the bull reaches back to at least 3000 BC, when early Hebrews carved the effigy of a God named El in the form of a bull at the head of their ritual staffs.

The bull is the archetype of brute masculinity, fertility, tyranny, and ferocity. In Greece it was sacred to both Poseidon and Dionysus. Zeus took the shape of a bull to seduce the mortal Europa; once she had been tricked into trusting the kneeling creature and climbed onto its back, it carried her away, an emblem of passion and lust. The bull also tested the strength of Heracles, who strangled the Cretan bull that was wreaking havoc and had it shipped away to Athens.

Bull Sacrifice

The ritual sacrifice of the bull is so ancient that its origins cannot be fixed. A painting in the Ellora Caves shows the Goddess Kali slaying a bull, yet the rite is far older than the artwork, which is dated to around AD 500 to 1000. To early people the bull was so supremely powerful that being splashed with its blood was thought to confer immortality. In Rome a bull cult introduced from Asia Minor in the second century BC inspired the taurobolium, in which an initiate stood in a trench beneath a board pierced with holes while a bull was slain above, so that the hot blood poured down over the devotee. The rite reenacted a Mithraic legend that named the bull's blood as the origin of all life, renewing body and soul.

The Spanish bullfight is a remnant of this same tradition and draws on the same Mithraic legend, which tells that the bull was the first creature on Earth and that when Mithras killed it, all other living things sprang from the blood spilled on the ground. Many of the oldest bullrings in Spain stand on or close to the sites of former Mithraic temples, and bullrings also appear in South America and France.

The Celts shared these beliefs and kept their own bull sacrifice, though theirs was shamanistic in purpose. The tribal seer ate the flesh and drank the blood in the hope of inducing prophetic dreams, specifically to choose candidates for kingship.

The bull is immortalized in the night sky as the constellation Taurus, one of the signs of the astrological Zodiac.

The crane is one of the most symbolically revered birds across world cultures, associated with longevity, fidelity, vigilance, and the capacity to bridge earth and heaven. Tall, elegant, and fiercely loyal to its mate, it carries a dignity that has made it a symbol of nobility and high office across Asia, Celtic tradition, and beyond.

Physical Description

A tall, long-necked wading bird, the crane measures between 50 and 60 inches in length with a wingspan of 70 to 80 inches and a weight of 10 to 15 pounds. Its plumage is predominantly grey or white. The sandhill crane holds the distinction of being the tallest bird native to North America. The whooping crane is critically endangered, with fewer than 500 individuals remaining in the wild.

Habitat and Distribution

Cranes favor wetland environments including marshes, bogs, and damp grasslands. Sandhill cranes are distributed broadly across North America, absent only from the northeastern regions of Canada and the United States. They migrate in large massed flocks.

Behavior

Cranes are monogamous and mate for life, maintaining their pair bonds even outside of breeding season. Their courtship rituals are elaborate and highly choreographed. When foraging, they wade through water and mud, bending low to probe for food. Breeding pairs typically raise young together and return to the same areas year after year.

Mythology and Folklore

The crane's fidelity and elaborate courtship dances have made it a widely recognized symbol of loyal partnership and successful marriage. Its fabled longevity links it to endurance, lineage, and family legacy. The English word pedigree may derive from the French pied de grue, meaning "foot of the crane," a reference to the branching shape of a genealogical diagram.

In Asian tradition, the crane is associated with healing, happiness, good fortune, and spiritual elevation. The practice of folding one thousand paper cranes as an offering for healing and success was brought to wide awareness through the story of Sadako Sasaki, a young girl who died from radiation illness following the Hiroshima disaster. Strings of paper cranes remain a common offering at temples and shrines. The crane was also believed capable of carrying the souls of the deceased to the heavens on its back, and in ancient China it served as the emblem of the highest-ranking officials.

In Celtic tradition, the crane held sacred significance. The crane bag of the Irish god Manannán mac Lir was said to contain some of the most precious objects in the mythic world, possibly including the staves of ogham, the early Irish writing and divinatory system whose angular forms are compared to a crane's legs.

A famous fable attributed to Aesop contrasts the crane and the peacock: the peacock mocks the crane's plain appearance, but the crane replies that while the peacock struts on the ground, the crane soars to the very heavens. The story is a reminder that inner capacity outweighs outward display.

The crane's legendary vigilance comes from an old tale in which it stands watch on one leg while holding a stone in the other foot. Should it fall asleep, the stone drops and the sound wakes it and its companions. This image appears frequently in heraldry as a symbol of alertness.

Omens and Divinatory Meaning

A crane seen in flight directs the gaze upward, toward trust, hope, and connection with something larger than the immediate moment. A crane seen standing still calls for watchfulness, patience, and careful attention to what is unfolding around you.

Colors

Grey, white

Feather Magick

Use crane feathers in charms and spells to impart wisdom and knowledge.

Longevity, the Sun, and the Alphabet

The crane is reckoned among the most ancient of birds, with evidence of its presence stretching back some ten million years, and with a lifespan that may reach fifty years it has long stood as an emblem of longevity. It is a symbol of communication as well: one legend holds that Mercury, or Hermes, devised the alphabet by watching the angular shapes the birds' wings made in flight, after which the letters were kept in a bag of crane skin. The idea reaches from the Greco-Roman world to the Bambara of Africa, who hold that the crane was present at the invention of speech.

For the ancient Greeks the crane was a solar bird, dedicated to Apollo, who is said to have taken its shape whenever he came down to visit the Earth; its exuberant dance was read as a celebration of life and a herald of spring and returning sunshine. In China and Japan the crane likewise stands for longevity and faithfulness, and is honoured as a messenger between the Gods and humankind and as a psychopomp, its dance picturing the flight of human souls to the Land of the Immortals. The Chinese spoke too of heavenly or blessed cranes that embodied wisdom and bore legendary sages upon their backs as they passed between the worlds.

The crow is one of the most widely distributed and symbolically loaded birds in the world, recognized across cultures as a creature of intelligence, magick, death, and transformation. A member of the Corvidae family, it shares deep kinship with the raven and carries many of the same associations, though where ravens lean toward transformative magick, crows are more closely linked with healing, prophecy, and psychopomp work.

Overview

The corvids are a large, widely distributed family of birds including crows, ravens, and jackdaws, powerfully associated with witchcraft and magick. Crows and ravens are big, loud, glossy black birds often referenced interchangeably. Ravens tend to be slightly larger with shaggy, disheveled-looking feathers, while crows are sleeker. Ravens are somewhat more solitary; crows may roost in communities numbering in the hundreds. Ravens hunt more actively, while crows are primarily scavengers. When mythology distinguishes between the two, ravens are usually associated with transformative magick while crows are identified with healing. Both are teachers and sponsors of magick and shamanism.

Physical Description

The genus Corvus includes approximately forty species worldwide. Crows are generally recognized by their glossy black plumage, black beaks, and black legs. The American crow measures approximately 17 inches in length with a wingspan of about 35 inches and an average weight of 16 ounces.

Physical Characteristics and Behavior

Crows are characterized by their shiny black coloring and loud, raucous voices. Diurnal birds, they noisily greet the sun each morning. Like baboons and roosters, crows are strongly identified with solar power and may be understood as venerating the sun themselves. In a Pacific Northwest myth, Earth is enshrouded in darkness and it is Crow who hangs the sun in the sky. Crows are classified among the world's most intelligent creatures, capable not only of tool use but of tool improvisation and construction. They also engage in play with one another and with other bird species. A collective of crows is known as a murder.

Associations with Death and War

Most crows are carrion eaters. They do not hunt or kill but consume the remains of the dead, wasting nothing and contributing to the cycle of decomposition and renewal. Historically, corvids gathered over battlefields to feed on the fallen, forging deep associations with death, war, and disaster. In Irish Gaelic, badbh, meaning crow, is also a word for witch, and is the name of the Celtic battle goddess Badb, one of the three aspects of the Morrígan alongside Nemain and Macha. Badb could take the form of a crow to fly over battlefields. The Scottish expression for death, "going away up the Crow Road," reflects the folk belief that crows serve as psychopomps, guiding spirits between the living world and the afterlife.

Oracular Nature and Associated Deities

Crows are oracular birds, evoking the spirit of prophecy and affiliated with divinatory traditions worldwide. Among the deities associated with crows and ravens are Amaterasu, Apollo, Badb, Cathubodua, Epona, Kali, Macha, the Morrígan, Nantosuelta, Nephthys, Odin, and Tlazolteotl.

Cross-Cultural Associations

In Hindu tradition, crows act as intermediaries during Shraddha, a ritual of ancestral gratitude in which offerings of food and water are brought to deceased relatives on the anniversary of their death. In ancient Egypt, the crow symbolized faithful love, a reflection of the bird's monogamous nature. In Chinese and Japanese mythology, crows serve as emblems of filial duty and familial devotion.

One of Aesop's most celebrated fables, "The Crow and the Pitcher," shows a thirsty crow unable to reach the little water remaining at the bottom of a jug. Rather than giving up, the crow drops pebble after pebble into the vessel until the water level rises within reach. The story encodes both a moral about patience and small persistent actions, and an observation about the crow's genuine capacity for problem-solving and creative tool use.

Trickster Heroes and World Mythology

Trickster heroes, Crow and Raven play an enormous role in world mythology across Celtic, Greek, Hungarian, Japanese, Jewish, Native American, Scandinavian, and Vietnamese traditions, but most especially in the indigenous traditions of Siberia and North America's Pacific Northwest. Crows truly are tricksters and clowns. They are assertive, unafraid of people, and as willing to play a trick on a human as on a dog or on each other. Shiny objects attract them and they have been known to steal. Crows coexist well with people and occasionally become companion animals, sometimes mimicking human speech or the sounds of other animals.

Post-Christian Demonization

The associations of crow and raven with witchcraft, magick, and shamanism predate Christianity. What shifts in the post-Christian period is the valuation of those associations. Rather than positive links with wise-women, shamans, and seers, crows came to be seen as signs of diabolism and sin. Their color, raucousness, sharp intelligence, and assertive nature led the Church to identify them with Satan as Lucifer, the fallen light-bringer. Legends emerged explaining why crows were black, typically framing their dark color as punishment for some ancient wrongdoing, once pure white but stained permanently by sin.

Omens and Divinatory Meaning

The crow urges inventiveness and lateral thinking when facing seemingly insurmountable problems. It asks what tools and skills are already at hand, and how they might be applied in unconventional ways. Change is the crow's central teaching. Death and ending are not losses but transformations, and every ending feeds what comes next. As a psychopomp, the crow is a companion through difficult transitions, whether literal or symbolic. If change feels overwhelming, the crow offers to walk through it alongside you. It also reminds you not to take the work of understanding life too seriously. Play is not a distraction from wisdom. It is part of it.

Symbolism & Medicine

Deer embodies graceful decisiveness and intuitive wisdom. She teaches the balance between careful observation and confident action, moving through life with both caution and certainty.

Behavioral Wisdom

Deer's medicine is never impulsive. She pauses first, feeling into each situation and reaching out with all her senses to assess the environment. Only after getting the lay of the land does she step gracefully and surely into action.

Magickal Applications

Deer offers support during life's cyclical changes and transitions, especially when one season ends and another begins. She gifts self-confidence and helps you make definitive decisions, then step into them with grace and trust in your intuition.

The Power of the Pivot

While Deer is a prey animal, swift and wily, she is far from helpless. Deer is known for duplicity, deceiving hunters into a false chase. She enters dense underbrush then gracefully and quickly pivots, running off in a different direction.

Reflection

Deer's tactical redirection illustrates how apparent vulnerability can be transformed through intelligent strategy. The pivot represents a sudden change of course that alters the balance of power, turning disadvantage into advantage through cunning rather than force.

Amulet Uses

A deer antler carried as an amulet promotes fertility, encourages quick gains, and attracts success.

The Celtic Otherworld

In the Celtic pantheon the deer is an otherworldly creature, belonging to the realm of the fairies and possessing magickal powers. Counted among the oldest of creatures, its home in the darkness of the forest lets it share in hidden secrets. Flidais, the Celtic Goddess of Wild Things, rode in a chariot drawn by deer.

Universal Symbolism

Some of the deer's meanings are found everywhere: meekness, gentleness, and swiftness. Despite the masculine energy of the stag, the deer is a feminine animal, linked to the Goddess in her aspect as a huntress. The antlers carry their own significance, standing for the tree of life and for fertility and vitality.

Psychopomp and Soul-Guide

The deer appears prominently in Paleolithic cave paintings, a reminder of how long it has been held significant. Shamans connected with the spirit of the deer by wearing its antlers and skins, believing the animal could speak with the Gods. For this reason the deer was also seen as a psychopomp, a sacred creature that guided the soul on its journey to the Afterlife. The Scythians reflected this by placing the deer motif on funerary equipment, hoping it would speed the soul to its final destination.

Buddhist and Hindu Lore

In Buddhism the deer recalls the teachings of the Buddha, who began his calling in a deer park. In Hindu stories the Goddess of Learning, Sarasvati, takes the form of the deer, and her followers hope that sitting on deerskin mats will help them absorb her knowledge.

The Hind

The hind, an old name for the doe, is essentially a female symbol, gentle and shy, at once a mother and a virgin. Several goddesses are bound to this lovely forest creature, among them Diana and Artemis, the goddess of the hunt, and the Celtic goddess of the woodland, Flidais. Genghis Khan was said to be the offspring of a hind and a blue wolf, an almost alchemical image in which the herbivore mates with the carnivore, the marriage of spirit and matter. The hind is also the shape taken by the Valkyries, who bear the spirits of dead warriors into the Afterworld.

The Ceryneian Hind of Greek myth is the origin of the Golden Hind, a creature with antlers of gold and hooves of brass that could run like the wind and was sacred to Artemis, the chaste goddess of the hunt, as the hind herself was chaste. Its capture was one of the labors of Hercules. For the Celts, the hunt for the hind was a metaphor for the search for wisdom.

The Stag and Masculine Power

The antlers of the stag mark it as a magickal and sacred animal and a potent masculine symbol, as horned creatures so often are. Through those antlers the stag becomes an emblem of fertility and male sexuality, and like the goat it lies behind the word "horny" for one who is sexually charged. Amulets shaped as the phallus were carved from stag horn, and some traditions of Chinese medicine grind the horn into an aphrodisiac.

Rebirth and the Sun

Because the antlers are shed and grown anew each year, they evoke the World Tree, and so the stag itself comes to stand for rebirth and, by extension, for the Sun. It is no accident that the Hopi cut their image of the Sun God from a piece of deerskin.

Pan, Cernunnos, and the Horned God

The pre-Christian God Pan wears the cloven hooves and horned headdress of the stag. Seeking to make the old Gods fearsome to those who had once worshipped them, and so to drive them toward the One God of the new faith, early Christians recast Pan as the Devil and gave him these same stag-borrowed features. The Celtic Horned God Cernunnos, Ruler of the Beasts and a God of Plenty, bears a striking likeness to Pan. So sacred was the stag to the early peoples of Switzerland that it was sometimes buried with full ceremony beside people and horses.

The Watchful Fighter

The stag's behavior shapes its meaning. It is a sensitive animal, catching scents on the air from far off, swift to act and able to cover great ground in little time. It is a courageous fighter as well, defending its territory with determination and clashing antlers against any rival that intrudes.

The White Stag

Wherever a white stag appears, in myth, in folktale, or in dreams, it signifies the world of spirit. In the Arthurian legends its ethereal presence sends the Knights off on spiritual quests. In China the white stag is the emblem of Shou-hsien, the God of Immortality.

Healer and Emblem of Christ

The stag is also credited with healing powers, and is sometimes shown with an arrow in its side and herbs in its mouth, for it was said to know the use of every medicinal plant in the forest and to eat them to mend its wound. The stag was believed to kill serpents as well, and where it is depicted trampling a snake underfoot it signifies the victory of good over evil. In this guise, and because it was hunted for sacrifice, the stag becomes an emblem of Christ, appearing then with a cross set between its antlers.

Overview

The history of dogs' ancient alliance with humans is shrouded in the mysteries of time. They have been our steadfast companions and guardians since time immemorial. Even cultures that historically do not domesticate animals, such as many indigenous cultures of North America, have maintained dogs as companion animals.

Because of this long alliance, dogs have intense spiritual associations with protection, healing, and death. In every one of these aspects dogs are understood to be guardian spirits: they protect people from spiritual and physical dangers in life, battle on behalf of their human allies during illness, and protect dead human souls, accompanying, guiding, and assisting them in their journey to the next realm.

Dogs and Death

Perhaps because feral dogs were observed lurking in ancient cemeteries ready to devour offerings and dig up bodies, dogs achieved early identification with death and funerary rites. Dogs also lingered on battlefields where they competed with crows for their share of the dead.

Guides to the After-Life

Although everyone dies alone, it was once commonly believed that without a dog's assistance one would never be able to locate the realm of the dead. This was a widespread concept although how it was interpreted varied. In some Central American beliefs, when one's soul begins that journey, a dog will be found waiting by a riverbank ready to serve as guide. Some cultures refused to take chances: dogs were sacrificed and buried together with a person so that they might start the journey together. The Aztecs evolved a happier solution: they buried their dead with terracotta dogs who, through ritual and spell-casting, were able to perform this function just as well as flesh and blood dogs.

Anubis and Egyptian Tradition

The ancient Egyptians may not have rigidly distinguished between jackals and dogs: Anubis, Lord of Embalming, Guide to the After-Life, may be understood as either species or both. His color is black, not because it is the color of death but because for the Egyptians it represented regeneration and rebirth. Anubis rules the Dog Star in conjunction with his adopted mother Isis, the first syllable of whose Egyptian name Au Set resembles a dog's bark: ow, ow, ow!

Norse Tradition and Hell-Hounds

The Norse Queen of the After-Life, Hel (Christianity borrowed her name for the eternal realm of post-life punishment) has her own companion pack of wolves and dogs that nibble arriving corpses. Vestiges of the ancient Indo-European custom of offering dogs a bite of the corpse may survive in this legend. These may be the original hell-hounds who will survive to ride with the Wild Hunt.

Hekate: Queen of Witches

Dogs are most profoundly identified with the Eurasian witch goddess Hekate, Queen of the Night, spirit of birth, death, magick, healing, witchcraft, travel, and victory. Hekate guards the threshold between life and death, serving as a psychopomp (one who guides the dead). Hekate also serves as the personal handmaiden of Persephone, Queen of Hades.

Hades is famously guarded by Cerberus, the monstrous three-headed hound of hell. Hekate's sacred number is three; she is typically depicted with three heads and very frequently assumes the guise of a dog. Cerberus may be Hekate's pet dog or he may even be Hekate in disguise. Whether Hekate transforms into a dog or is in fact a dog spirit who transforms into other shapes (old crone, seductive beauty, occasionally even a black cat) is a little like asking which came first, the chicken or the egg.

Deities Associated with Dogs

Dogs serve as sacred companion animals to many spirits, most having to do with healing, death, war, and protection: Artemis, Asklepios, Babalu Ayé, Epona, Erinyes (justice spirits who chase sinners like bloodhounds in pursuit), Hekate, Hel, Hermes, Nehalennia, Ogun, and Sirona.

Hekate originated in what is now Turkey. In Sumer, another goddess was intensely linked to dogs: Bau, the daughter of Sirius the Dog Star. Sometimes depicted as dog-headed, it's tempting to associate her name with "bow-wow." In her later Babylonian incarnation, Gula Bau, spirit of healing, walks Earth accompanied by her pack of hounds.

Divine Transformation

Hekate is not the only deity to transform into canine form. The Middle Eastern and North African spirits known as djinn have been known to lurk in the form of dogs, usually loitering in the marketplace just before dawn. In Jewish mystical folklore, Lilith and Asmodeus, respectively Queen and King of Demons, travel incognito disguised as large black hounds.

Black Dogs and Witchcraft

Black hound is the key: although to some extent all dogs have associations with funeral rites, magickal healing, and protection, the dog most powerfully identified with magic, witches, and witchcraft is the black dog, the bigger and blacker the better. Large black poodles have particularly strong associations, perhaps in honor of magician Cornelius Agrippa's beloved pet, Monsieur.

In addition to serving as witches' familiars, black dogs may be transformed witches or witch goddesses. Nicholas Remy, the merciless witch-trial judge from Lorraine, alleged that women transformed into rabid dogs and wolves.

European Witch Trials and Satan

In witch-crazed Europe, dogs were understood as the devil's favored companion or maybe even his favorite disguise. According to witch-trial transcripts, Satan routinely appeared at the sabbats he hosted in the shape of a massive black dog.

Spectral Black Hounds

Dogs are believed to venture out at night to do battle with evil spirits. This is not an untypical international belief: lone dogs at night, particularly large black ones, are understood to either be evil spirits or out battling evil spirits. British folklore is full of stories of spectral black hounds mysteriously appearing to guard, guide, and accompany lone travelers, particularly when venturing through forests. Once the journey is over or safety is reached, the dog vanishes as mysteriously as it arrived.

Fidelity and Second Sight

One traditional pet name for the dog, Fido, comes from the same Latin root as "fidelity," and the trust shared between a dog and its owner defines their bond. The dog's keen sense of smell takes on an almost supernatural quality, a power denied to people, which is part of why the dog acts as a mediator between the seen and unseen worlds, seemingly gifted with second sight.

Hunters and Guardians of the Dead

Supernatural dogs gather across the northern myths. The Hounds of Annwyn hunt alongside Odin, and the greatest Celtic hero, Cuchulain, bears a name meaning "Hound of Culann," an echo of the dog's importance as a hunter. In Teutonic myth the dog Garn stands at the gates of Niflheim, the land of the dead, much as Cerberus guards the gates of Hades. The same figure surfaces in a modern form as Fluffy, the great three-headed dog of the Harry Potter stories.

Shamans and the Mexican Dog

Shamans took on the magickal nature of the dog by wearing robes of dog skin to reach its otherworldly powers.

⚠️ The following is a closed practice, sacred to its Indigenous Mesoamerican originating culture, and recorded only for understanding. The Ancient Mexicans sacrificed the dog whose master had died and laid its body on the grave, so that the creature could walk with its master one last time through the nine rivers of the Afterworld until they reached their journey's end.

The Unclean Dog

Although much of the world treats eating dog flesh as a deep taboo, and many peoples revere the animal, followers of Islam regard the dog as unclean. Mohammed decreed that any bowl a dog had eaten from should be washed thoroughly seven times before it was fit for human use again.

The Yellow Dog and the Sun

The yellow dog is a symbol of the Sun. In Persian myth Ahura Mazda keeps a yellow dog that drives away evil spirits, just as the sun drives away the night and the darkness.

Alchemy and Self-Sacrifice

In alchemy the image of the wolf devouring the dog stands for the purification of gold by antimony, the next to last stage of the great work of transformation. The close kinship of the two creatures here points to the need for self-sacrifice in order to reach a desired aim.

Overview

Foxes are intensely identified with witchcraft in East Asia, and most profoundly in Japan where they are the witchcraft animal supreme. Fox-owning is a specific form of witchcraft, unique to Japan.

Inari and Sacred Origins

The fox's role in witchcraft may derive from its ancient importance in Japanese spirituality. Inari is the ancient but still immensely popular Shinto spirit of rice, food, and nourishment. Inari brings prosperity, fertility, and abundance and has shrines in every Japanese farming village. The fox is Inari's sacred animal, messenger and, sometimes, alter ego. Stone or wooden foxes are always found in front of Inari's shrines. The fox and Inari merge to form one being: the question of which came first, the fox or the human shape, is irrelevant. They are parallel forms of the sacred being.

Inari's gender remains subject of debate. Today Inari is most commonly depicted as a bearded man carrying bundles of rice, however Inari also manifests as a beautiful woman or as a female fox. Inari's female manifestation is believed to be older, predating the introduction of Buddhism into Japan.

Female Fox Spirits Across Asia

Inari in her feminine aspect is also intensely involved with sex, fertility, reproduction, and the magickal arts, not only agricultural abundance. Similar but exclusively female fox spirits possessing strong ties to magick and witchcraft exist in China, India, Korea, and Tibet.

Shifting Perceptions

Once upon a time, Japanese fox spirits were protectors, teachers, and sponsors of witchcraft. Even now some fox spirits are saintly and helpful. The foxes that serve as Inari's messengers are miracle workers, understood as sacred and godly. However, as centuries passed, attitudes towards witchcraft became more ambivalent, and fox spirits became feared.

Fox Possession

Fox spirits are held responsible for illness and misfortune. They possess victims, similar to possession by demons or zar spirits. This isn't ritual possession or channeling; it's involuntary and unpleasant. Sometimes full possession results; sometimes only individual symptoms. Symptoms of fox possession include hearing voices, insatiable and indiscriminate appetite, nocturnal feelings of suffocation plus increasing facial resemblance to a fox: The person begins to develop a visible "snout."

Eventually the fox may push the true individual out, taking over body, soul, and personality, either full-time or just intermittently. The fox spirit speaks through the person's mouth, often indulging in obscenities, frequently sexual, which the person would normally never use.

Fox-Owners and Familiars

Specific individuals and families are believed to control fox spirits. The solitary fox-owner is most frequently believed to be a corrupt and degenerate sorcerer or exorcist, the proverbial shaman-gone-bad. Although fox familiars are disproportionately female, those humans who put them to evil use are usually male.

Solitary sorcerers dispatch foxes to carry out nefarious deeds. The old extortion racket may be at play: what seems like a perfectly respectable exorcist who specializes in ridding people of fox-spirit possession may actually be the source of that possession, the one who sent the fox. Fox spirits may also be rented out to others for a fee, to perform their secret, dirty work as well. Fox spirits tend to run in packs. The fox-owner may have a large number of fox spirits to work with. Seventy-five is a typical number, although there may be less.

Fox spirits are fed daily; in return the familiar performs various magical services on the person's behalf. It is a mutually beneficial relationship although neighbors may see the fox-owner as threatening and possessing unfair advantages.

Hereditary Fox Families and Social Stigma

Fox spirits run in families. Families who are hereditary owners of foxes typically transmit this hereditary power through the female line. For centuries tremendous fear and social stigma have been attached to families rumored to be fox-owners. Not only is it hereditary, fox-owning may be contagious too. One becomes contaminated (at least by the social stigma) by living in a house formerly occupied by a fox-owner or by possessing their property.

Contamination may be avoided by avoiding the fox family: don't visit them, don't socialize with them, don't engage in any financial transactions with them, don't be friends with them but don't offend them either, and don't marry into their family—most especially don't marry their women.

Japan has never had European-style witch-hunts; few witches have been killed. Instead their punishment is intense social ostracism. Occasionally ostracism has evolved into violence: houses burned down as retribution and entire families banished. This isn't ancient history: in 1952 a young couple committed suicide together because the woman came from a family with a reputation for fox-owning and the man's family forbade their marriage.

Fox Spirits as Thieves

Just like real foxes are believed to surreptitiously raid chicken coops, fox spirits are believed to rob the neighbors. Fox-owners are believed to gain wealth at the expense of others. To become suddenly, mysteriously wealthy is to leave oneself open to accusations of malevolent witchcraft, particularly if anyone else in the area is simultaneously suffering misfortune.

Chinese Fox Spirits

In China, fox spirits retain their positive identity. Among their primary roles is the protection of archivists and librarians. Should a document be lost, missing or otherwise unable to be located, offerings are made to the fox spirit. After the offering is made, the archivist leaves the room for a little while to give the spirit space and opportunity to work its magick. Upon return, the document, book or scroll should stick out or somehow draw attention to itself.

The Izuna Rite: Obtaining a Fox Familiar

A late seventeenth-century work contains an account of the Izuna Rite, the magical ritual by which people gain power over fox familiars: Find a pregnant fox. Feed her, care for her, form an alliance with her during her pregnancy but especially afterwards when she's needy and vulnerable. You cannot take a cub, no matter what. If you are meant to have a fox familiar, when the cubs are sufficiently grown, the mother will bring you one and tell you to name it. Name the fox but keep the name secret. Henceforth, if you call the name, the fox will come to you in invisible form. No one else will be able to see the fox spirit, only you. Nothing is ever entirely hidden, however, so be prepared for others to attribute supernatural powers to you.

Red Fox: The Shape-Shifter

Vulpes vulpes

Despite being a redhead, Fox understands camouflage's subtleties. One moment she appears as a small dog, the next a log, then moves gracefully as a cat. In Asia, she's been seen wearing a beautiful woman's face and sometimes an old man's. Fox is said to gain a tail as she masters her magic—a fox with nine tails knows many things including invisibility and the shape-shifting art.

Fox is a starlet-turned-spy, ready to stand out or blend in, possessing the wisdom to know which is needed. Fox teaches that your exterior is an ever-changeable illusion. If she has appeared, see if it's time for a shift, or perhaps someone is being shifty with you.

Fox has no ego attachment to being seen, content to move through shadows unidentified. The red coat that marks the Red Fox as visually distinctive represents only one aspect of fox medicine. The complementary aspect is the capacity to blend into the background, to become effectively invisible. These two qualities, conspicuousness and concealment, constitute the dual nature of fox symbolism.

The Fairy Bells of the Fox

In Norse and Finnish telling, the fairies gave the fox the secret of the foxglove. The fox slips the bells onto his paws to move silently into the chicken coop, and rings them softly to send a sound that only other foxes can hear, warning the pack when a hunter is near. In Finland the fox is a sacred animal, and the aurora borealis is called foxfire, the sun reflecting off the tails of magickal foxes running across the sky. See Foxglove.

Amulet Uses

A foxtail carried as an amulet promotes cleverness and swiftness.

Symbolism

Wiliness, slyness, cunning, craftiness, trickery, and guile, paired with genuine wisdom, are the qualities attributed to the fox across much of the world. It is an intelligent animal, and Reynard, the celebrated fox of fairy tales, is given human characteristics, often conversing with men and women in their own speech.

The first recorded fox hunt with hounds dates to the sixteenth century, though the practice is thought to be far older. The animal was pursued for its handsome pelt, yet the chase frequently became so bloody an affair that the fur was left useless. Why the creature was persecuted beyond simple culling remains a mystery, though it may grow from the early Christian belief that linked the fox with the Devil, the most cunning of tricksters.

Because foxes live in holes and tunnels in the ground, they are attached to the earth element and so become the totem animals of several earth deities. The fox is also the emblem of the seducer, and more dangerously the seductress, the figure aptly captured in the phrase foxy lady. It is the totem animal of Dionysus, whose seductive priestesses wore fox skins.
